en: "Buddha-vision" (buddhadarśana) is the compendium of the Buddha's teachings.
The meaning of the word "Buddha" is one who possesses perfect knowledge (*samyak-jñānin*). This term refers to that person by whom the reality of the Dharma has been revealed.
By this, the vision of the Buddha is established.
This is the meaning: the trainings of the Buddha are truths established by their own nature; they are not some entities that were manifested by the Buddha, nor were they created as something new.
Those truths shine by their own nature,
regardless of whether or not there was a birth of a Buddha,
or whether or not they were revealed by him; thus, they have no dependence upon those [conditions].
Nor have they been discarded;
those [qualities] are common to both.
They do not abide within the domain of anyone.
These always abide by their very nature;
they do not arise through the conceptualization or the effort of a Buddha or anyone else.
This is the specific excellence of this method of training: that this method is not rooted in agitation.
Rather, he exists transcending all;

designated by the name "Buddha" in a subsequent time, he was the promulgator of this Dharma. By means of his absolute nature, he churned the ocean of knowledge and likewise, through the power of inward vision, obtained the perfectly complete jewel of wisdom.
It was not created by him as something new;
rather, the essential meaning is that it was manifested directly through his novelty.
In this regard, he too possesses no claim of exclusive ownership.
This is noble and common to all living beings;
however, within the Buddhist perspective, there exists a certain distinction regarding that refuge which is difficult to find in other religions.
In the Buddhist religion, that refuge is known as the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*), wherein the inclusion of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is observed.
For the Buddha was never a messenger sent by God, nor was he the Supreme Brahman;
rather, he was an ordinary soul, much like his circle of disciples.
It is merely that his character is distinguished as being free from impurity.
Purity of mind, possession of right knowledge,
and compassion for all beings.
Endowed with these qualities, his selfless service to humanity has become firmly established in the world; even now, it remains rich with the essence of life.
Yet, it is not a mere particularity of creation.
Here, the light of the Supreme Truth has dawned—that truth which, due to ignorance, had never before been heard among men.
Immediately after the manifestation of that Truth, he began to propagate it among those people capable of understanding it.
The Dharma existing in this regard is indeed the teaching of the Buddha;
it is recorded in the Pali Vinaya and Sutta Pitakas, whose literal meaning, ideal, and practice constitute its essence.

After the disappearance of the Buddha, for the sake of perfect knowledge, assemblies known as *saṅgāyanā* were convened from time to time by his devoted followers who followed the path of self-restraint (*damma*).

Thus, in later times, the Buddha’s teachings were divided into three collections called the *Piṭakas*, namely the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, the *Sutta-piṭaka*, and the *Abhidhamma-piṭaka*, wherein the term "examination of the mind" (*manas-samīkṣaṇa*) appropriately applies.
The compendium of the teachings of the Buddha, whose subject matter is the Dhamma, is solely for the sake of attaining this Truth; it is indeed the manifestation of that Truth in embodied form.
This alone is capable of creating a community for any person, wherein the simultaneous presence of both the Buddha and the Dhamma is perceived.

From this, the following truth emerges: the term *ratnatraya* (the Three Jewels), through its connection with various subjects, indicates a twofold meaning. On one hand, it implies the presentation of physical forms, books, attire, and ornaments—objects that are both visible and tangible.
On the other hand, this term conveys a more subtle, spiritual meaning, referring to *guṇa*, *dharma*, and *sattva*, wherein the convergence of these three aforementioned elements is realized.
Although the previous explanation has reached a state of brevity and appears somewhat coarse,
nevertheless, this present explanation attains an indispensable status in the minds of ordinary people, as it specifically reminds those who have attained a higher degree of excellence.
We recollect the Buddha’s qualities of purity and compassion.

Furthermore, the existence of the Saṅgha-deśa indicates a courageous group of individuals within the common assembly of disciples who follow the footprints of the Buddha; therein, the Dharma in the form of the Dharma-texts serves as a staircase upon the path of Dharma for the sake of easy understanding by ordinary people, leading them all forward,
and thereafter transcending them.

For, in truth, that which is called the Saṅgha—being an awakener who has awakened to reality and resembling a Buddha—is indeed released for the sake of all those who strive to attain right knowledge during his lifetime;
it is not a state reckoned as a social convention accepted by the people.
Thus, whether it be a boy, a girl, an ordinary devotee, or a monk, such a person may become this Saṅgha, and that person exists in the form of a pure deity.
In the administration of the teaching, the power of the noble-born is seen where a certain assembly was established by the Śakyas;
the lord of this assembly was Śuddhodana, who was known by the title of King,
and his queen was Māyā, also called Sirimahāmāyā.
Once, on the full moon day of the lunar month known as Vaiśākha, this pair of parents gave birth to a son who would become most renowned throughout India and the world.
His manifestation took place in a certain grove of trees at a location situated between the city of Devadaha, belonging to Queen Māyā, and the city of Kapilavatthu.
Because he had achieved his purpose, his name was Siddhārtha.
Endowed with all the mental qualities appropriate for a prince—consisting of proficiency in every art—as well as physical strength and beauty, he became accomplished.
Having completed all that was to be learned, he married a charming maiden named Yaśodharā, who gave birth to a son named Rāhula.
At that time, Siddhārtha was a youth of nineteen years.

This was precisely the time for his life’s transformation, when the call of compassion arose most intensely within his heart, and the light of supreme knowledge shone more brightly in his mind. [He realized] that the sufferings and hardships which arise for human beings stem from the sacrifice of one who bears a body under the sway of desire, from the realization that sin takes on another form, and from the deliberations on identity and difference born from the manifestation of distinctions between castes.
Along with them, the physical and mental sufferings born of old age, disease, grief, death, and despair—which had remained dormant within the mind of Siddhārtha—awakened.
An unceasing thirst for truth impelled him toward an investigation into the secrets of life.
Siddhārtha realized that the answer could not be found through a way of life immersed in sensory pleasures.
Driven by an irrepressible ambition, he set out to find an answer at whatever great cost it might entail, and he found one that became a source of immense assistance for both himself and others.
He realized that Siddhārtha, desiring to help others, would first strive to accomplish something for himself.

Then, having spent his time in vain amidst the pleasures of the senses, and being impelled by a doctrine of radical renunciation, he became a practitioner (*vratin*) for the sake of realizing the secret of life.
This very state is what is called "Great Renunciation" (*mahāsannyāsa*); there is no exaggeration here. Thus, he became renowned as a man of perfect knowledge, or as the Buddha.
The attainment of Buddhahood occurred for him on the full moon day of the month of Vesākha in his thirty-fifth year.

From that time forward, he surrendered himself in order to share the bliss of the supreme truth longed for by him with ordinary people. Prior to his acquisition of Buddhahood, he had voluntarily undergone such hardships among those familiar with him who were capable of enduring similar suffering and perceiving the majesty of the Dharma.
He took up the burden of propagating the Dharma;
for this reason, both princes and those who live by begging,
both the wealthy and the destitute—
He honored those who were healthy;
for it is said: "Princes and those who live on alms, the wealthy and the destitute,"

Whether they were healthy or lacking in health, he had a connection with all people who would certainly hear his words or strive to attain them; there was no distinction whatsoever regarding external appearances or artificial thoughts transmitted to him.
Therefore, whether after or before his attainment of enlightenment (*bodhi*), the life story of the Buddha is not considered separate from his deeds.

In the context of selfless service and in the context of the practice of patience, reflection, and discernment, both will serve as aids by virtue of being adorned with qualities rooted in illustrative examples.
That is to say, while wandering from village to village throughout India, the Buddha always remained in contact with ordinary people living by agriculture;
accepting whatever kind of food they offered, he would remain engaged in personal conversation, present his own teachings, and bestow instruction.
In this regard, even the immediate objective of the individual’s mental tranquility should not be considered inferior.

From the words of the Buddha spoken in the Catukkanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Buddha’s method of instruction is understood. For it is said: "The propagation of the Dharma is intended for the sake of attaining reality."
This propagation of my Dharma is never for the sake of being unperceived; it proceeds solely through the light of reasoning. My reality does not fall into the state of being devoid of logic.
"My instruction on the Dharma is accompanied by wonder, whereas this one is devoid of wonder.
Thereupon, various sequences of conduct were established for people in diverse circumstances, according to their various purposes.
The fundamental principle for them is *nīti* (right conduct), which is to be applied both to renunciants and to ordinary people alike.

To overcome an inclination toward negative desires, vain egoism, and other such inferior qualities, a certain Buddhist, through the power of meditative yoga, experiences the capacity for compassion, pity, affection, and equanimity toward those who are happy;
thus, two distinct divisions exist within the teachings of the Buddha.
First is the mundane, and subsequently the supramundane.

In the Pali language, these are respectively called *lokiya* and *lokuttara*. For those people who desire a higher rebirth or a better life, the "mundane" teaching is intended; however, for those for whom worldly happiness or rebirth is utterly insignificant, the "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) is intended.
It was devised for the sake of those humans who desire liberation (nirvāṇa);
however, in reality, both systems maintain a certain equality in achieving their intended purpose.
In both cases, the cessation of suffering alone is the ultimate goal.
In the first field [of merit], it is by way of a portion (*aṃśataḥ*), whereas in the second field, it is in its entirety; such is the distinction between the two.
That is to say, in the first field, only a mere fraction of suffering remains, while in the second, once the root of suffering has been destroyed, the complete cessation of suffering arises.
An illustration of this is seen in the *Catukkanipāta* of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*.
Regarding this, the Buddha said: "O monks,
this pure nirvāṇa is not intended for the deception of men, nor for the sake of gaining their faith,
nor for wealth or fame."
Familiarity with him in the form of a new teacher or as one who performs new consecrations is not intended by his purpose; even the proclamation of a goal is not desired.
In that regard, he takes as his goal pure living, self-restraint, renunciation, dispassion, and liberation.
That Dharma is released for all human beings;
therein, no distinction is reckoned based on birth, caste, status, age, gender, or physical appearance—thus, monks, as well as ordinary people, all who are devoted to the Buddha know this well.
The Buddha’s teachings are manifold and extensive.
Nevertheless, it is divided into three parts:
namely, for the performance of what is auspicious and for the removal of what is inauspicious.
And for the sake of achieving purity of mind,
her state at that time was one of matted hair;
and people were immersed in such beliefs and practices as had been described.

For that purpose, it was necessary for them to engage in wise conduct together with him. At the time of undertaking the work of pioneering the mission, the Buddha’s method of propagation was as follows:
one characteristic of the Buddha’s teachings was their orientation toward transformation.
The intention behind this is described as a fundamental and complete transformation of the material basis and the general practice of "dhāraṇā" or "acceptance" that was prevalent at that time.

Specifically, the Buddha rejected the practice known as "self-mortification" (attakilamathanuyoga), which involves the act of self-restraint; instead, he established the teaching of relying upon the Middle Way.
The religious instruction given at Sārnāth, beginning with the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*, should be considered here;
that is to say, a new meaning relevant to the objective is presented.
For instance, according to Hinduism:
This is the established rule: that a certain person may become freed from evil through bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Here, the Buddha has introduced a new meaning;

having explained this statement by means of a metaphorical sense, the Buddha demonstrated that in his Dharma, a certain person can become freed from evil by bathing in the river of moral conduct (nītinadī).

Through the two aforementioned methods of teaching the Dharma, Lord Buddha would have become familiar with the Hindu religion in its form of well-known traditional rites, just as the group of Indian scholars including Svāmī Vivekānanda and others was at that time.
However, because it possessed a certain novelty, the Buddhist religion, for the sake of re-establishment, truly became entitled to honor and fame as a new religion.
"The Four Noble Truths" is the preeminent example of reality here.
This is the primary subject of the first teaching in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*.
For indeed, Buddhist doctrine maintains that at this stage of existence, human life is the most excellent opportunity for attaining *nirvāṇa*.
A human being is the master of what he accumulates;
therefore, it is the tenet of the Buddhist religion that one partakes of the fruit of the karma accumulated by oneself.
Nowhere is there the notion that virtuous action must be performed for the sake of obtaining the grace of a supreme deity.
In this very context, the establishment of human rights and self-determination is supported through reasoning, without distinction based on birth, caste, or tradition.
Any person who commits an act of killing, theft, or any other criminal offense is considered guilty by the Buddha;
there is no consideration as to whether that person calls themselves a Buddhist or not.

Likewise, by performing actions rooted in transgression, one will inevitably become a partaker of suffering; in that case, the necessity of embracing righteousness is not negligible. Similarly, the person who performs an auspicious action will inevitably experience an auspicious result.
Whether he becomes a Buddhist or not is a matter of no consequence whatsoever. There is no power or existence that can create an obstacle to the attainment of the accumulated fruits of merit.
In the crafting of one's own destiny and the determination of one's self, no other principles have proclaimed such a powerful realization as this human equality.
At that time, he wandered everywhere throughout Bhārata and taught those people who adhered to the dharma of all castes.
There, for the remaining twenty *ghaṭikās*— spanning four *ghaṭikās* of sleep and excluding only the time for rest— his selfless service to humanity remained unimpeded and free from weariness.
For this reason, his teachings possess such diversity and vastness that, according to some, those teachings are said to consist of eighty-four subjects; and these are divided into three heads. Thus:
These are intended for the common disciples of the monks;
these are employed in the order of those who are currently active and seeking.
In that regard, for any person—
There is no mention of a soul or a substantial entity;
this indeed is what is called the sacred Dharma-book of the Buddhists.

For those who are unable to reach the further shore of all the various domains [of the teachings], there is seen a most concise distillation of the Buddha’s instructions intended for monks, known as the *Ovādapātimokkha*. It is stated therein:
"And accomplish the purification of the mind."

In this context, that which is called the "body" is visible or tangible, external, composed of the elements (*bhautika*), and appears to be relatively stable when compared [to the mind] or at first glance.
The mind (*citta*), however, is non-material (*abhautika*), a subtle entity, and likewise invisible and intangible.
This [mind] is perceived as being more prone to oscillation and unfit for restraint.
However, through discipline and restraint, this mind—which was previously very slight and wavering—becomes increasingly firm.
For this very reason, the first step in the Buddha’s instructions regarding the method of discourse on mental self-control and mastery of oneself is established.
Their manifold nature and multiplicity of stages are clearly observed.

Among these, the group of five is prescribed with a view toward the possibility of ensuring the fixed conduct of common Buddhists. The group known as the eight, called the *upoṣadha*, is for the observance of common Buddhists during specific ritual performances.
The group of ten instructions is set forth for those who are new.
However, that which exists as the collection known as the *Pātimokkha*, consisting of two hundred and twenty-seven precepts, is prescribed for the monks as well as for Buddhist renunciants,
both in terms of physical and verbal conduct.
Offenses such as killing pertain to individuals;
offenses such as theft pertain to property;
and offenses such as adultery with another's wife are included among bodily offenses pertaining to men and women.
False speech is primarily understood as verbal misconduct.
Such evils arise fundamentally from delusion (*saṃmoha*).
Substances such as liquor and other intoxicating drugs are the principal causes of this delusion.
These medicines that accomplish what is harmful dull the mind;
therefore, a person falls away from the restraint of the senses.
To prevent this, a certain method based on fundamental principles has been set forth by the sages.
This [set] is seen here within the fivefold group of prohibitive precepts;
these faults are collectively and comprehensively familiarized by the designation "the five precepts" (*pañca-anuśāsana*).
For the sake of accomplishing auspiciousness and for the purpose of prescribing faultlessness among all people, these precepts have been composed in the form of aphorisms (*sūtra*).
Their protection brings about happiness and peace not only for those on the side of devotion, but for all people associated with them as well.
According to some, by protecting these [devotees], no negative result arises;
rather, through that, the prosperity of the country is furthered.
The renunciation of these [five actions] also achieves the progress of the country by way of the nature of reality as it is inherently established.
For instance, the absence of practices such as killing and counter-violence makes the country peaceful and prosperous in another sense;
that which is designated as "Dharma" also incidentally teaches the fivefold set of actions.
And thus, it establishes a complete list of good governance practices;
namely—namely—the noble lineage system (*abhijātatantra*), the monarchical system (*rājatantra*), the republican system (*gaṇatantra*), and so forth.
Nevertheless, within Buddhism, the scope of governance carries a more extensive significance than that of the aforementioned systems.
For all the arrangements of a political administration are intended for the individual efforts of its constituent states;

however, the sphere of the Buddhist Dharma encompasses the human race as a whole. This subject indicates that its own governance is attained through two principles: shame regarding the nature of evil and apprehension concerning the fruits of unwholesome actions.
In terms of its transformation, this world is protected from falling away from reality;
however, it is a factual truth that only a few individuals reach the goal while others do not.
To remedy this deficiency, the Buddha established the Four Noble Truths.
To explain: the principle of *chandas* (will) is the joyful eagerness for the performance of what is to be done.
The principle of *vīrya* (energy) is the power of volition (*icchāśakti*) that accomplishes the action intended by one's resolve.
The principle of *citta* (mind) is the determination regarding its object.
Even when fearsome calamities and problems arise, one who is fearless and resolute in the performance of action—

whether through mental composure or deep contemplation— possesses the capacity to determine what is beneficial or harmful regarding any task and to eliminate confusion and error. This is the principle [of *vimanasanīti*].
All these qualities are well known for awakening the application of the mind and its focused grasp;
however, they are generally treated with contempt and forgotten,
and for that reason, people are unable to reach their desired goal.
For instance, in the case of prohibitions, there is addiction to drinking intoxicants,
the habitual preparation and consumption of harmful medicines,
and gambling.
Respect for improper conduct toward women and men, friendship with wicked people, and being devoted to indolence.
And they remain without going to places where they are not needed (*Aṭṭhaka-nipāta, Aṅguttara-nikāya*).
One must certainly refrain from such conduct in order to be free from transgressions that are considered contrary to the principles of purposeful conduct.
Otherwise, there would be an unbearable loss of accumulated wealth;
likewise, even the mere expectation of someone who consists only of expectation causes distress.
For instance, there is toil in study.

The acquisition of wealth through virtuous means such as industry, agriculture, knowledge, and giving; thereafter, skill in the protection of the acquired wealth— meaning, having ensured its protection from loss due to theft or other causes, one establishes the wealth in a secure place free from calamity.
Association with righteous people will provide assistance for each individual to practice virtuous conduct accordingly;

likewise, certainty regarding the prosperity of wealth and livelihood will arise. Regarding the management of income according to one's means—wherein a long-term plan consistent with economic policy is indicated as appropriate.

These function together as follows: the accumulation of a specific portion of income for the sake of future requirements or for use during times of adversity; providing assistance to one who requests aid at a time of need; and the application of funds to ensure the security of financial policy.

Elsewhere as well, skill in preserving wealth acquired is described as being accompanied by a sense of gravity, wherein the causes for the destruction of a prosperous retinue are revealed by the Buddha. For instance:
wandering at night;
Generally, giving assistance at festivals and the like, addiction to gambling,
and friendship with people of immoral conduct;
Laziness regarding one's work;
the causes for obtaining prosperity when surrounded by a complete retinue have been examined below.
Otherwise, that wealth, out of regard for one's welfare, achieves what is even more harmful.
The Buddha has prescribed the appropriate means for the application of wealth; for instance,
having divided the wealth therein according to its form and capacity,
it should be given to deceased persons for the sake of merit.
To the king, to the country,
(for the purpose of taxes and for hospitals and so forth), and to the deities.

Prior to investigating the Buddha-dharma, we must briefly resolve such questions as: what is Dharma, what does it accomplish, and what goal does it aim toward in social life and in the life of devotion?

Dharma is the transformation of a human being characterized by longing and intention; it exists for the sake of overcoming internal suffering, and especially for the attainment of mental and spiritual happiness.

Having transcended the various stages of development over the course of time, whatever skill and knowledge have been accumulated, as well as whatever disposition and trust have been gathered— all these are considered here within the Dharma.
Although a person has come from the primordial birth after traversing a vast distance,

nevertheless, because it accords with the principles of both the mental and the physical, it is a true statement that within a person, the stream of the primordial birth flows in a gradual sequence starting from the beginning.
The quality of initial engagement does not reside in that person in common;
when the person becomes civilized, that [quality] is later abandoned.
Furthermore, when a person moves toward [the goal],
Then he runs toward the new price;
in the new state, he disciplines himself and effects the purification of the initial impulses and so forth.
However, just as an infant is cherished within its swaddling clothes,
so too can human beings never be liberated from their primordial activity.

Therefore, especially in the sphere of dharma, the Primordial Man continues to dwell among men even now, together with all the qualities, knowledge, dispositions, and convictions that have been accumulated in every way.
This being the case, the ancient dharma was such that its root was agitation rather than being grounded in reasoning.

Nevertheless, at the conclusion of time, once a greater accumulation of higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) has been achieved, the previously mentioned existential certainties (*bhāvapratyaya*) are gradually transformed by means of the teachings of others and so forth,
until the moment arrives when the knowledge thus acquired— having purified and perfected its application and so on— reaches the ultimate stage of manifestation.
In the first age, the administration of the teaching was governed by the Kulapatis.
A universal faith arose in the Vahnīśvarīya Prāṇavāda.
This faith was born from the anthropomorphization of beings and natural phenomena, as well as from a fear rooted in ignorance.

For instance—the first man perceived himself among all kinds of elemental forces with compassion; yet those elemental forces were not within the scope of his understanding. Moreover, thunderbolts, lightning, earthquakes, floods, and cataclysms did not remain subject to his control.

Subsequently, the realization arose among them that behind those objects there must necessarily exist some power or some possessor of power; thus, the conception of a person standing before terrifying things took the form of the later concept of God. However, the first man did not conceive of a single God as the sole agent in every activity.

However, he conceived of many gods who presided over each individual region of the earth; because of this conception, two doctrines—the doctrine of a single God and the doctrine of many gods—were created. Over time, human society became increasingly vast.
That governance, having become impossible according to the *kulapati* system,

was then taken up by a certain controlling personage endowed with the power of comprehensive resources. Gradually, a complete state administration was seen to evolve within the system of governance, wherein a king or an emperor became established as the ruler.
The territory of that sovereign’s dominion was known by the name of a kingdom (*rāṣṭra*),
and its citizens were recognized collectively under the designation of a caste (*jāti*);
along with this, religious activity was also pursued.
The number of Lords has been reduced through the process of dhāraṇā;
consequently, there has appeared the manifestation of a certain divine form endowed with complete power.
This specific individualized form is designated as the Father of the universe in the heavenly realm.
As the Supreme Lord in the form of the possessor of unique supreme power, he was worshipped by all;
even beyond that,
by further disseminating human knowledge, he became the foundation for individual self-realization— in which the Supreme Lord’s own maintenance did not attain such a degree of centrality.
The conception of a single sovereign authority (ekacchatra-bhāvanā) adopted a new significance: that human fortune, due to its helplessness, is dependent upon the Supreme Lord or subject to His will.
In this regard, human destiny, instead of remaining under divine control, became subject to human will.
In this manner, Dharma is reckoned as being broadly twofold.
To explain: 1. The doctrine of faith (*āstikyavāda*)—within which are included the doctrine of a single God (*īśvaravāda*) and the doctrine of many Gods (*bahvīśvaravāda*).
That is to say, Hinduism, Christianity, [and so forth].
1. Islam and other such [religions]. 2. Nihilism (nāstikyavāda): No worship of any being designated as a Supreme Lord is prescribed here.
Buddhism is, in truth, a religion enriched by nihilism.

Dharma is externally conjoined with religious, social, and customary practices; however, primarily, that Dharma is social—such a Dharma is generally observed within every human society. In societies established in the present age, even apart from various systems sanctioned by politics, pedagogy, and economics, Dharma exists as a weight-bearing institution within the organization of the entire community.
It has been accepted;
nevertheless, dharma is neither like a command nor synonymous with legal procedure.
In that regard, the granting of forgiveness and the restriction of forgiveness are indicated as interconnected realities.
This is not equivalent to the establishment of a legal doctrine (*ārthanītika-pratiṣṭhāna*), wherein desires for production, enjoyment, and accumulation are intertwined.
Furthermore, this connection is neither established nor regulated by a retinue (*parivāra*).
It appears that Western scholars connect it with the phrase "dharma is [performed] by someone."
Dharma establishes the relationship between man and *tathatā*.
Through Dharma, the ontological purport of that which is designated as *tathatā* is realized;
this Dharma is itself connected with that very [reality].
Briefly stated, Dharma is that which transcends the limitations of human beings, serving as the supreme and peerless embodiment of all human aspirations.

It possesses distinctiveness by being the locus of political wisdom, serving as the gateway for social bonds and individual tranquility, acting as the means for social regulation, and constituting the fruit of a great civilization.
Now is the time for the answer: what indeed does Dharma accomplish?
Does it fulfill the goal in its entirety within human life as well as social life?
Indeed, in the field of constructing the entire social order, Dharma is said to be one among those institutions that carry great weight.
A society is defined as the dynamic equilibrium of its constituent institutions,
which establish certain exemplary actions based on both conventional consensus and foundational principles.
This synthesis of institutions collectively constructs the social order, wherein each part is interdependent upon the others.
In that regard, if a transformation occurs,
then that transformation exerts its influence upon the entire social order; such being the case,
in these circumstances—
Dharma is not a distinct subject apart from human social conduct as it has evolved through its structural forms.
Within the framework of the entire social order, there are certain social institutions that possess specific functions, both manifest and latent.
Therefore, within the total structure of society, what are the various latent and unmanifest functions of religious institutions that serve to maintain equilibrium?
It is said in general that dharma serves to establish human ethicality;
it fosters the development of the entire range of valuable mental dispositions.
For instance: faith through tradition, unity through proximity,
and daring as well as trust in the midst of a battle crowded with problems and in the face of the possibility of death.
Dharma bestows upon human beings that capacity by which they are able to confront and reconcile adverse fortune;
moreover, Dharma grants us a state beyond mere knowledge,
conferring a defined status and a security that transcends human relationships.
But it is said specifically that Dharma, in the field of action, harmonizes the individual with tradition,
sustains them in uncertainty,
and provides consolation in the absence of security.
He remains engaged in achieving social goals,
promotes ethical conduct,
and furthermore,
Dharma provides the instruments for the cultivation of individuals.
This Dharma, through the mechanism of social regulation and the strengthening of established foundational goals, [fulfills its purpose].
He strives to establish the unity and stability of society by providing the means for overcoming defects and passions; furthermore,
he is capable of accomplishing even that which is the sole ground of prophetic instruction,
and thus:
In a particular society, this dharma spreads an influence that is devoid of order and rooted in destruction.
Whether from the perspective of the individual or the perspective of society, the role of dharma may be either commendable or not;
such a role either preserves an unconditioned existence or serves as a foundation for the removal of undesirable objects.
For instance— when Dharma performs its function as a means for the restraint of the senses and for the curbing of the path of impulsive actions,
then that Dharma is said to accomplish an action characterized by destruction.
This is the action denoted by the term *neti*.
On the contrary, when dharma establishes itself by effecting social restraint, nurturing established values and goals, and providing assistance for the maintenance of social unity and stability,
then that dharma performs its true function of preserving uninterrupted existence.
By virtue of habituation, human beings are self-centered.
Even though he is educated, refined, and holds a social position, he is generally overcome by desire, hatred, and other such passions.
Furthermore, although in reality a human being is a rational creature, he is by nature an experiencing soul.

Secondly, there is the construction of its setting, wherein appropriate mental engagement is not provided.
Human social behavior and its establishment reveal something as a necessary requirement, wherein the central theme of the suffering created by the Buddha exists.
The human being is a dependent soul;
he lives by such powers as are near him, yet he is shrouded in darkness until those shackles of his are broken.

As long as an individual does not become self-reliant and diligent in his own right, he lives outside of social conduct; therefore, as the architect and builder of culture, he is only capable of conceiving and creating the social projections associated with his own fetters. Our present undertaking is directed toward that living being to whom the Buddha imparted perfect knowledge—a being struck by spiritual urgency—and it has reached a boundless depth through this [work].
It has attained expansion along with social dimensions.
In the view of the Buddha,
a person's life necessarily passes through the midst of a particular primary cultural nursery school.
That unconscious force, known as craving (tanhā), is a harsh impulsion that bestows its own mode of life upon society.
Everywhere, man creates his culture and ideal and transmits it through the lineage as if with a lack of attention.
At its origin, the primary activity is one initiated by the child, by which a person becomes a victim of those states situated in the lowest depths of the conscious mind.

In the teachings of the Buddha, topics concerning the analysis of social virtues and defects, along with an examination of the conduct of an individual within society who is characterized by many questions and inquiries, are observed.
Here, we are connected to these subjects:
we are related to the human being who is the creator of culture; he creates ideals for other men, and likewise, through the thread of social giving and receiving, [he sustains] the lineage.
He sends them forth, saying:

"We are joined with such a state as this of this man; dwelling by means of the power of the sent-forth life-form and through the force of the unconscious sending of the Yuga-power, the man will inevitably grasp the subjects of his questions within the assembly."

Relying upon those objects of sense while failing to recognize the measure of one's innate capacities, one accomplishes diverse actions and likewise engages in conflict with those very powers. Regarding the nature of the disjunction between the human being and their conditioning, no more certain determination of faults has been established anywhere on this earth than that which is found in the teachings of the Buddha.
Manifestation (*vyakti*) refers to the final form of living beings in a long lineage;
from one, another follows, being born again and again.
Each individual soul, having pervaded a greater portion of life, is driven by a state of delusion through the dictates of cause and effect.
In these teachings, a certain prospect is promised for the pacification of the conflict that generates ill-being between the individual person and the social structure.
The inherent dichotomy between the individual and his culture is one of the primary discoveries made by the Buddha;
its significance is particularly profound within the modern institution enriched by the idealistic imaginings of human science.
The interpretation of human conduct—both social and spiritual—has captivated the minds of great scholars everywhere;
it describes a successful incursion into those realms where, at one time, ignorance, false impositions, and deceptive narratives reigned supreme through a lack of competition.
By this very means, a vast truth is made known, by which we come to understand why a human being does what he does.
Among its primary elements is one called the humanization of knowledge,
which is an intricate arrangement of social reactions that is transmitted from generation to generation solely through social actions and reactions.
In this arrangement, our second nature is observed.
A certain person dwelling in the deepest ocean, who remains perpetually submerged in its waters, forgets that water;
and it is only when he somehow rises from the ocean floor and comes above to behold the vast expanse that he first manifests his own existence.
Thus it is said.
Such a discovery has been achieved within modern disciplines concerning the nature of culture.
By examining each individual culture, we have attained a completely new perspective regarding the formative power of all cultures.
In this regard, our own culture is also included.
For this very reason, we have introduced a portion of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) into our knowledge, which is rooted in the media accepted by society as pervading human life.
Nevertheless, even knowledge that is highly capable of being relied upon strives to conceal that subject matter which is not contained within it.
Especially when an external object remains unconnected with our inferences,
the grounds for trust therein are precisely these:
that which has been acquired by human personality through its engagement with cultural sciences is generally full of hyperbole.

And thus, the field of social and spiritual exegesis—leaving aside questions that are disconnected from prior inferences—is described by the modern man as being endowed with new and even unrefined material; because of this, activity toward various evasions leads to a lack of progress for knowledge in that corresponding field, making it prone to the construction of speculative theories concerning cultural subjects. Within our own domain, there exists an almost inexhaustible accumulation of knowledge regarding diverse cultures.

In this regard, it is observed how the class of individuals accumulates expertise through the various channels of each society in order to refine its junior members, whereby they acquire maturity as living embodiments of diverse cultural traditions.
This earth is the gathering place for these diverse and generally dualistic social forms, much like a pen for the collection of animals and birds.
Human beings here exercise a boundless capacity,
by which they create, preserve, and likewise send the most diverse paths of life from one family to another.

In the view of Western scholars of human science, it appears that humans are capable of dwelling in a state where social conditions are characterized by marvelous adornment and a sense of satisfaction.
Among people possessing the Dōvuyān culture, two primary characteristics exist within their social conduct: doubt and counter-doubt;
whereas in the peripheral regions of the Nigini country, the essence of compassion was established within their culture.
Among the foreign people, due to their preoccupation with other matters and their way of life, a tendency to flee like clay was observed everywhere.

Among the "Manusānāṃ," however, those who were well-integrated with their cultural ideals became capable of engaging in the most fierce competition against their neighbors, just as the British-Indian Koyakīūt people advanced upon their territory after abandoning their own property.
In these cultures, each reveals through its mere tendency toward change an underlying agitation and a void of hope,
by which a group certainly learns to struggle;
yet people are generally more capable of maintaining a connection with despair than with that which is called for.
Furthermore, within each culture, there exists a complex and intricate arrangement of various social strata that is difficult to comprehend,
wherein diverse inclinations contribute only marginally to the formation of social relations. Within each culture, there is scope for certain individual differences.
In all these cultures, diversity and unity exist surrounding the primary mode of life.

And thus, through the light of a transformed state, human individuality demonstrates a capacity to manifest a marvelous power for generating means to reconstitute the ancient ideal and to undergo a transformation of form.

From these facts—namely, the truth, the consensus, and the disjunction—it generally follows that this established conclusion is difficult to refute: that knowledge transmitted by another culture bestows upon human beings the capacity to overcome the attachment rooted in universal subversion. Prior to the advent of modern society, each culture, along with its dispersing lines of communication, was relatively undisturbed in its manifestation of the fullest possible potential.
There were expectations within society that were extremely significant regarding the sphere of one’s own lifestyle.

Formerly, isolation based on caste, language, and sect, as well as fragmentation, empowered the human race for the sake of movements rooted in diverse cultures, wherein the tradition of the supreme right pertaining to the essence of life was enshrined.
Now, various cultures endowed with distinct characteristics perform the function of mutual giving and receiving among the lineages of living beings for the sake of their recognition.
Now, that state of fragmentation which was concealed through the succession of ancestors becomes obsolete;
thus, each culture remains bound above all other cultures by the thread of a nature characterized by mutual interdependence.
We observe that a cultured person, even when establishing a new relationship with other cultures alongside his own,
does so with certainty; for every culture today necessarily possesses a measure of understanding and tolerance,
by which it becomes capable of following a way of life.

It revolves solely within its own orbit and provides cooperation to those questions by which the life-journey of all becomes beset with calamity. Regarding culture and personality, the conceptions that are formed in Western sciences— conceptions particularly described by Gardiner Murphy— are as follows:
‘We shall now learn to speak to one another and to grasp this [truth] in such a way that it is not presented as an example for any particular age, gender, caste, religion, or community,
but rather solely as a matter of individuality.’
That individual who, as an exemplary manifestation of humanity, produces within us something resonant with the very first echo;
now we behold the necessary fundamental offering.
Marphī says:
Taking this as its object, our mechanical age divides itself into two ways of speaking regarding human mutual affection. This is one of the favorite imaginary worlds of the modern man;
now his vision is the vision of science directed toward the construction of a divine city.

This [work] is not fundamentally independent of the perspectives of the eighteenth-century philosophers of the great continent of Europe. A cultural being, a human being, everywhere on earth manifests his creative genius in order to reveal a new cultural ideal for the solution of his problems; he manifests a new way of life in his actions in order to fulfill his grinding desire; and he effects change even within the existing mode, provided that mode—
For his gain and for his happiness, it would be useless;
he now becomes intent on creating some new culture that embraces the earth,
wherein the primordial attachment to the ancestors will recede far away.
This dream-like hope receives support from the vast array of incidental subjects within cultural diversity,
for which reason the abundant illumination of human knowledge signals our prosperity.
In our view, it is possible that our cultural transmission, scholarship, and universal knowledge may not be sufficient to create a necessary detachment regarding the domain of action;
in such a state, research transmitted through society and sanctioned by the principles of the mind indicates a lack of skill regarding the ultimate goal.
That which, through familiarity with those people, enables one to engage in conversation freely;

the transformation occurs such that they become more at ease in the constraints of social conduct and in responding to the currents of cultural trends. Now, we have psychotherapy, which assists in establishing individual social relations; by doing so, this therapy eliminates the sense of pride.
In the lower stage of social aspiration, one views life as something light;

We see that we are fit for faith when opposition within opposites and the sharpest edge of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator become, through excessive discourse, objects of tolerance.
People are eager to act in exactly the same way as they do when performing any of the plays composed by Samuel Beckett;
what do they do?
They converse;
with reference to what do they converse?
They converse by taking up those very questions of theirs.
These efforts regarding consciousness and the science of arts and crafts attempt to resolve extremely difficult questions in order to bring the entire environment of civilization under control;
yet they generally do not produce any truth.
For instance—for what reason is it so impossible for people to change their cultural ideals?
When, for the most part, each individual perceives that this alone is the peerless path for avoiding miserable rebirths,
how does culture establish such an obstacle to transformation? Or why does rapid social change exhibit a tendency to render the refined members of a certain culture devoid of ethical conduct?
For what reason does the transformation within the mental dispositions and modes of perception hidden inside people generally proceed as slowly as crossing a mountain?
In short,
have we revealed any connection whatsoever between the human being and his culture?
Formulating our inquiry regarding the separation of people from their traditional way of life, we observe three types of social conduct that are now primarily observed in Western countries.
For instance, there is the person who follows tradition and conducts himself entirely in accordance with it.

The person who follows internal instruction is one who, from childhood onwards, performs actions by following several straightforward internal objectives. The person who follows external instruction, on the other hand, is one who conducts themselves by following whatever others practice.
These three types of character are merely different forms of a single fundamental question.
That question was indeed anticipated by Rieff:
How is it that people initially conform to a uniform pattern where cultural ideals are observed?
And how is it that people are seen everywhere adopting their culture, taking those behaviors as the primary determinants?
How do they proceed to adopt the ideals of their society as the primary means for understanding its meaning?
How do the ideals of conduct become generalized within party membership through the firm grip of resistance to necessary change in party activities?
This is precisely the question at hand.
In this regard, the intention is not that people will accept the prescribed ideal of their society like machines;
rather, many stand in opposition to them and engage in rebellion,
while others, following their own social positions and perspectives, effect changes to those ideals through more natural means.
However, the ideals of civilization stand like pillars upon which meaningful social conduct is constructed;
regardless of what may be reported in the cultural background concerning the individual—
be it the contributions of Marguerite Bourjois, Freud, Marx, Malinowski, Hui-ai, Spengler, and others.
Western sciences bypass the question of how it is that people actually practice what their culture teaches them for the sake of achieving;
regarding this matter, they offer at most a minimal light,
stating that those people fulfill the satisfaction of their various desires within the boundaries prescribed by their culture.
Since those very desires were here clearly kindled and universalized as social phenomena,
this question was consequently neglected.
It is likely that Erich Fromm was the first to cast a dense light upon this primary question, which had not been addressed by anyone else.
In his view, the modern person is not a liberated individual who governs himself;
rather, he conceives of himself as performing actions by discerning utility through means appropriate to the time.
Thus, he conducts himself according to whatever current or role he attains from society, following the rewards associated therewith.
On the contrary, Professor Frazer argues that the man who takes pride in his efforts and exertions accomplishes more through social restraint than by relying on his own imagination.
By engaging himself within social conditions, a man internalizes those dispositions which impel him toward the performance of his duties.
However, even Mr. Parkman approaches our question as if he were touching upon it.
In his analysis, conduct is defined as the form fundamentally driven by the system of human nature’s impulses projected onto the canvas of social ideals.
Yet he does not ask the question: how does this social ideal establish itself as a barrier to change within such a human nature—where, on one hand, there is the flash of light?
*Kṛta*— that object which is presented as one of the specific characteristics of society itself.
Furthermore, in Frazer’s view,
changes in social conditions give rise to changes in social customs.

That is to say, regarding new purposes and anxieties, one thing becomes clearer: this is not a mere change, but rather a necessary engagement within conduct rooted in the ideals approved by culture, which requires explanation. As for the answer to this question, it is utterly insignificant.

In this regard, this very origin is the reason why all the endeavors of the science recognized by human social practice in Western countries—whether conceived as conscious or otherwise—act like a prior hypothesis regarding the question at hand: namely, the establishment of a higher-order relationship between individuals and their social ground and condition;
and likewise, [the following].
The mutual creative engagement among social groups:

this possibility did not arise for students of Western education who were close to the human individuality, because these questions regarding the formation of social associations could only be resolved at the final stage, provided we are able to understand the more fundamental question: how do individuals and groups function within social endeavor and conduct during a fundamental transformation?
They create a more powerful obstacle for the opposing side.
This is the fundamental question for both: he who lives to preserve the established social ideal, and he who acts against it by being inclined toward transgression.
