However, if he remains in the company of women or partakes of food provided by women, [he will suffer even more].
If one wears the garments and so forth of women, then one will take birth once again in hell, and there one will experience suffering for a long time.
And thus, through various other clear examples, Gotama makes his doctrine known: in what manner should the monks practice their training?
That is to say, if they follow the Buddha's instruction, then the use of their alms-food as well as their clothing and other requisites will be appropriate.
He said: "O monks,"
You should practice by means of the following method:
"We, being afflicted, enjoy alms-food, clothing, shelter, and medicine;
those donors who give these things obtain great fruit as well as benefit."
Our practice of generosity shall receive its due reward;
it will be fruitful and shall not go to waste.
"O monks, you must practice by means of the method described above.
O monks, if you perceive what is beneficial, then you must exert yourselves with diligence."
If you perceive the welfare of others, then exert yourselves with diligence;
if you perceive the welfare of both, [then do so likewise].
Therefore, you must strive with diligence.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya, 4.124–354) In this section,
it is clear that the preceding statement concerning the use of a monk’s necessary requisites indicates an improper means.
This is not true enjoyment because it is unaccustomed;
a monk who indulges in that which is for the sake of satisfying the senses will take birth in hell.
Therefore, one should perform actions that benefit the giver and accomplish deeds that bring about welfare useful for a righteous life.
The dialogue with the flame of fire was so powerful that by its influence sixty monks vomited blood.
Sixty monks abandoned their renunciation, while another sixty monks became fully liberated. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.135)
The *Ṭīkā* on the *Kṣudrakavastu* explains that after the instruction on the flame of fire, the Buddha remained in seclusion for a period of time.
When he emerged, he saw people gathered in small groups (*Aṅguttara-nikāya-ṭīkā*, *Manorathapūraṇī* 2.69).
His younger brother and companion, Ānanda, said that many monks have abandoned the life of renunciation because they experience that they are incapable of maintaining a righteous way of life,
and they experience that if they engage in improper conduct, then the enjoyment of wealth provided by trusting donors will become improper.
Buddha, being amazed, said: "During his period of living in seclusion, no monk explained to him the 'cause for easy breathing' (*assāsakāraṇa*).
Through practice of that, the monks will certainly come to know whether they are conducting the transactions of the goods entrusted to them in accordance with the facts."
In the *Kṣudratarachoṭikākāṭīkā*, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "Just as there are many paths leading to the ocean, so too there are many means for attaining ease within his teaching.
(*Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā*)
*Manorathapūraṇī* 1.70):
He commanded Ānanda to summon the renunciants.
Then he gave him a face-covering, saying: "O monks!"
The very first stage of love (*prema*) is the sole cause of a happy breath (*sukhaśvāsa*). Here, there exists only a connection with living beings for the sake of accomplishing their welfare;
this is not yet compassion (*karuṇā*) in its true sense.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā* (1.70) that, in order to explain the "drop of reflection" (*ālocanā-bindu*), the Buddha introduced a very brief narrative concerning the snapping of fingers.
(*Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā*, 1)

70) Thus, by means of the analogy of a "smaller spark" as a summary of the "flame of fire," it indicates that path wherein the first stage of compassion is explained as the cause for easy breathing. This is to be noted: as seen in the *Ṭīkā*, the Buddha establishes three stages for the mind consisting of compassion (*karuṇāmayacitta*).
For instance: (1) the initial stage, wherein there exists merely the desire for the welfare of living beings;
(2) the gateway of entering compassion, wherein one-pointedness gains birth;
and thereafter, (3) the stabilization of one-pointedness, wherein meditative concentration (*samādhi*) finds its place.
Generally, the term *karuṇāmayacitta* (a mind imbued with compassion) expresses any one of the three aforementioned meanings. In the dialogue with Cūḷa-Taṇhāsaṅkhya, the first meaning was revealed.
In the account of Cūḷa-Taṇhāsaṅkhya, Gotama explains that if any monk nurtures a mind imbued with compassion for even the duration of a finger-snap, he is a monk in the true sense of the word.
It is said:
A mind consisting of compassion establishes contact with sentient beings wherever there is a desire for their welfare.
(Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā, 1.70)
He possesses a universal boundary: "May all living beings be happy"—such a wish arises in his mind.
The manner in which the monk nurtures such a mind is explained in the commentary as follows:
he nurtures it.
How does he nourish it?
When he reflects, then he nourishes this;
when he knows, [then he nourishes this].
Then he nourishes this;
when he sees,
then he protects this mind.
At the time of establishing the definitive conclusion, he protects this;
at the time of applying power, he sustains this;
and through the attainment of knowledge, he nourishes this.
When he knows that object through direct perceptual knowledge, he maintains a mind imbued with compassion. At the time of abandoning the object to be abandoned, he cultivates this;
at the time of contemplating the object to be contemplated, he cultivates this.
Even at the time of directly perceiving the object that is to be realized in its true nature, he nourishes this [attitude].
Furthermore, this activity of nourishing the mind may be found to arise solely from a desire for the welfare [of others] and through a feeling of affection associated with sentient beings;
this indeed is the primary synonym of love.
In this way, a monk ought to always maintain a mind imbued with compassion during every act pertaining to the Dharma.
If he maintains his mind in the primary state of love and compassion for even the briefest moment, such as the snap of a finger, then he is reckoned as a true monk.
By acting thus, he performs his duties in accordance with the instructions.
He practices meditation and enjoys the pleasures of sovereignty as is appropriate;
he is thus able to breathe with ease. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.20)

The commentary on the *Kṣudrakavastu* brings forward that reading where it is stated as follows: "This is not 'eating' (*bhuñjati*), but rather 'enjoying' (*paribhuñjati*). In the *Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā* (1.70), "enjoying" (*paribhuñjati*) [the flame of fire] is cited as one principal term.
"By joining this word with the expression 'a mere snap of the fingers,' weight is attributed to the contact between the two dialogues.

In the commentary it is said: 'How can a monk, while maintaining a mind full of compassion even for the duration of a finger-snap, consume the food of the kingdom without causing depletion? (He eats)."
"He enjoys it.
Enjoyment is of four kinds:
enjoyment by theft, ...
The enjoyment of debts, the enjoyment of inheritance,
and enjoyment by way of sovereignty.
In this regard, when a monk who is engaged in wicked conduct partakes of a gift, it is called "enjoyment through theft."
When a monk endowed with virtuous conduct enjoys a gift given without anxiety or debt,
it is called the enjoyment of a debt.
When the seven assemblies of those seeking training enjoy a gift, [it is likewise].
Then there is the enjoyment of inheritance.
If a monk enjoys a gift after destroying its harmful influence, then it is called enjoyment by means of mastery.
In this regard, the monk (as described in the Kṣudrakavastu) partakes of the food of the kingdom without any reduction [of its size].
In this regard, there are two reasons:
first,
that monk who nourishes compassion for merely the duration of a finger-snap;
By virtue of his authority, his freedom from debt, and his status as an heir, he enjoys the enjoyment of the kingdom.

This is precisely the reason why he consumes the food of the kingdom without any diminution. Furthermore, there is a great power in giving even for the duration of a finger-snap to a compassionate mendicant.
Whoever offers an offering to such a monk obtains from that offering great fruit, great benefit, and great merit.
This is the second reason why a monk enjoys the food of a kingdom without having performed any reduction [of his own defilements].
(Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary, 1.72; cf. Visuddhimagga)

That monk who protects his heart, even for a moment, with love and compassion associated with the primary sequence of practice, acquires that Dharma which is acquired by such a monk; he who contemplates the nature of generosity,
and who becomes one among those seeking the seven trainings.
Or rather, he alone is worthy by whom all detrimental powers have been destroyed.
(The members of the group of seven, seeking training, directly perceive the path.)
Or alternatively, stream-enterers, once-returners,
and non-returners;
And they realize the fruit of arhatship.
When a benefactor comes into contact with a monk who practices a mind full of love, that benefactor becomes vitalized by that monk’s conduct, deportment, and so forth.
This beneficial encouragement will serve as the foundation for a reward that bestows joy.
(Commentary on page 18,

verse 35) This is sufficient for the nourisher to cultivate as a seed for the practice of subsequent qualities. One who protects the compassionate mind and practices assiduously is the supreme example of a righteous life.
He alone eats alms-food as it truly is, without deficiency.
A mind endowed with love that has consumed the sequence of immersion is specifically understood by the term "compassionate mind" (*kāruṇikacitta*).
For instance, in the sequential statements:
The Buddha instructs the householder Anāthapiṇḍada— the foremost among those who practice the Dharma and bring forth its fruit— (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.364–85):
"Giving alms to many people and supporting a person of right view [leads to] stream-entry."
(Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā, 4,185) Moreover, that will be nourishment for a bhikkhu who is a once-returner, for a bhikkhu who is a non-returner, and so forth.
To the Arhat monk,
to the Buddha who is oriented toward primordial wisdom,
to the one possessing perfect knowledge.
To the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha as their preeminent leader, the construction of a Buddhist hermitage,
and the taking of refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The thorough examination of the five types of teachers, the drawing forth of a compassionate mind for even a moment, and the direct realization of impermanence.
The series of primary effects demonstrates the relativity and gravity of the discussion concerning the compassionate mind (*kāruṇikacitta*).
However, this discussion remains subordinate to the discourse on the inner vision directed toward liberation.

Regarding the explanation of the compound term *kāruṇikacitta*, the commentary states: "The very mind associated with a living being who possesses the desire to accomplish the welfare [of others] is the compassionate mind."
Furthermore: "This, through the practice of concentration, becomes internally assimilated according to its true nature" (Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary, 3.4.197).
Thus, in this context, the mind of compassion, having been assimilated by means of concentration, remains entirely imbued with love and compassion.
In the *Krakacadṛṣṭāntasaṁvāda*, Gotama instructs the monk Moliyaphagguna that he should not nourish a mind of anger, but rather maintain a compassionate mind (*Majjhimanikāya* 2.122–29).
Moliyaphagguna had become excessively attached to female renunciants.
Therefore, if anyone pointed out a fault in the female renunciants, he would become exceedingly angry;
and such was the reaction of the female renunciants.
If anyone perceived a fault in his conduct,
the Buddha, upon hearing it,
would summon Moliya and tell him that excessive attachment toward female renunciants was improper for renunciants.
Therefore, if anyone perceives a fault in the conduct of the female renunciants, they should cultivate such a mental disposition as this: "May my mind not turn toward sense objects;
may I not utter wicked speech."
"I shall cultivate a sense of shared experience for the benefit of all;
my mind, being compassionate, will always remain free from anger.
(Majjhima Nikāya 1.123)
The Buddha teaches humility: that one should cultivate an evenness of mind whether someone perceives his faults, or whether someone strikes him or a female ascetic (sannyāsinī).
Gotama instructs the monks—not only in terms of discerning the virtues and faults of others—

Moreover, at all times when discerning the virtues and faults of others, one should nurture a compassionate mind. In his discourses, the Buddha Gotama explains that if anyone wishes to correct the faults of another, they should do so at the appropriate time.
Then, with a compassionate heart, he would speak the truth,
speak what is peaceful,
and act for the sake of producing benefit.
Having instructed them on how they should converse with one another, he further enjoined that all monks should always engage in peaceful discourse with everyone.
Regarding the words of the Middle Way, Gotama taught that no person should entertain considerations of caste, but rather draw forth a heart full of love.
(Majjhima Nikāya,
2.151) This practice is not only to be performed by everyone, but it also serves as a means for the completion of the internal path.
In the discourse titled "The Lion’s Roar to Kassapa," Gotama describes the monk who maintains a compassionate mind.
When all harmful influences have perished,
he is appropriately called a "wandering mendicant" (parivrājaka, i.e., śramaṇa), or else he is called a "brahmin."

In this passage (Dīghanikāya 1.169), Gotama describes the Dharma as a mirror; by means of that mirror, there is a purpose for the position of the individual, provided that the individual wishes to become either a wandering mendicant or a brahmin.
In the *Vaktṛtāmālā*, there is a list (*sūcī*) of objects that cause the outflows (*āsava*). (From the *Majjhimanikāyaṭīkā*, *Papañcasūdanī*, 2.326)
In that context, what are called "harmful objects" are craving,
rebirth,
and ignorance.
And what is seen is desired.
Those objects have been explained in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) as follows:
namely, thirst for the sense-faculties (*indriyatṛṣṇā*).
The desire for rebirth,
ignorance,
and deluded views.
(Visuddhimagga 22.56) Those sense objects have been completely relinquished by the Arhats alone;
the nature of the earthly environment is impermanent.
That *prakṛti* does not produce satisfaction for the Arhats;
they perceive *prakṛti* in its subtle state according to the sequence,
and thus they experience the flavor of *nirvāṇa*.
Consequently, they are no longer drawn by the pleasures of the senses of a worldly ruler.
Thus, neither impermanent pleasure nor the suffering of rebirth is able to affect them.
By such people, all forms of mental darkness as well as deluded views have been cast far away.
Therefore, the term "one whose taints are exhausted" (*kṣīṇāsrava*) is indeed a synonym for the state of an Arhat, meaning "one by whom the power that causes harm has been destroyed.
Furthermore, if such a person draws forth a heart full of love, then he may truly be called a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) or a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*).

In the sequential discourses, the Buddha said to the monks that one should not fear the performance of wholesome deeds (*sukarman*), because the term "wholesome deed" is by its very nature a synonym for happiness. (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 6.88–92)
He reflects upon his own knowledge, noting that the virtuous deeds he performed over a long period have resulted in bliss.
And the fruit of this is as follows: in a previous birth, he protected a compassionate mind for seven lifetimes;
therefore, he now enjoys a multitude of joys consisting of bliss.
Having pervaded seven yugas during both the universal illumination and the universal expansion, he was not born again upon this earth.
During the time of universal illumination, he took birth in the divine world (*ābhassara*);
and again, during the time of expansion, he took rebirth in the divine Brahma-palace.
There, in the form of Mahābrahmā, he exercised sovereignty;
he was Sakka,
the lord of the world of desire.
Thirty-six times,
having been a universal monarch many times over, he governed according to the Dharma;
at that time, he drew forth a compassionate mind.
By means of this, he attained a fruitful result;
his mind, consisting of love, had been experienced as the initial stage on the path of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In another discourse, the Bodhisattva’s compassionate and loving mind is described as being worthy of depiction.
In a dialogue concerning fear and terror within the forest life, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi questions Gotama regarding the dangers encountered therein (*Majjhima Nikāya* 1.26).
The Buddha informs Jāṇussoṇī that the minds of those wandering mendicants and brahmins dwelling in the forest were filled with anger and impurity;
therefore, they are overcome by fear and distress.
(Majjhima Nikāya 1.18)
He explains to Jānussoṇi that once, when he himself was a Bodhisattva,
he lived in the forest during his time of training for Buddhahood;
however, there was no anger in his heart.
His heart was filled with love.
Having manifested such a compassionate mind, the Bodhisattva was never at any time seized by doubt,
nor did he become afraid or terrified.

The connection with the commentary (*ṭīkā*) is as follows: "My mind was not full of anger. This has the following intention: "I possessed a single heart consisting of compassion; within that heart there was the desire for [their] welfare. Such was the Bodhisattva. (*Majjhimanikāya-ṭīkā*)
Papañcasūdanī 1.116):

Following this, Gotama describes his perfect knowledge in this discourse; it would be logical to infer that this reflection concerning the Bodhisatta’s life in the forest points to the period prior to the attainment of enlightenment by Gotama.
In several dialogues, it is seen that the disciples were practicing acts of body, speech, and mind characterized by love;
or rather, it is seen that they were being instructed to act in such a manner. One disciple was inspired toward their exaltation.

Since he possesses a compassionate mind— as previously demonstrated— that mind must be associated with the love experienced during the initial stage, or else associated with the love experienced during the stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

According to the commentary, both types of mind remain capable of accomplishing deeds consisting of love. These reflections shed light upon actions impelled by empathy, wherein the characteristics of love and compassion belonging to the initial stage of that empathy are clearly manifest.
In a discourse concerning the great liberation from the wheel of existence, it is seen that Ānanda began to weep upon seeing that the lineage of the Teacher was nearing its end.
At that time, Gotama reminds Ānanda of his very own teaching: "All things that bring happiness are subject to change and disappearance. (Dīghanikāya, 2.143)
The Buddha consoled Ānanda, praising his service characterized by love: "Ānanda,
for a long time you have performed service to me as one who is ever-united with me— through acts of love consisting of body and through acts of love consisting of speech."
And by means of mental actions consisting of love;
those actions are beneficial and bring about happiness.
They are non-dual and devoid of measure. (Dīghanikāya 2.144)

The analysis according to the commentary is as follows: regarding the phrase "by bodily actions consisting of love," "bodily actions" refers to acts such as offering gifts, washing the face, and so forth, which are impelled by a heart full of love.
Regarding the term "beneficial," those actions are meant which are performed for the increase of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
"Bringing happiness"—this is the intended meaning: actions are performed with ease and joy, not with pain or hardship.
"Non-dual"—the sense is this: how many people [act] merely in the presence of others?
These [actions] are not beyond their perception;
they perform physical actions consisting of love and so forth.
Others, however, are merely beyond the perception of others.
They do not accomplish their tasks in his presence;
however, Ānanda did not accomplish his acts of loving-kindness by dividing them in such a manner.
And thus, those physical acts of love performed by him became non-dual;
"devoid of measure" means without limit.
He intends to say: "Your physical acts of love are exceedingly abundant in measure."
However, this world is exceedingly crowded,
and even the pinnacle of existence is extremely short.
Because there is no room for the abundance of activities within this petty world of goodness (*sāttvika*), it is said that actions are devoid of measure.
Acts of speech consisting of love—here, by the term "acts of speech," activities such as washing the face and making proclamations at the proper time are indicated.
These are sent forth from a compassionate mind.
Furthermore, if someone, having heard the voice of instruction, says:
"O noble one, you have spoken well"—this is an example of action consisting of speech imbued with love.

Regarding actions of the mind consisting of love, the intention is as follows: having exerted himself in the body according to the occasion, he sits in a secluded place and reflects in this manner: "My teacher..."
"May he be freed from disease and from affliction;
may he be happy.
(Dīghanikāyaṭīkā)
In the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* (2.584–85),
it is also recorded in the *Saṃvādasutta* that among themselves, those monks practiced acts of loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind.
In the *Gosiṅgasāvakasutta*, Gotama [addressed] Anuruddha...
He went to see Nandika and Kimbila;
those monks were staying in the Gośīrṣa garden.

(Majjhima Nikāya 1.206–207) The Buddha asks the renunciants: "Having obtained sufficient food by way of alms, and dwelling together in comfort like milk mixed with water, are you well, or not? They reply: "Indeed, we are well, and we have sufficient food by way of alms."
Under the leadership of Anuruddha, they each speak of the Buddha, dwelling together in happiness like milk and water mixed.
In their view, living together with such fellow-practitioners as monks is indeed a great gain;
for the sake of one another’s welfare, they perform actions of body, speech, and mind imbued with love.

In their presence and even behind their backs, Anuruddha described his devotion to those other people, saying: "I think of myself as lowly; have I surrendered my own mind for the sake of serving such friends?
And is my life truly for the sake of serving them?"
"...O noble one, although our bodies indeed remain separate from one another, nevertheless our minds have certainly attained unity. (Majjhima Nikāya, 1.206–207)

The commentary explains in detail the description of Anuruddha’s actions of body, speech, and mind consisting of loving-kindness (*premamaya*). Regarding the phrase "actions of body consisting of loving-kindness": here, bodily actions—whether others possess knowledge or lack it, whether they are present or absent—are [performed] because of his compassionate heart.
In this context, physical and verbal actions toward others occur only when a person dwells together with them;
the opposite occurs if people dwell separately.
Mental action occurs in all states.
For instance, Anuruddha saw that two monks were living with him;
one of them came back after having left outside without unfastening his belt.
He does not reveal his detachment through reflection, thinking, "By whom was this used?
Rather, he takes up those objects and places them back in their proper positions,
just as he himself would discard or retrieve them.
Alternatively, one exerts effort toward the object of desire;
these very actions are called affectionate bodily deeds in the presence of others.
For instance—some monk goes outside.
He discards his bed, his seat, and any necessary articles outside,
just as previously arranged by Anuruddha.
If he were to act in that very same way, then his series of affectionate physical actions would remain hidden from others;
for instance, when Anuruddha dwells with two other elders and converses with them in a sweet and pleasant manner.
Then that action is called an affectionate verbal act performed in the presence of others.
If one employs those two for conversation that is easily accessible through friendship or rooted in kindness, even then it would be an affectionate verbal act.
Furthermore, when one asks such a pair of questions or provides an answer to them— such an action is also called vocal karma. Moreover,
when two elders are traveling elsewhere and they are not present, if one praises their virtues, saying, "My dear kinsmen," [that too is vocal karma].
Nandiya and Kimbila, who were advanced in years, were endowed with such virtuous conduct;
they practiced in this very manner.
Such an action performed behind the backs of others is called a verbal act consisting of love.
Mental action consisting of love arises only when, whether others are present or absent, one thinks:
"May my dear relatives, Nandiya and Kimbila, who are aged, be freed from enmity and hostility;
may they both be happy."
Noble sir, our bodies indeed undergo separation;
for bodies are reduced to powder like wheat flour or like clay,
and they never again attain unity.
Nevertheless, our minds certainly partake in unity.
This is the intention: when we maintain our presence together in one place, we never remain separate from one another.
When we never engage in dispute and always cultivate harmony, then our minds attain unity; that is to say,
mental oneness arises.
How do they cause their own minds to be relinquished and engage them in service for others? For instance: one person has a vessel that is flawed, while another has a soiled garment.
Furthermore, there may be an action requiring repair.
In this situation, one who possesses a bowl with a flaw says: "Friends, my bowl is flawed."
"This must be washed," yet others do not say, "I have a garment that requires washing.
Or else: "I have those who wash their garments for me."
They also perform the work of preparing others;
even with just one of these other [factors], a similar cooperation occurs during the first proclamation:
"O kinsman," [they say].
"My clothes are soiled; they must be washed.
Or else, "My hut is falling into a state of ruin."
"His funeral rites must be performed.
(Majjhimanikāyaṭīkā, Papañcasūdanī, 2.239–40)

In the "Instruction to Siṅgāla," Gotama instructs the householder Siṅgāla: "Serve the wandering mendicants and brahmins with acts of love through body, speech, and mind; open your door for them, and give them material goods for the sake of sustaining their lives."
Even wandering mendicants, being sustained by shared experience, will accomplish acts of service in return.

It is stated in detail in the *Ṭīkā*: "By means of bodily actions consisting of love"—in this regard, when bodily actions are performed, if the individual creates a heart consisting of love, then those actions are said to consist of love.
When some worldly person, thinking "I shall converse with the monks," goes to the Buddhist temple and,
having arrived there, takes a water vessel and sprinkles water;
Massaging the feet or back of the monks— such actions as these are called physical actions consisting of love (*premamaya-kāyika-karma*).
When a worldly person sees that "the monks are entering the village for alms" and,
with faith, says to them, "Give them food, or milk, or something to eat," [that is also such an action].
At that time, such actions are called acts of speech consisting of love.
Furthermore, when one listens to the Dharma with faith and from within, and says, "Well said by you," then such actions are described as acts of speech consisting of love.
When a householder thinks,
"May those elder relatives of ours who remain within this cyclic existence be freed from enmity as well as from calamities," such speech is called an action born of a compassionate heart.
In the *Mahāparinibbāna-saṃyutta* of the *Bhavacakka-vagga*, Gotama instructs a bhikkhu: "There are six conditions by which gain arises" (*Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, 3.957).
[Also in the] *Dīghanikāya*, 2.80–82.
For instance: performing physical, vocal, and mental actions imbued with affection toward fellow monks, whether in their presence or in their absence;
receiving and sharing the alms-food obtained from fellow monks;
and conducting oneself according to virtuous conduct.
The Buddha said: "The cultivation of views for the sake of the absolute destruction of suffering— so long as you observe the aforementioned eightfold group,
you will certainly be fit for exaltation."
It is explained in the *Ṭīkā*: "Those very same bodily actions that are performed with a compassionate heart are characterized by affectionate tenderness (*prītisnigdha*).
Likewise, vocal action accomplished by a mind of compassion and fear is called 'consisting of love' (*premamaya*);
mental action accomplished by a mind consisting of compassion is called 'consisting of love'."
In this teaching, such a collective aggregate of actions is prescribed for renunciants;
nevertheless, even a householder is capable of performing such action.
When renunciants, impelled by hearts full of compassion, accomplish virtuous conduct, that action is called "action of the body characterized by affectionate joy."
When householders go to the remaining shrines to demonstrate their faith,
or go to the Bodhi tree, or go to invite the transmission of the Dharma;
Seeing a monk coming to the village for alms, they go out to see him;
they take hold of his alms-bowl and detain him so that he must sit down.
When they go together with them, such actions are called "actions of the body characterized by affectionate joy.
When renunciants, impelled by a compassionate mind, always teach proper conduct, [that too is so described].
When they explain the object of meditation and teach the Dharma, these actions are called "actions of speech characterized by joy and affection."
Furthermore, the Buddhist religious scripture is called the Tripiṭaka. Within it, there are the words of the Buddha in the form of questions and answers.
This scripture is an act of speech consisting of love.
The verbal acts of affectionate joy of householders occur only when they say,
"We are going to the common support (aviśiṣṭādhāra) in order to demonstrate our faith," or "We are going to the Bodhi tree for the sake of worship."
"Let us create the opportunity to hear the Dharma that is worthy of being heard.
"Let us perform worship with lamps, garlands, and flowers.
"Let us carry out the three types of noble practice."
"Right conduct, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
"We shall provide appropriate food and other necessities. "During the rainy season, we shall offer a gift to the monk who observes the retreat day."
"Today we shall provide the four requisites used by the spiritual tradition (namely:
clothing, an alms-bowl, a bed,
and medicine)."
"Let us invite the members of the spiritual community and prepare hard food for them.
"Show them seats for them to sit upon.

Through complete awakening regarding that object, he removes the desire for repeated rebirth.

And so, the *Kṣudratarachoṭikā-ṭīkā* states: when a renunciant perceives an object through direct knowledge, he nourishes a mind consisting of love—even though this love is generated through the door of profound inner vision or the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, ordinary compassion does not enter into this context. Nevertheless, apart from the aforementioned metaphorical usage of "compassion," all examples associated with compassion recorded in the dialogues undoubtedly— whether explicitly or implicitly— shine forth in conjunction with the power of either the stage of entry into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or the stage of stabilization (*sthāpanā*).

9.36) For rebirth stands spread out for us over an indefinite period of time extending into the future.

Having accepted every kind of decline for himself, he protected us with great effort; yet now we foster enmity toward him. For a long time, this person, acting as our father, underwent arduous labor for our protection.
"In the form of our sisters or in the form of our brothers, these people have rendered us assistance through various means.

If the practitioner [extends it] toward himself...

Then, through such practice, the practitioner increases the number of living beings who have come within the sphere of his compassion;

In the words of the *Sagāthāvagga*, the householder Manibhadra speaks this verse to Gotama: "A person of noble mind is always fortunate."

With whom does he have no enmity?
(Saṃyuttanikāya, 1.208).

The commentary explains that in the second verse uttered by the Buddha, the person indicated is an *arhat*;

and thus he becomes liberated from enmity.
What is the meaning of this commentary? Following the *Visuddhimagga*, it is stated that mindfulness or heedfulness is a beneficial mental object.
(*Visuddhimagga* 14.133)
In the commentaries, this is the established conclusion (as stated in a certain sub-commentary): that beneficial mental objects cannot coexist with unbeneficial mental objects.
When a beneficial mental object—such as one termed "dignity" (*manasvitā*) or "heedfulness" (*sāvadhānatā*)—is present in a non-sustained manner, then no unbeneficial mental object [can remain].
It is not fit to remain there.
Thus, if one who practices meditation reflects upon the previous moment of anger, then his mind becomes naturally free from anger in the present moment.

confidence, and so forth.

solitude,
and modesty.
freedom from aversion, absence of greed,
and equanimity toward all living beings;

Dexterity,

"For a person such as this, the future is more beautiful"—
