"Just as this mind— unshakable, free from enmity, vast, expansive, and immeasurable—
is like a person who, with a shovel and a basket, is not capable of destroying the vast earth" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.127).
Likewise, the five kinds of speech are unable to overcome a person whose mind is moistened with compassion because of their disagreeable nature.
Just as the earth repels being stepped upon due to its depth and immeasurability, (Majjhima Nikāya 2.200).
In the same way, with a mind moistened by compassion,
Gotama instructs the monks that they shall maintain compassion;
by acting thus, their minds will become indescribable, like a region of unbroken space.
It will become like the Ganges, impossible to burn.
By rubbing it with a piece of wool, the rough cat-skin pouch becomes well-sewn and no longer coarse.
Monks, if you follow this instruction, [it will be so].
In that case, their minds will not suddenly become deluded, inflamed, or harsh.
Regarding the words of his own kinsmen, Gotama teaches that in whatever household there are many women but very few men, [the mind becomes agitated].
That house is entered without effort.
In the same way, that monk who does not accomplish liberation of mind through the form of compassion will certainly be harassed by non-human powers.
(Saṃyuttanikāya, 2.254)
Furthermore, just as a house where there are many men but very few women is not suddenly attacked by bandits,
so too a monk who achieves liberation of mind through compassion is not overcome by non-human powers.

Then he instructs the monks for the practice of compassion. In the "Discourse on Compassion" within the fifth collection of discourses (*Saṃyutta Nikāya*), Gotama instructs the monks on how one should meditate—
by means of which meditation the fear of evil spirits does not remain.
The monks are not harassed by them.
When a person skilled in practices that produce gain knows a state full of peace, what would he do?
He is capable.
He is a virtuous person, straightforward and firm,
and capable of grasping [the truth].
He should be worthy of salutation, disciplined,
contented,
and nourished by happiness.

With very little work and very few possessions, and with senses capable of discernment, the man of knowledge, having distinguished himself from action and emulating the worldly, would never at any time practice base conduct.
The practice of that [knowledge] produces the discernment of virtues and defects by one who acts as a knower.
(He should fulfill these desires:
"May all living beings dwell in happiness and fearlessness."
May they all be happy in their hearts;
whoever possesses life,
whether stable or unstable, provided there is no transgression.
Whether long or broad, medium or short, subtle or gross, visible or invisible, far away or near— whatever living beings there are, or those yet to be born, may they all be happy at heart.
No person whatsoever should deceive another.
No person should become proud on account of receiving honor from anyone, anywhere;
no one should harbor thoughts of harm toward others; and one should maintain a boundless attitude of mind toward all living beings, whether out of anger or even hatred.
Just as a mother protects her only son even at the cost of her own life,
so should one nourish a boundless mind of love toward the entire world— above, below, and in between— free from obstruction, anger, or hostility.
From side to side;
while in the posture of standing like a staff,
with feet together.
Whether sitting or lying down, he should maintain his dignity and remain firm in his resolve.
This very state is proclaimed here as the noble (udātta) sentiment.
Having abandoned false views, practicing truth, and likewise relying on the vision of truth, he should cast away attachment to objects of desire; thus, he will certainly not enter a womb again.

According to the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha* (8–9), when monks understand the subject matter contained in the aforementioned discourse and follow its instructions while cultivating compassion, then the obstructive deities,
having failed to create any hindrance, become satisfied and happy, acting as fellow practitioners, allies, and helpers.

(Khuddakapāṭha, 252) Thus, the power of compassion exists for the sake of overcoming the forces of fate; this doctrine is supported by the narrative of the monk named Viśākhā, through whose cultivation of compassion non-human powers dwell in his presence in a state of mutual peace.
Even if those powers do not enter into association with monks who practice the cultivation of compassion,
they will still be unable to harm those monks.

In the Saṃyutta Nikāya, in the Discourse on the Gotamas, Gotama says: "If non-human beings cause trouble for monks who are engaged in the practice of liberation of mind through compassion, then those [non-humans] themselves will become exhausted.
(Saṃyutta Nikāya, 2.265)
Nevertheless, one who practices [meditation] does not desire protection from the afflictions created by non-human powers out of fear or servility;
rather, having abandoned defects such as fear, attachment, and pride, they draw forth compassion in the form of mental liberation—the noble state.
(Aṅguttaranikāyaṭīkā)
2.47; Visuddhimagga 9.44) Then his mind becomes steady, attained to equanimity, and likewise filled with supreme bliss.
(Visuddhimagga 9.111)
And thus that mind becomes an obstacle to all kinds of mental failure.
This is what is meant by saying that one who practices [this meditation] is protected even from physical calamities.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.72; 12.30–35)
For instance—Sāmāvatī, the daughter of Sāma, was the chief female disciple of Gotama.
While practicing the cultivation of compassion, she became capable of resisting her own suffering through that very compassion.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya, 2.26)
Lacking confidence in her continued devotion, her husband prepared to end her life with an arrow;
however, Samavati, together with her friends, captivated her husband with love and compassion,
so that he was unable to carry out his intended killing.

Nevertheless, Samavatī herself fell victim to transgression. Although she was skilled in the cultivation of compassion, she died from the burning of fire as a result of the consequences of an action she had committed that caused harm.

Although there is no explicit example in the dialogues (*saṃvāda*) to show that the compassion of one who practices is capable of turning the mental disposition of another person toward what is wholesome,
nevertheless, it is stated in the *Viśuddhimārga* that compassion possesses such power.
For the sake of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the practitioner begins to meditate appropriately upon any one of the forty objects.
Alternatively, one strives for the elevation of inner vision.
Therefore, it is taught that one should first protect compassion through the method described below:
A monk who has taken up the object of meditation should first define the boundaries of the tradition of the monks associated with his place of worship.
Then, for their sake, he should cultivate compassion with such a thought as this: "May they be happy, and may they be liberated from affliction.
Thereafter, he should cultivate compassion for the deities dwelling in the village.
Then, he should cultivate compassion for those people who stand in the position of leaders and who provide him with food and other necessities;
furthermore, he should practice compassion for all human beings as well as for all living creatures.
Through the compassion he maintains toward the monks associated with the monastery, he generates a tender heart within his companions.
They dwell together with him happily in one place.

Out of the compassion maintained for the deities associated with the sanctuary, those deities, being of tender heart, protect him fully by providing appropriate protection. Out of the compassion maintained for the village-dwellers who stand in the position of leaders, they, being of tender heart, serve him diligently by providing necessary supplies as required.
Through compassion cultivated for the sake of humanity, those people become pure-hearted;
consequently, when he wanders as a mendicant, they will not show him contempt.
When compassion is cultivated toward all living beings, a monk becomes capable of traveling everywhere without hindrance.
They do not create obstacles.
(Visuddhimagga 3.58) There is fear in the aforementioned practice;
There is attachment.
Due to that duality, the practice of what is beneficial may become tainted with defects.
Nevertheless, one should practice with equanimity, discernment, and confidence.
By grasping other objects through the medium of the object of meditation, one who practices in this manner will indeed protect compassion.
As a constituent part of common karma, he must certainly act in this way (*Visuddhimagga* 3.59) in order to establish the sequence of practice according to its proper order.
Meditation filled with love and compassion is the ground or the soil upon which either the drawing forth of concentration or the drawing forth of inner vision is performed.
Even after the attainment of right knowledge, such a drawing forth remains unimpeded.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.282–284)

Beyond the path of purification, there is no further statement in either the dialogues or the commentaries; it is merely an illustration where it is clearly stated that the cultivation of compassion in the form of meditative absorption immediately and effortlessly influences the mental state of another person.
This teaching reveals an extraordinary degree of compassion drawn forth within the state of being absorbed in meditation.
Those who practice can assist others not merely through teaching or by accepting alms, but also by their own conduct.
Not by establishing examples drawn from the lives of righteous individuals,
but rather by the means of elevation consisting of meditation permeated with compassion;
perhaps.
This very thing is called "the attraction of joy through sympathetic experience.

In his gradual discourses, Gotama explains that a certain monk was bitten severely by a snake because he did not establish a connection with the four classes of snakes through a heart moistened with compassion.
The Buddha said: "If a monk were to establish a connection with the four families of snakes while his mind is moistened with compassion, he would not be bitten.

Thus, for one who practices in order to protect himself from snake bites, he should establish a connection with the four families of snakes through a mind imbued with compassion; having reflected in this very way—"

I have compassion for the sake of the Virūpakkhas; I have compassion for the sake of the Erāpathas; I have compassion for the sake of the Chabyāputtas as well as the Kaṇhāgotamakas. I have compassion for the sake of those who are footless, and likewise for the sake of those endowed with two feet.
I have compassion for those who possess four lines,
and also for those with many lines;
may those devoid of lines not cause me harm.
Nor [should there be] those with two legs;
may those with four legs not do me harm, nor those with many legs.
May all sentient beings,
all living beings endowed with breath, together behold pure sights;
may no evil come upon anyone.
The Buddha is immeasurable,
the Dharma is immeasurable, and the Saṅgha is immeasurable.
But snakes, scorpions, leeches, spiders,
chameleons, and mice— all these are finite in number.
I have extended protection;
I have established protection.
May all living beings flee!
I praise the Blessed One, who is without equal in fortune;
I praise the one possessed of the seven right knowledges.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya, 2.72–73)
When Gotama said that the Buddhas and so forth are immeasurable, his intention was this: [regarding] that Buddha, the Dharma, and...
And he points out the virtues of the Saṅgha. (Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary,
3.103) There is a measurable virtue in [beings such as] snakes and so forth.
In the *Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā* (3.104),
Gotama shows the monks that by means of these two beneficial actions— namely, the cultivation of compassion and the exposition of the truth of the Dharma— they are able to protect themselves.
Having abandoned the state of deficiency and having moved far away from lives that cause harm, they remain.
Furthermore, in the discourses of the *Sagotrīya*, Gotama instructs the monks that they must be able to protect themselves through compassion;
in this regard, there is the example of the wrestler Mallavīra and his student.
Regarding the matter of self-protection, the two maintain differing views.
Mallavīra said, "I shall mark you, and you shall mark me.
In this way, through mutual marking, our protection of one another will be possible,
and our wrestling match too will reach its conclusion without obstacle."
Furthermore, the seeker of training said: "I observe myself; may you also observe yourself.

Gotama explained that the agent should follow the seeker's method to its successful conclusion, and likewise concluded that the agent should emulate a manner consistent with the establishment of self-respect.
It is expressed by other words:
O monks, for the sake of their own wisdom and exaltation, they should practice mutual cooperation, which will, in turn, accomplish the benefit of others even when they are not present.

The monks, with their tranquil mental applications and through various means, will demonstrate examples of those who have attained excellence in a life lived according to the Dharma, and they will likewise provide encouragement to others. The Buddha said: "Monks," [he continued].
He who protects himself also protects others;
or he who protects others also protects himself.
Monks, how does one who practices self-protection protect others?
Again and again, by means of meditative concentration and retention, by the extraction of what has been retained, and through the practice of meditation.
Monks, one who thus protects oneself protects others; monks, how does one who protects others protect oneself?
Through steadfastness and through being free from decline.
Through the state of compassion and through the state of effortless affection;
monks, in this way, one who protects others protects oneself.
If one who practices applies effort toward their own mind, whether with reference to themselves or others, then it becomes a benefit for both oneself and others.
The commentary states clearly: "having protected," [the self and others].
Having reflected upon the objects of meditation, monks, one who thus protects oneself also protects others.
That monk who, having abandoned the worldly pleasures found within the realm of kings, maintains and cultivates the primary objects of meditation day and night, attains the state of an Arhat.
Then another person, seeing him, thinks:
"This is a supreme monk;
he must have practiced accordingly."
"Having nourished this doctrine concerning association with monks, he will attain heaven;
thus, 'he who protects himself also protects others.
The meaning of 'with fortitude' is through steadfastness and through endurance."
The meaning of "by way of being free from loss" is: together with the compassion found in the first stage, [it is] by means of sympathy (*anukampā*).

The meaning of "by way of the state of affection" is: together with the love found in the first stage, [it is] by means of endearment (*prīti*). The meaning of "by way of the state of affectionate effort" is: together with the bliss of shared experience found in the first stage, [it is] by means of service accompanied by affection and by means of the happiness of shared experience.
He who protects others also protects himself. In this context,
the monk’s compassion—
Regarding the three sublime states— love (*prema*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*)— he practices absorption in meditation through the first three stages day and night.
By doing so, he understands the excellence of objects that are still subject to dependence and attains the state of the Worthy One (*arhat*).
Thus: "He who protects others also protects himself" (*Saṃyuttanikāya-ṭīkā*, 3.287).
An Arhat is a person who, through his righteous life, serves as a mirror for others to behold the foremost qualities they ought to attain.
When a certain person, upon beholding an Arhat, becomes joyful and gains firm conviction,
and is further sustained by that person’s conduct,
at that moment he becomes one whose heart is intent on benefiting others; in the future, he creates the causes for attaining the state of an Arhat himself.
Because he has cultivated this universal and benevolent mind, that person, acting as its agent, will be born in heaven after death in a state far superior [to his former one].
Thus, the practitioner who protects himself through his own cultivation becomes a worthy person (arhat) and protects others as well.
Although love—

Through the cultivation of these three noble qualities— compassion, sympathetic joy, and [equanimity]— the practitioner brings about benefit, welfare, and manifest influence upon others; nevertheless, there is no mention of other objects in the dialogues.

It is better that the person who draws these objects [toward himself] protects his mind from anger, cruelty, and the perception of faults where there are no faults, respectively; thus, they attribute a sense of gravity to the constraints regarding sensory objects.

In the previously mentioned dialogue, Gotama describes how one who practices [meditation] relates to others regarding their state of mind: with composure, without deficiency, and with a state of compassion.
And through a state of affection and effort, one protects his mind.
To bring about the realization of the three sublime states—compassion (*karuṇā*), love (*prema*), and sympathetic joy (*sahānubhūtānanda*)—the final triad of states is explained.
This is the intention: these states are understood as universal love and so forth during the stage of absorption in meditation.

The intention of the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*—in the context of being absorbed in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), those states are understood as universal worldly love and so forth (*visuddhimagga*, 9.45).
(*Aṅguttara-nikāya*, 3.224–25; *Visuddhimagga*, 9.45).
These elevated states protect the practitioner from unwholesome states such as anger.
Indeed, these three aforementioned states are designated as the root of inner vision;
for through inner vision, the practitioner becomes foremost in abandoning all forms of mental corruption for a long time.
By acting in this way, he liberates himself from rebirth along with all forms of incidental suffering;
consequently, he becomes an Arhat.
Thus, by maintaining an attitude toward others as toward himself, that practitioner protects his own mind.
Thus, the protection of oneself reaches completion.
This discourse places greater emphasis on the role of examples for practitioners in their ritual actions as well as in their commitment to spiritual prosperity (*dharmīyasamṛddhi*).
Although there is no explicit mention here of instructions regarding social duties,

Nevertheless, it is understood from an extensive examination of teachings associated with empathy that, for those who practice them, the agitation experienced in the heart is primarily manifested through training as a commitment to action (*karmaniṣṭha*). Furthermore,
we observe that there exists an inevitable connection between social agitation and its consequential action.
The stream of all previous perceptions flows uninterrupted until the very end;
however, the Buddha did not experience such inevitability here.
It was accompanied by simple compassion.
In teachings characterized by compassion and imbued with these three qualities— especially in those teachings rooted in empathy— he perceives the connection between social action and social anxiety.
He does so both in the individual sphere and in the work of his assistants and brothers, where there is a practice of engagement together with others.
He attributes the weight of that [teaching] to its subsequent synonyms.
He felt no need to establish a connection between those teachings— consisting of meditations associated with love and compassion— and the subsequent actions rooted in the welfare of others,
because he had already imparted the teaching on that subsequent subject elsewhere.

However, this is understood here: that through the pursuit of such meditation, there remains a natural inclination toward such supreme altruistic actions. At the time of cultivating the vision of love and compassion, Gotama brings forth unprecedented qualities—qualities which are generally not considered in the context of "empathy," "straightforward compassion," or "acts of love."
These unprecedented virtues have as their objects the preservation of those [virtues];
they are personal gains as well as gains recognized by the principle of the mind (manas-tattva),
and they are also gains for future life.
In his gradual discourses, Gotama teaches that there are eight gains (*lābha*).
A certain person is capable of acquiring these gains through liberation of mind characterized by compassion,
or when [compassion] is intense.
It becomes accepted, increased, and transformed into a formal promise.
(Aṅguttaranikāya, 4.250) "A person sleeps rightly; he wakes rightly."
He does not see bad dreams;
he becomes dear to human beings;
he becomes dear to non-human beings.
The deities protect him;
he is not overcome by fire, poison, or weapons.
If his perception does not become more expansive, then he ascends to the Brahma-world (*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.250).
The commentary analyzes it as follows: "He does not see terrifying dreams."
Even though he sees them, nevertheless those dreams are merely auspicious dreams;
he sees himself.
For example: he seems to offer his faith in the remaining supports; or [faith] in the Buddha, the Dharma, and—
He honors the Saṅgha as it were;
unlike other people who see dreams, he does not see them.
Others see him as if surrounded by bandits, struck by serpents, or fallen into the midst of a chasm;
yet he is not overcome by fire, poison, or weapons.
In this context, some tell a story about cows:
one cow, standing on her hind legs, was giving milk to her calf.
Another man, a hunter, holding a spear in his hand, thought to himself:
Thinking, "I shall strike this ox," he hurled a spear; once the spear had struck the body of the ox, it returned just as it was, like a palm leaf.
In this case, the compassion felt during the sequence of its entry was not the cause.
Or rather, compassion is not merely a state of being established through its synonyms; rather, it is the cow’s extremely intense longing for the welfare of her calf.
Thus, compassion possesses great power.
In the *Aṅguttaranikāyaṭīkā* (5.82–83),
it is stated that the gains arising from liberation of mind through compassion (*karuṇā*) and form (*rūpa*) have indeed been mentioned above.
However, it has never been stated in either the discourses (*saṃvāda*) or the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) that these gains are compatible with all states by their very nature.
Even Gotama, despite possessing the great power of compassion and empathy, was not devoid of enemies;
his envious brother Devadatta serves as proof of this.
One should observe the equilibrium between the mind’s capacity across various conditions and its functional efficacy toward the welfare of others.
Empathy is not specifically endowed with any particular power of the mind.
Those who practice it teach others,
and they receive alms from others.
And they establish the example of a life dedicated to the welfare of others.
In all these fields, compassion is designated as the sustaining power. Acts moistened by compassion rely upon a certain power of a mind consisting of compassion.
Those actions are assistants to the welfare of others;
although the specific nature of the benefit that liberation of mind in the form of compassion accomplishes for others has not been examined here,
it is nevertheless understood beyond doubt that the drawing forth of compassion makes one's empathy toward another firm and intense.
And thus, it manifests power in subsequent altruistic intentions and altruistic deeds;
it is the potency of a certain mental state and the gains arising therefrom.
When the remedies for those defects are clearly demonstrated in one place beyond doubt, then among them, direct yoga is seen.
Co-experience is a state of mind that is naturally graspable;
therein lies the power of dispatching [the mind].
Such a shared experience is never justified by either present circumstances or future rewards.
The compassionate mind found in the first stage of practice is capable of sustaining the mendicant’s enjoyment of alms, his cultivation of meditation, and his bearing of the name of a monk.
Moreover, actions characterized by compassion, which are mutually dependent and impelled by a compassionate mind, lead to the prosperity of the Saṅgha.

Nevertheless, the attainment of the mental liberation consisting of compassion, as well as the remedies for its defects, are exceedingly diverse and abundant; for it is precisely for the sake of attaining the extraordinary gains born of the mind when it has reached a high stage that ultimate mental application is bestowed.
This is stated without doubt: even such mental power as this produces gains born from even a slight state of meditative concentration.

Having reflected upon the gains born of compassion in the aforementioned dialogue, Gotama praised the blossoming of compassion and said: "The fetters of that wise person, whose nature is to draw forth immeasurable compassion, come to an end; he perceives that the very foundation of the wheel of saṃsāra is destroyed."
The person who cultivates compassion solely for a particular living being becomes a benefactor through that specific act;
however, the great man who possesses a disposition of empathy toward all living beings accumulates abundant merit.
Kings equal to sages conquer the earth, which is filled with sentient beings.
And thereafter, he becomes one who observes the vow for the performance of several sacrifices;
namely, the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and the human sacrifice (puruṣamedha).
The *Sammāpaṭha*, the *Vājapeya*, and the *Niraggala*—

whatever merit a person acquires through the proper nourishment of a mind full of compassion, you do not accumulate even a sixteenth part of that merit, nor even a sixteenth part of a sixteenth part of it.
They shine like the stars in the lunar orb;
he who does not kill, nor causes others to kill,
and who does not practice banditry—
Nor does he cause others to act as plunderers;
for one who possesses compassion for all living beings does not nourish enmity toward any person whatsoever.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya, 4.74–49)
The fetters go to destruction;
he perceives that the foundation and root of the wheel of saṃsāra is destroyed.
This is the intended meaning: the person who has attained the state of an Arhat abandons the ten fetters.
Included herein is the destruction of the very foundation of the wall of the wheel of saṃsāra.
This state is attained in due order through the inner vision;
it possesses compassion, which serves as an uninterrupted cause.
Alternatively, "fetters go to destruction.
The meaning of this is: fetters associated with both aversion and non-aversion go to destruction.
He perceives that as the destruction of the root of the wheel of saṃsāra.
For, being endowed with compassion, he perceives the destruction of that which is called the root of the wall of the wheel of existence (*saṃsāracakra*) whose nature is defilement (*dūṣaṇa*).
(Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā, 4.68).
In the discourses, ten kinds of fetters (*nigaḍa*, i.e., *saṃyojana*) are spoken of.
Those fetters bind a person together with the wheel of saṃsāra;
for instance, false views regarding the self and doubt.
Attachment to the performance of rituals such as sacrifices,
longing of the senses,
and anger.
Longing for the world of form, longing for the world devoid of form,
and the insentience of abiding in a state.
Delusion and ignorance;
since these fetters are cast off by the Arhat person,
he thereby effects the destruction of the entire foundation of the wheel of saṃsāra (the upadhā).
By this, no cause remains for a renewed birth characterized by repeated suffering and the like.

To abandon the criticisms examined in various commentaries (*ṭīkā*), the commentary sets forth two clear methods. Namely: the method for the abandonment of persistence (*sthāyiparityāga*) through the uprooting of criticisms by means of internal vision (*antardṛṣṭi*), which is the abandonment through eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
And by the subduing of faults through the gateway of concentration, there is the means for the relinquishment of the unstable (*vikkhammanappahāna*).
First, the discourse points out the Noble Person (*arahantapuruṣa*) as the immediate cause; together with immeasurable compassion, he maintains inner vision.
In brief:
Having maintained meditative absorption through meditation upon compassion— up to the point of being immersed in the state of concentration— he will remain therein.
Then, arising from that state of meditative immersion, he directs his exceedingly sharp mind toward entering into the specific and general qualities of both the mind and the body.

Having observed that both the mind and the body are, individually, non-abiding with respect to their objects, subject to change, and likewise incapable of being satisfied, his mind naturally establishes a connection with that *nirvāṇa* which exists by transcending all worldly transformation and instability.

When a profound inner vision arises concerning the world that is subject to change and *nirvāṇa* which is free from change, there occurs the liberation from the bondage of mental shackles such as sensory desire and the like.
Tendency fades away;
this newly manifested awakening does not justify those various reactions that must be abandoned for a long time.
According to the second interpretation, it separates a certain person mentioned in the dialogue from whom one possesses only immeasurable love.
Such a person remains completely liberated from all objects rooted in hatred for a short time.
Here, "fetters related to hatred" point to the harmful mental defects associated with hatred;
namely—envy, and so forth.
Sañjaya and agitation (*Visuddhimagga* 14.170):
When the Buddha said,
"He sees the destruction of that which is called the wall and foundation of the defects of the wheel of saṃsāra," [he refers to this].

Then, with concentrated love, he points out the impermanent nature of faults. Although the faults of one who practices may even come within the range of vision during a state of absorption in meditation,
nevertheless, at the time of meditating on love, the person absorbed in meditation experiences a supreme, satisfying bliss along with the equalized subduing of those very faults.

Through the nourishment of immeasurable love, he is assisted toward the attainment of inner vision (antardṛṣṭi-bhakti) by way of such mental states serving as the foundation, or by way of the enjoyment of the supreme bliss born from such mental states.
In the chapter concerning the eleven gains (*ekādaśalābha*) within the *Kramika-vacanāni*, Gotama provides a list of these eleven gains.
The person who accomplishes mental liberation in the form of love attains those benefits.
This is the conjunction with the eight benefits previously mentioned: "He quickly brings that mind into a state of concentration;
his complexion becomes radiant."
"He dies without agitation" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 5.342).
Without doubt, for the sake of all these benefits, Gotama further teaches that which pertains to the *cāndrāyaṇa* vows (*upoṣadha*).
The disciples of the great teachers practiced for the sake of all beings in order to bring about an immeasurable expansion of the heart imbued with love and compassion (*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.390).
Brahmā draws in and protects [beings] through the states of equanimity, joy, sympathetic joy, and compassion (*Majjhima Nikāya* 1.370–72).
(Aṅguttaranikāya-ṭīkā, 2.204) Therefore, during the period of one's life, the cultivation of the aforementioned qualities is itself the specific method for attaining union with Brahmā.
Gotama describes this method as follows: "Vāseṭṭha," [he said].
A certain monk, with a mind endowed with a state of evenness accompanied by compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, remains constantly connected with living beings in one direction;
and likewise in the second, third, and fourth directions, and above.
He behaves in such a manner even toward those at his feet, at his side, or at his back;
he establishes a connection with all beings everywhere through equanimity— with a heart full of love—
wherein the mind remains undisturbed.
Free from enmity, vast, extensive, and likewise immeasurable.
Vāseṭṭha, a single powerful conch-blower, with a slight effort, was able to produce an echo in the four directions.
In that state, measurable karma does not remain immeasurable.
Through the means of liberation of the mind, which is endowed with the equal functioning of compassion, shared experience, and bliss, such a state arises.
Vāseṭṭha, this alone is the path to union with Brahman.
Furthermore, a certain monk establishes constant contact with beings possessing life in one direction (such as the northern direction) with a mind full of loving-kindness.
In the same way, in the second, third, and fourth directions, above, and below.
He establishes contact side by side;
he remains connected with all beings everywhere through equanimity— with a mind full of love— wherein the mind is undisturbed and free from desire.
It is vast,
extensive, and likewise immeasurable.
Vāseṭṭha, a single powerful conch-blower is able to produce an echo in the four directions by means of a mere slight effort.
In that state, measurable karma does not remain immeasurable.
A state arises that is equal to the means of liberation through a mind consisting of love.
Vāseṭṭha, this alone is the path to union with Brahman.
When love and the other qualities are cultivated in accordance with the instructions previously mentioned, they are then called sublime states (*udātta-bhāva*).
In the dialogues (*saṃvāda*), the definitions for compassion, love, sympathetic joy, and equanimity were not formulated within the first fourfold compendium.
Nevertheless, through the commentaries and the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*), the characteristics and explanations of those subjects have been established.

Because each sublime state possesses its own distinct excellence, when one state is present, the absence of other states is understood. Compassion has the specific characteristic of taking the form of devotion toward the removal of the suffering of others.
The function of compassion (*karuṇā*) is precisely the state of being distressed by the suffering of others (*Visuddhimagga* 9.94).
Indeed, the cultivation of compassion through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) yields especially abundant fruit for the purpose of counteracting violence.
There is a characteristic that bestows joy upon one who has experienced bliss together [with others].
(Visuddhimagga, 9.85)
Freedom from envy is his very practice.
(Visuddhimagga,
9.95) For the cultivation of meditative absorption experienced together with joy is especially fruitful for the prevention of discontent.
There is a characteristic that has attained a state of mental equilibrium through evenness (Visuddhimagga 9.96), which is the mental state that persists in sentient beings. (Visuddhimagga 9.108)

Beholding all living beings with an equal state of mind is the very function of equanimity (*samavṛttitā*). The cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) characterized by equanimity is particularly fruitful for the purpose of counteracting attachment (*rāga*).
The state of *udātta* (the sublime), which consists in equanimity, is distinct from the experience of equanimity itself.
In the former case, there exists an independence regarding conscious living beings; however, in the latter, there is no such [independence] regarding pleasure.
Nor does the experience of suffering persist;
rather, it arises as a companion to the conscious mind throughout its various states.
(Visuddhimagga, 4.158, 162)
The activity of these four states indeed has its root in sending forth people.

It bestows the essence of the supreme light through such a thought as, "May all living beings be liberated from these sufferings and the like"— for compassion is the state of longing to remove the pain and suffering of others.
Love is the state of longing for the attainment of happiness and welfare through such a thought as, "May all living beings be happy. [It is expressed as:
"May you experience bliss;
it is good that you experience bliss."
The state of constantly desiring to accomplish the happiness and welfare of others, accompanied by the thought "This is exceedingly good," is itself the bliss of sympathetic joy (*sahānubhūtānanda*).

The state of being fully cognizant of the happiness and suffering of others, accompanied by the thought "The happiness and suffering of people arise solely from the causes of the fruits of past actions," is itself equanimity (*samavṛttitā*).
Furthermore, in the depiction of character and in the compendiums of essential points, an apparent contradiction is observed.
For instance—love (*prema*) is characterized as devotion (*bhakti*) for the sake of accomplishing the supreme auspiciousness.
Love, indeed, is the state of desiring the means to happiness.
In this context, the promise regarding the fruit of action (*karma-pratiśruti*) is understood.

Nevertheless, the wish that "all may be happy" constitutes the very essence of love—a state in which the utility of ritual action and its rewards appears minimal. Perhaps the reason for this is as follows: the teachings concerning love and compassion found in the dialogues merely indicate the cultivation of these dispositions through the yoga of meditation.

For this very reason, the teachings merely involve the cultivation of such wishes as "May all be happy" and "May all be free from suffering. Furthermore, Gotama never uttered any connection between meditation on love and compassion and any incidental action performed for the sake of others. Nevertheless, it is understood that by drawing forth these states of mind, a transformation of the practitioner's brotherly actions is indicated both in their nature and in their extent.

There is no fixed rule that one who practices with concentration and cultivates universal love and compassion will necessarily become deeply moved for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others; however,
there are teachings regarding acts of love, simple compassion, and empathy.
Among these, the aspect consisting of action regarding love and compassion has been described;
even a mere drop of these teachings is not limited to the context rooted in meditation.
It is understood that among these teachings, Gautama instructs on the sending of communal labor.
In those dialogues concerning love and compassion, the gravity of a state rooted in excessive concern for one's own religious life was not slight;
nevertheless, Gautama did not mention it—namely, that if suffering arises, then compassion becomes false.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.94) Although compassion is manifested simply by the manifestation of suffering,
nevertheless, such a state does not exist within compassion itself.
"May all beings be liberated from suffering"—this kind of wish alone constitutes compassion.
Overwhelmed by the suffering of others, we fail to provide them with assistance.

On one hand there is heartlessness, and on the other, agitation caused by the suffering of others; between these two, there exists a dilemma regarding effort that cannot be resolved without suffering itself.
At the time of drawing forth compassion, one who practices in order to remove the suffering that has arisen should be constantly mindful.
First, with reference to those beings afflicted by extreme suffering, he wishes: "May they be freed from suffering. Then, for his dear ones, and so on.
One draws forth compassion for those who are indifferent and for those who occupy the position of enemies (*Visuddhimagga* 9.80).
If a question arises concerning the object of an enemy, then the aforementioned counteractive measure is applied.
Just as compassion takes the form of a sublime state, so should one practicing the cultivation of it bring about equanimity in that compassion.
One should strengthen and universalize this point:
that which the word *prema* indicates in the Pali dialogues and commentaries is a meaning distinct from the meaning of the word "love" in the English language. This is worthy of note.
In dialogues, there is no mention of conjugal love or carnal love.

In a certain profound dialogue, Gotama explains the nature of the marital relationship as follows: that the husband should serve his wife, and the wife, in turn, should be characterized by compassion toward him.

The instruction that the manifestation of love toward an object contrary to one's own nature should not be made for the sake of intensifying sublime love is given to those who have newly received initiation;
for if it were done otherwise, love would easily transform into mere craving.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.4, 6)
The practitioner should always be attentive to avoid attachment; otherwise, the unfolding of love will not occur as it should.
This is possible when effort is exerted. (Visuddhimagga, 9.93)
The meditator first expands the sphere of love toward oneself through a gradual intensification of affection,
and thereafter toward the venerable teacher and toward a friend.
Toward indifferent people and, by elimination, toward hostile people,
his aim should be equanimous love for all the world.
Then he will certainly bring this about:
One should thus consolidate and expand it.
In that regard, universal loving-kindness does not make a distinction between self and other.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.40–48)
The meaning of shared joy (*sahānubhūtānanda*) is a state of delight in the success of others;
it occurs when there is either jesting or intoxication in this regard.
Alternatively, when someone becomes self-forgetful through the success of another, then a false semblance of shared joy arises.
(Visuddhimagga,
9.95) There is a need for equanimity toward the side of those who act for one's benefit as far as possible;
however, when others achieve success, a loss of equanimity arises due to the power of excessive intimacy.
That loss leads to one's own detriment;
thus, through falling away from pure practice, there will be a decline.

For the sake of attracting the bliss experienced together with a dear friend—whether that friend has come, gone, or is yet to come—one undertakes the attraction of bliss with a view toward its fruitfulness.
(Viśuddhimagga 9.87) Thereafter, he draws forth shared joy with respect to the success of both indifferent persons and hostile persons respectively.
In this way, whatever is performed toward the fields of loving-kindness and compassion, he performs it as well through its incidental applications.

Equanimity is a state of perfectly balanced mind resulting from the observation of the happiness and suffering of others. It is the drawing forth of equanimity in the fourth stage of the exclusive absorption in meditation.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.111)

The meditators are sent forth for the purpose of drawing out equanimity (*samavṛttitā*), because they perceive a somewhat meager fruit in the first three exalted states (*udāttabhāva*). Among those exalted states, each individual state is drawn into one of the first three stages of absorption (*dhyāna*) during whichever stage is appropriate.
(Visuddhimagga,

9.111) By nurturing such a wish as "May all beings be happy," one feels a sense of agitation toward those living beings who are capable of experiencing joy. One's initial three noble qualities become endowed with such agitation.
(Viśuddhimagga,
9.88) However, equanimity is free from such agitation.
Furthermore, in the first three sublime states, there remains the operation of either rejoicing or aversion.

(Visuddhimagga, 9.83) Love must certainly be guarded; otherwise, love is transformed by attachment. Compassion also must be guarded accordingly; otherwise, compassion is transformed by aversion toward the conditions of others or by the perception of their suffering.
Thus, accompanied by experienced bliss, it ought to produce a state of intoxication.
When an equalization is performed through comparison, the aforementioned calamities are seen to result from its being of little fruit;
nevertheless, there is no purpose in protecting this kind of equalization by such means.
In the remainder, the first three states are accompanied by the experience of pleasure,
because those states are indeed the means for liberation from enmity, violence, and discontent.
All of them, moreover, are again joined with suffering (*Visuddhimagga* 9.88.111).

When a comparison is made between the experience of equanimity (*samavṛttitānubhava*)— which occurs in the fourth stage of absorption (*dhyāna*) together with the state of sublime form (*rūpodātabhāva*)— and that which arises in the first three stages of absorption:
Only gross happiness is seen as supreme;
if equanimity is absent there, it is false, for in that case there exists only a lack of knowledge.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.96)
When impartiality has been cultivated accordingly, this realization arises: that other people are the performers of those actions.
And thus, their future state will reflect the perspective of the principles governing present actions.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.96)
When dharma conduces to a good fruit, likewise adharma results in the opposite fruit. (*Visuddhimagga*, 9.23–24).
Other people will certainly take up the burden of their own destiny at the time of its ripening.
And thus, as he practices, he will take up the burden for its sake;
regarding this subject, the meditating person, being attentive, frees his mind from mental states that produce inauspiciousness as well as from the hatred directed toward the conduct of others.
Furthermore, in the fourth stage of absorption, he cultivates a beneficial impartiality free from partiality.

Having already practiced the cultivation of equanimity prior to the intensification of the sublime state (*udātta-bhāva*), he should nourish one of the other sublime states up to the third stage of absorption.
(Visuddhimagga 9.104) Rising from that state of meditative composure, he maintains equanimity toward ordinary people who are indifferent, as well as toward friends and enemies.
In subsequent turnings, he acts as before.
When he exerts himself with resolve for absorption in meditation through this state, he necessarily proceeds to the fourth turning;
this alone is the deviation.
This indeed is the very nature of the noble state (*udāttabhāva*).
Having understood that nature, we are able to respond to the previously mentioned simile of the conch-blower. The commentary explains: "Vāseṭṭha,"...
There was once a certain powerful conch-blower;
likewise, there was a certain weak conch-blower who, at the time of blowing his conch, was not capable of producing an echo in the four directions.
He was not able to cause the resonance to spread everywhere.
Furthermore, a powerful conch-blower is able to spread sound everywhere by means of drawing forth the mind and its liberation; in this context,

that which is compassion is what is applicable when the occasion for compassion arises— namely, the compassion belonging to the stage of entry (*praveśa*) or the compassion belonging to the stage of stabilization (*sthāpanā*).
Nevertheless, when the occasion for the liberation of the mind arises, then compassion, existing solely as a mode of stabilization, becomes applicable to its object.
That action which operates within the sphere of desire is called limited action (*parimita-karma*).
That action which has as its object both that which is endowed with form and that which is devoid of form is called immeasurable action (*aparimeya-karma*).

Because it transcends measurable action, this action is called immeasurable action; and because it extends through a network of connections in the four directions both specifically and generally, this action is called immeasurable action.
It does not abide in that object; it does not become established in that object.
This action, characterized by desire for an object, does not persist for long in an act, whether it be one consisting of form or devoid of form.
This does not find a firm footing therein.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that it does not perceive a basis for its action—whether that action consists of a form characterized by desire, or whether it is an action devoid of form.
One does not attain a proper yoga for the sake of one's own stability;
rather, action consisting merely of form, or even that devoid of form, pervades and exceeds the action directed toward objects of desire.
This [latter] attains a proper yoga for the sake of one's own stability.
This undertaking is like the great ocean.
Just as the great ocean, having surpassed small reservoirs of water and having found its own place, remains established;
so too does this form or that inferior form cast aside the fruit of action pertaining to the sphere of desire on its side.
"This alone conduces to union with Brahmā" (*Dīghanikāyaṭīkā*, 2.405–406).
The commentary explains that this indicates compassion as it pertains to the mode of entry or the mode of establishment.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) pertains specifically to the category of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), that is, to being immersed in *dhyāna*, or alternatively, to the category of immersion in *dhyāna*.

Although this compassion accords with the usage of compassion as it is explicitly explained in the dialogues (*saṃvāda*), nevertheless, it is understood here as the very compassion situated within the category of establishing [the mind] through mental liberation (*manomukti*).
Such a qualification should be employed together with love (*preman*) and shared joy (*sahānubhūta-ānanda*).
It may also be employed together with equanimity (*samavṛttitā*).
Equanimity is applied in the sense of equal-mindedness with respect to sentient beings.

Just as a certain powerful conch-blower is able to produce echoes in the four directions with minimal effort, so too a certain practitioner, by drawing forth the mind, may become endowed with a connection to the living beings existing in the four directions. This occurs when the powerful conch-blower produces an echo in the four directions.
It is expressed by other words;
there is no place where sound is not heard.
Even in the fields of liberation such as compassion and the like, such a state is observed.

But what is the meaning of this practice? First, regarding the mental state, one must bear in mind this gravity: that the word ‘ek-tibbati’ (Pāli: *kammaṭṭhāna*)— [The text continues: ...is a term for a subject of meditation. It is not merely a matter of physical posture; rather, it refers to the internal condition of the mind. Therefore, one should reflect with reverence upon the significance of this practice. Furthermore, it is essential to understand that the purpose of this work is not to achieve some external goal, but to cultivate a profound inner transformation. Thus, one must approach this task with a sense of solemnity, recognizing that the purification of the mind is the primary objective. In this regard, the practitioner should maintain mindfulness and alertness at all times, ensuring that the mind remains focused on the chosen object of meditation without distraction. Only through such earnest application can the true benefit of this spiritual discipline be realized. Finally, it is important to remember that progress in this path is gradual and requires patience, as the seeds of virtue must be nurtured over time to yield their full fruit. Therefore, one should persevere with diligence and a steady resolve. This concludes the preliminary reflection on the nature and purpose of the practice. May this effort lead to the ultimate liberation from suffering. [End of text]
Volition indicates bodily action (Visuddhimagga 19.24).
By substituting "consciousness" (*cetanā*) for "action" (*karman*) in this passage, the position of the commentary becomes refined.

Just as the measurable flood of sound produced by a weak conch-blower is limited, so too is consciousness regarding its object of desire limited. When a person attains absorption in meditation, [the mind becomes immeasurable].
At that time, the mind remains in a world composed of form (*rūpamaya*) when endowed with the first four stages of absorption (*dhyāna*),
or it exists in a subtler, formless (*arūpa*) world when joined with the state of great expanse attained through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is because the mental state associated with sublime qualities (*udāttabhāva*) persists within the first four stages of absorption.
Consequently, that state is indeed the world consisting of form (*rūpamaya-jagat*).
Consciousness (*cetanā*), when accompanied by that mental state which has form as its object, becomes entirely liberated from states such as passion (*rāga*) and the like—
those states of passion and so forth which bind the mind and create a limit for its range of movement.
(1.58–59) That consciousness is said to be immeasurable.

Furthermore, one who practices with a delight in drawing forth the state of exaltation expands those [powers] either through a specific increase or gradually, individually, toward each of the directions as if they were existing entities;
or else, generally, he expands them simultaneously everywhere.
(Viśuddhimagga, 9.45–47) Thus, when one who practices with objects that have come within range of their consciousness examines them, an immeasurable volition arises.
When immeasurable compassionate volition is present,
At that time, the measurable consciousness directed toward objects of desire does not remain.

Having illustrated the metaphor of the ocean and the lotus pond, the commentary points out the further meaning of the statement, "Whatever action is measurable does not remain in that context," by noting that if a person,
at some point in their life, draws forth one of the noble states of being (*udāttabhāva*), [the measurable consciousness does not persist].
Thus, at his death, the consciousness imbued with these dispositions attains meaningfulness and is prepared for rebirth in the world of Brahmā.
At that time, no karma directed toward finite objects of desire remains meaningful.
In this way, the power of sublime states of being is established for rebirth in the world of Brahmā.

This explanation provides a genuine occasion for the simile of the powerful conch-blower, in order to include within the synonyms for absorption in meditation (*dhyāna*) the fruits of drawing forth compassion and other qualities that liberate the mind.

At the conclusion of the discourse, Gotama said: "The man who draws forth the four sublime states (*udāttabhāva*) by means of the previously mentioned method will become liberated from the afflictions of mental corruption, such as association with women and the calamity of enmity."
And thus, he acquires mental strength.
Endowed with the qualities of Brahman, this person goes to the world of Brahmā after death, provided there is love and compassion.
When one experiences shared joy and practices the fourfold equanimity by following the method of the four types of instruction, those qualities are called sublime states (*udātta-bhāva*).
(The Brahma-vihāras)
Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.225:
In terms of sound, for exalted states are indeed the means for the livelihood of life,
like the Brahmās (the deities).
(Brahmā),
or rather, those states are the supreme means for the journey of life. (Visuddhimagga, 9.105)
Each individual state is an elixir that destroys the harmful defects such as anger and violence.

Thus, all four states are beneficial for one who practices them. Even so, at the specified time, a certain meditator may consider one state to be more helpful and feel entitled to accord it greater importance; yet Gotama [regards] the state of compassion as universal among all beings.
He attributes great importance to these gains, for all his teachings regarding compassionate deeds and shared experience are permeated by compassion.
Any increase in compassion brings the subsequent two to life; that is to say, it enriches and adorns both the sending and the manifestation of the entire life of the Dharma.

Four exalted states— whether the Brahma-vihāras or the states of equanimity (*samavṛttitā*)— reflect the attainment of what is considered the true nature of the mind; among these, while the first three share the quality of equal footing,
the state of equanimity is the supreme station.
In one commentary, the sequence of their development is demonstrated. A comparison is made between the sublime states and those emotions which parents experience for the sake of their offspring;
when the infant is within the womb, [the comparison is drawn].
Then, with hearts full of compassion, the parents think, "When shall we see our son endowed with all his limbs and restored to health?
Furthermore, when this tender infant lies on his back and cries out or wails due to being stung by lice, flies, and the like, or because of an interruption in his sleep;
Then, hearing that, the parents experience a common compassion.

Moreover, during those most longed-for years, whenever the child runs about or finds rest during playtime, upon seeing him, the hearts of the parents become as tender as balls made of soft cotton soaked in the finest, purest butter.
The minds of the parents become fully satisfied and gladdened; then, a shared joy arises between them. Consequently, when the son is able to provide ornaments for his wife and dwells in his own home,

At that time, his parents, being endowed with even conduct—that is, maintaining an even-mindedness—thought, "Now our son, being under our own authority, ought to remain [with us]. Thus, at that moment, they cultivated equanimity toward him. (Aṅguttaranikāyaṭīkā, 2.104)
By such a means,
he who practices and draws forth sublime states first nurtures compassion.
At this time, he desires the welfare of sentient beings.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.109) Then, when he sees—

When one hears and reflects that those living beings are subject to suffering (*Visuddhimagga* 9.109), then one draws forth a love in the form of affection for the purpose of taking upon oneself the suffering of others.
(Since this passion is drawn forth during the state of being absorbed in meditation,
the practitioner, through the power of practice, becomes concentrated for the sake of expanding his inner disposition in relation to his actions.
By the drawing forth of compassion, the practitioner desired the welfare of those [toward whom he felt it].
When the practitioner of meditation sees the prosperity of those living beings, he wishes, "May their suffering be far removed," and thereby he becomes joyful.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.109)
Here, the meaning of "he sees" is that the meditator observes the prosperity of others in the present, or contemplates their past prosperity or future prosperity.
His contemplation remains limited solely to the objective sphere of the thing itself. (Visuddhimagga, 9.84)
Thus, by drawing forth the bliss experienced together, the practitioner fulfills the manifestation of interconnected phenomena for the sake of others;
nothing remains unfulfilled.
He is able to draw forth equanimity.
That equanimity is not a state of equal-mindedness toward those in whom devotion has arisen;
being impartial, he regards all living beings with indifference.
(Visuddhimagga, 9.109)
The practitioner, sent forth to preserve one of the noble dispositions for the sake of individual gain as well as for the attainment recognized by the mind-as-such (*manas-tattva*),
begins to protect the aforementioned fourfold set of dispositions by means of the poison-destroying medicine that is anger and its like.
Following the sequence of expansion taught, he conforms to the mirror of the four fundamental countermeasures.
By repeatedly following this mirror and practicing, one begins to contemplate most deeply for the sake of others; his capacity also becomes endowed with equanimity.
This is stated without doubt: through meditation, the drawing forth of noble qualities is beneficial, as it influences the response given by others in their actual circumstances.
By that power, the intensity, utility, and stability of the remedy undergo transformation.

Gotama never asserts that the fourfold teachings concerning the sublime states belong exclusively to him alone; nor does he say that a person who practices the sublime states in isolation is acting rightly. Gotama clearly demonstrates the incompatibility of practicing the sublime states in isolation alongside the instructions on the Eightfold Path for liberation—according to the fourfold teachings: [The fourfold teachings: "Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages (*ariya-vamsa*). What four? Here, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, any kind of almsfood, any kind of lodging, and any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. He takes delight in renunciation, takes delight in solitude, takes delight in non-distraction, and takes delight in the factors of enlightenment. These, bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages. By means of these four noble lineages, [he shows] the incompatibility of the mere practice of the sublime states. Thus it is said: "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardently, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, then, bhikkhus, this bhikkhu is said to dwell in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Teacher's instruction, and in accordance with the sublime states. Therefore, one should understand that the mere practice of the sublime states is not sufficient for the attainment of the goal. One must also cultivate the path consisting of the eight factors. This is because the fourfold teachings are intended to show the way to the cessation of suffering through the cultivation of the eightfold path. Thus, the Blessed One teaches that the fourfold teachings are the means for attaining the cessation of suffering by means of the eightfold path.
