The mere cultivation of compassion and the other [immeasurables] is for the sake of turning away from [suffering],
for non-attachment,
and for tranquility.
It brings about benefit for the sake of dispassion, direct knowledge, right knowledge, and nirvāṇa.
However, rebirth occurs only in the world of Brahmā.
My practice brings about complete detachment from sense objects;
moreover, that practice leads to the abandonment of attachment to sense objects and the cessation of sensory enjoyment.

It serves as an aid in attaining the state of perfect tranquility, in acquiring direct knowledge, in acquiring right knowledge, in attaining nirvana, and especially in relying upon the great eightfold path.
— (Dīghanikāya,
2.352) The mere cultivation of sublime states is sufficient for rebirth in the Brahma-world; however,
that [cultivation] is not capable of effecting either the liberation from defilements or liberation from rebirth.
Even Brahmā and the other gods fall under the sway of suffering, old age, death,

and rebirth (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.104). Only by following the path taught by the Buddha can a person ultimately attain the peace of nirvāṇa and achieve liberation from rebirth, cyclic existence, suffering, and the like.
Nevertheless, all people, being incapable of adopting the instructions of Gotama for the sake of warding off suffering, flee from them;
therein, those people who are incapable are instructed otherwise.
However, the highest goal is not accomplished there;
rather, it is taught by Sāriputta to a brahmin named Dhānañjāni that one must cultivate noble states of being in order to take rebirth in the Brahma-world at some point (Majjhima Nikāya 2.195–96).
Having done exactly that at that very moment, he was reborn in the Brahma-world after death.

Having understood all this through his divine vision, Gotama said to the returned Sāriputta: "Sāriputta, did you not once rise up and abandon the Brahmin Dhānañjāni, who had established himself in the inferior Brahma-world?"
"But what was the matter that he had to accomplish even more?
(Majjhima Nikāya 2.195–96).
Sāriputta explains that he established that brahmin in the Brahmā-world, because the Brahmā-world belongs to the brahmins alone.

The Buddha’s question indicates that a teacher of the Dharma ought never to become complacent for the sake of the welfare of his disciple. The teacher, too, at the appointed time, should gladden the disciple as much as possible;
for in the Brahma-world, the taking of rebirth is considered inferior to the attainment of the inner vision.

If a disciple is zealous for the sake of supreme prosperity, then the primary duty of the teacher is to give closely integrated instruction. When a person endowed with profound inner vision draws forth sublime states of being, [that is the time].
At that time, the aforementioned faults do not persist, because they are drawn away from there toward their respective objects.

Gotama describes that there is a clear distinction between the drawing forth of noble qualities by an ordinary person acting as an agent and the drawing forth of noble qualities by a great teacher who is a wise disciple.
(AN 2.224–29) When an ordinary person cultivates sublime states, then after death he is reborn once again in the Brahma-world.
However, at the end of that residence, he will again take birth as a denizen of hell, or as a hungry ghost afflicted by hunger, or as an animal.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya)

2.129 Except for the Arhat who is liberated from all forms of rebirth, the wise disciple— intent on drawing forth a noble state of being under a great teacher— will be born again in the world of Brahmā after death; however,
through the continuous cultivation of that noble state, he becomes an Arhat there.
When that life has reached its end, he is not born again thereafter; rather, he attains the security arising from immortal nirvana.
Gautama’s compassion and love—
Experiencing joy together with others and maintaining equanimity;
furthermore, Gautama, through the attainment of perfect knowledge, followed the method of the fourfold teachings and continuously cultivated all four types of sublime states.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya, 1.183) It was clear to everyone that the Buddha was skilled in drawing forth all four classes of beings.
In one discourse, the householder Jīvaka Komārabhacca said: "Venerable sir! I have heard that Brahmā dwells in compassion."
"Brahmā alone is fortunate (the Buddha);
I see this clearly.
For, O good sir, the fortunate one (the Buddha)..."
He dwells in compassion. (Majjhima Nikāya, 1.369–70) Because this state remains, the gods belonging to the Brahma-order [attain] compassion.
Having brought about love, the bliss of compassion, and equanimity,
Jīvaka establishes that Gautama is Brahmā.
Because he saw that Gotama was dwelling there out of compassion,
Gotama replied, "Jīvaka,..."
He who was formerly possessed of the defects of longing, aversion, delusion, and pride becomes angry;
for that reason, those defects have been abandoned and severed from their root.
Deprived of their roots and like palm trees, they are destroyed; in future times, they will not be capable of arising again.
Jīvaka, regarding this matter, as for what you have said—
"That is accepted by me" (Majjhimanikāya 1.370).
Thereupon, Jīvaka and Gotama felt affection for one another.
Concerning their shared experience of joy and their state of equanimity, they engaged in mutual reflection.
Gotama informed Jīvaka that, due to the faults of longing, aversion, delusion, and doubt, there may be violence— whether it occurs or not—
as well as dissatisfaction and a state filled with malice (*vihesā*).
Possessing aversion and possessing resentment,
they have gone to destruction.

Thus the Buddha spoke with reverence to Jīvaka regarding how his arising of compassion and other qualities was produced in dependence upon longing, aversion, delusion, and renunciation. In this discourse,
Gotama establishes that anger, violence, discontent, and hatred are the opposites of love and the other [wholesome] states.
In the commentary, this statement of Gotama is explained as follows: "Jīvaka, regarding this matter, what you say may be so— Jīvaka,
the Great Brahmā abandons anger and the like by relinquishing his prideful nature."
He dwells thus with compassion; I abandon those faults through the renunciation that consists of rejection. If that which you say regarding this matter should come to pass.
The meaning of this is: "If this is as previously stated, then I shall accept your word. Jīvaka accepted this proposal.
Thereupon, the fortunate Buddha gave him the aforementioned instruction in detail, concerning the remaining sublime states.
(Brahmā abandons the obstacles to compassion and the other [immeasurables] by means of non-restraint;
however, at the moment of attaining right knowledge, Gotama uprooted all mental defects.)
Thus, at the time of drawing forth compassion and the other [immeasurables], he did not make an effort to subdue those faults because there was no purpose in doing so;
rather, by means of drawing forth the inner vision, they were all completely eliminated.
To cause the inner vision to expand, a person first engages in pure conduct.
And he relies upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Pure conventional practice always serves as the foundation for what is purposeful,
by which one may become free from the remorse arising from unwholesome conduct.
(Visuddhimagga, 4.23) Pure conduct nourishes a mind intent on benefit in the present time, and it also produces a mind intent on benefit in the future time.
(Visuddhimagga,

14.35) Standing right in the midst of a common configuration associated with being beneficial, any person who desires to establish well-prepared states for a concentrated mind ought to do so regarding the forty objects suitable for concentration. (Visuddhimagga, 3.104)
A meditator, following the instructions of his teacher, desires either one or more [objects].
(Visuddhimagga, 3.129) Thereafter, the meditator employs the mind, sharpened by concentration as a tool, in order to enter into the subtle nature of the mind and its objects.
He draws forth the internal vision.
If one who possesses internal vision and practices meditation draws forth the states of concentration belonging to the exalted moods,
then, by virtue of the clarity of his object of practice, he becomes proficient in both objects.
Nevertheless, by unifying both objects together through the form of combined practice, he is able to draw them forth.
In the *Atthakanāgarasutta*, the worldling Dasama asks Ānanda whether there is a single practice taught by the Buddha that accomplishes liberation of mind and destroys harmful influence.

"And from bondage, it brings forth a liberation that cannot be transcended" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.349). Ānanda, having enumerated eleven practices that accomplish the goal, provides the following answer.
In that regard, one instance is as follows: a certain monk, with a mind constantly filled with love, establishes contact with the *bhūtas* residing in one direction,
and likewise with those residing in the second direction.
Together with the spirits situated in the third direction,
together with the spirits situated in the fourth direction,
and likewise above.
Below,
he establishes contact with the people situated on every side;
he constantly and everywhere establishes contact with equal-mindedness toward all beings in the entire universe— with a heart full of compassion.
That mind which is stable,
free from enmity,
and expansive—
It is extensive and immeasurable.
Then he reflects thus: "This liberation of mind in the form of compassion also arises and is desired.
Whatever arises, or whatever is desired, that very thing is impermanent."
That very [attainment] depends upon cessation.
For him, such realization occurs;
being established therein, he accomplishes the destruction of the power that causes harm.
If he performs [the rite] there,
then he effects the destruction of the fivefold fetters belonging to the sequence of lower realms;
thereafter, his rebirth occurs spontaneously in the heavenly world.

Following the method previously described, the meditator first draws out the inner vision by means of one of the exalted states through natural methods. Thereafter, he emerges from this state of meditative absorption;
however, the purity of mind attained during that absorption remains for some time even after the specific state of meditation has ceased.
(Visuddhimagga, 22.111) He abandons the nourishment of the state of loftiness.
At that time, he [sees] whatever nature exists in the reality of things and likewise in the nature of the mind.
For the sake of investigating that [object], he immediately applies his sharp mind;
various functions of the objects of the mind persist,
and likewise, there exist material causes for the construction of the body.
What is the nature of those means?
Or what is the nature of mental activities?
He who perceives the distinction between these two is the practitioner of yoga.
For instance—there exists a certain state of compassion that is suitable for establishing the mind upon living beings as well as for nourishing the mind.
When that state is accomplished, an enthusiasm consisting of bliss arises.
Without inner vision, [it does not arise].
Establishment, nourishment, and the state of blissful enthusiasm— these three mental functions are experienced as inseparable and indivisible states of the mind through the yoga of inner vision,
yet they are perceived individually.
In this manner, such a connection has been made repeatedly in many contexts and in various mental tasks. (Visuddhimagga,
18.3) (Visuddhimagga, 11.112)
In the same way, when the meditator realizes through direct perception that the collection of indivisible entities is constructed from various material causes,
he then acquires purely physical mastery over the locations of mental fixations such as "the living being," "the arm," and "the head."
Therein, one perceives its hard parts or soft parts, its warm parts or cold parts.
That which was previously understood as a collection of indivisible entities is now seen to be constructed through the cognition of unconnected material elements.
An individual existence is constructed from how many real and mental constituent factors?
When those factors are clearly manifest, their common characteristics become apparent.
(Visuddhimagga 10.3)
Then, both the mental and the physical components are perceived individually.
How so? As being subject to change, unstable, and devoid of essence.
In that regard, there is no movement within substances from one moment to the next.
Thus, all those things produce dissatisfaction.
A person of meditative concentration proceeds to directly perceive and realize the objects that must be witnessed daily.
Since even consciousness, though it is being cognized, is subject to destruction,
it is clear from this that when one moment of consciousness has completely dissolved, another moment of consciousness arises.
(Visuddhimagga, 18.13)

Thus, within the existence of individuals, amidst the surrounding environment, and regarding insubstantial objects subject to change, the meditative person— failing to perceive the self as a stable refuge— regards every object of experience as impermanent,
as suffering, and as affliction.
as bursting forth, as an arrow, and as agitation;
By way of being an affliction,
by way of being of a different class,
and by way of being dissolved.
He sees it as empty and as devoid of its own purpose.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya, 2.130)
Thus, by directly perceiving the reality of things through their ninefold nature, the yogi naturally desires liberation. He realizes this liberation upon the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, having transcended all forms of impermanence and change, he attains a concentrated knowledge of whatever state is presently occurring.

In the first [chapter], within the initial series of discourses on the elimination of views, by means of a most acute direct perception of the incorrectness experienced with a concentrated mind, he realizes to what extent his previously well-established view of the world was inverted;
thereafter, through the attainment of Nirvana, he understands the nature of the peace that is the subject at hand.

Having experienced supreme power, he will likewise not be seduced again by the most alluring attractions of earthly sovereignty; for on one hand, the incapacity of all things to provide lasting satisfaction and their impermanence are as clear as can be,
while on the other, [he has realized the truth].
From that very state, the realization of Nirvana becomes clear and free from transgression.

A person who practices meditation should, by means of constant meditative absorption (*samādhi*), necessarily bring their mind to a state of tranquility. Even though one has entered the stream (*srotāpanna*) after transcending the three stages enriched by profound realization, the meditator must always maintain inward vision.
In this way, the nature of the objects of the sensory domains (*gocaravastu*), which produces dissatisfaction, gradually becomes clearer and clearer.
Similarly, the pure, integral nature of *nirvāṇa* constantly moves toward greater clarity.
Through the attainment of the fruit by the Arhat, his inner vision becomes complete.
Being liberated from rebirth, after death he attains the state of nirvāṇa, which is free from death.
By such means,
the collection of noble qualities is designated as the foundation for supreme liberation from the wheel of existence.
Even through mere perception, a yogi who practices the entry into the stream is capable of instructing other people in the path of inner vision.

Fifth Chapter: The Antiquity of the Purāṇas and Their Primitiveness. Regarding the history of the study of Sanskrit learning in modern India, when we entered the present era of the printing press, the minds of scholars as well as lovers of Sanskrit were drawn toward one particular subject among many ancient things.
The very purpose of printing the great texts of Sanskrit literature lies in that very matter itself.
Composed in the Sanskrit language, the Mahābhārata is the greatest book of the land of Bhārata, and its greatness is renowned throughout the entire world.
It is precisely regarding the publication of that work that the pride of the age and of human endeavor is indicated.

From the year 1834 to 1839 CE, the Sanskrit Mahābhārata was published by scholars through the patronage of the institution known as the Asiatic Society in Calcutta. Prior to this, the late Mr. Sir William Jones had introduced Sanskrit for his own sake as well as for the sake of the Western world.
By him, one Sanskrit version of the minor poem titled *Ṛtusaṃhāra* composed by Kālidāsa was brought to light;
by him, an edition of that minor poem titled *Ṛtusaṃhāra* composed by Kālidāsa was published. That *Ṛtusaṃhāra* is a lyrical poem based on descriptive description.
In that regard, there is a description of objects according to ancient Indian tradition.
In the year 1792 CE, he published the *Ṛtusaṃhāra* in Bengali script from Calcutta;
however, after the first edition of the *Mahābhārata*, the interest of the circle of scholars—both within India and abroad—became centered upon the study of Sanskrit learning.
The first edition of the Mahābhārata was not based on critical analysis;
it was prepared simply by following as many manuscripts as were available to the editors.
This is one beautiful edition;

many scholars have fulfilled its intended purpose, yet it has indicated its own true voice. From this, we have obtained a vast and preeminent literary work that demonstrates German scholarship in Sanskrit.
When the German scholar Max Müller, residing in Oxford, first published the Ṛgveda— divided into six volumes and accompanied by Sāyaṇa’s commentary—
in 1849–1870, it was the oldest work [published] in India as well as in the Indo-European world;
this was the first printed edition enriched with critical scholarship.
Not only the manuscripts in his possession, but also with the assistance of numerous living pandits— meaning those Indian scholars who had committed the entirety of the Veda to memory—
the venerable Max Müller strove to establish the pure text of the Veda.
Those pandits served Max Müller for the purpose of correcting the text by means of the manuscripts.
Thereafter,
in fact, a glorious history of Sanskrit publication was commenced by scholars both in India and abroad.
Hemacandra Vidyāratna, a resident of Calcutta, published an edition of the Rāmāyaṇa based on Bengali manuscripts.
The Italian scholar Gaspare Gorresio (1843–1850) produced the first critical edition of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, accompanied by an Italian translation, from the city of Paris.
This was his period of activity both within India and outside of India.

For the sake of attaining the highest excellence in publication, scholars have exerted great effort; for that purpose, several publishing houses have been established, such as the publishing institution founded by Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara in Calcutta,
and the Caukhambā Saṃskṛta Mālā established by Haridās Gupta in Vārāṇasī.
The Nirṇayasāgara Press, operated by Tukārām Javajī, in the city of Bombay; the Ānandāśrama Press, located in Pune; and the Vāṇīvilāsa Press, situated at Śrīraṅgam.
And thus, many renowned publishing houses have emerged throughout the whole of India;
consequently, the Asiatic Society and other institutions have also undertaken such work.
For instance, through the Asiatic Society, there is the Bibliotheca Indica series, along with its associated Sanskrit publications.
Edited by T.R.S.
Ayyangar, Madras E.I.
Yajurveda Research Society, Publication Department of the University of Madras.
Generally throughout India, there are institutions affiliated with universities, scholarly societies where research and editorial work are conducted,
as well as publishing houses for Sanskrit texts.
These literary forms are joined for the dissemination of the excellence of Sanskrit. The vastness of Sanskrit literature indicates a sense of wonder;
one of its most noteworthy characteristics is contained within the Purāṇas and Upapurāṇas.
After the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*,

their arrival occurred once again in the year 1918 CE. At that time, the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune undertook the effort to publish a critical edition of the *Mahābhārata* under the inspiration of the venerable Rāmakṛṣṇa Gopāl Bhaṇḍārkar.
This work was a great and unprecedented undertaking in the field of Sanskrit, and likewise the very first of its kind in India.
The responsibility for this project was entrusted to the hands of Dr. B.S. Sukthankar, one of the foremost Sanskrit scholars of modern India.
For the purpose of editing the ancient text, he established several principles which have been universally accepted by the scholarly world for their soundness and accuracy.
During his tenure and under his guidance, the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute has brought to light a unique and critically analyzed edition of the Mahābhārata—
an unprecedented demonstration of Indian scholarly excellence— in which modern literary criticism is harmonized with ancient Sanskrit learning and textual philology.
All the manuscripts that existed within India as well as those outside of India were collected.
Furthermore, the incidental literature obtained from countries such as Śyāmājābha outside of India, which contains variant readings of the Mahābhārata, was also secured through our requests.
Consequently, the Great Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata was adopted as a model;
this standard was subsequently accepted by other universities and institutions.

Furthermore, even apart from other editions of the Rāmāyaṇa, a critical edition of Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa—based on the textual tradition of the Mahābhārata—was produced by the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute.
It was accepted.
Gujarat University, situated in Ahmedabad, undertook the task of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
Indeed, the Purāṇa is the very face of Indian culture.

A person desiring to know the Bhārata seeks assistance or utility from the Purāṇas. Since ancient times, the civilization and culture endorsed by the Purāṇas, as well as the Paurāṇika Dharma, [have been central].
The Puranic vision and the Puranic faith have been faithfully welcomed and accepted throughout all directions of the earth;
therefore, the very dynamism inherent in the existence of the Purāṇas has become self-evident truth.

The modern Indian society, too, is able to regulate itself based upon the Purāṇas. In fact, the corpus of Purāṇas is the continuous cause and the source of inspiration for the intellectual progress of the land of Bhārata.
Although modern research demonstrates that the existing Purāṇas, which consist of very small collections, are logically established as being of ancient origin.
Nevertheless, the origin of the Purāṇic literature must belong to the very era of the composition of the Vedic Saṃhitās.
The oldest mention of the Purāṇa is observed in two hymns of the Atharvaveda,
where it is stated that one of them possesses a sacred value equal to that of the Ṛgveda verses.
The Purāṇas are always mentioned as being of the same nature as the Sāmans, the Chandas, and the Yajus.
They are recorded alongside Itihāsa in one of the two fields [of literature].
In many works of Vedic literature, the Purāṇa is mentioned either separately or together with Itihāsa.
For instance— in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,
the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad—
In the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,
and the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
In the *Sāṃkhyāyana-Śrautasūtra*, the *Āśvalāyana-Gṛhyasūtra*, and other such works;
moreover, the acceptance of the Purāṇa is established even in other ancient and sacred texts.
For example— in the Āpastamba-dharmasūtra, the Gautama-dharmasūtra, the Vyāsa-saṃhitā, and the Uśanas-saṃhitā.
In the *Manusmṛti*,
in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*,
and in the *Śabarabhāṣya*.
In the Śāṅkarabhāṣya, the Vātsyāyanabhāṣya, the Tantravārttika, and so forth.
According to the *Nirukta* composed by Yāska,
even the *Ṛgveda* mentions a mantra that is "mixed with history" (*itihāsa-miśra*), which is further subsumed within three categories of the Veda.
In his view, that which was ancient and yet becomes new is precisely what constitutes a *purāṇa*.
In the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, Pāṇini states that what existed in a former age (*prācīna-yuga*) is called *purāṇa* or *purātana*.
According to the view of the *Vāyupurāṇa*, it is called *purāṇa* because it was lived in ancient times (*purātaneṣu divaseṣu*).
The *Padmapurāṇa* perceives another, distinct meaning for the term *purāṇa*.
The very same ancient readings that relate certain interconnected narratives constitute the Purāṇa;

"it was thus in ancient times, and therefore it is called a Purāṇa"—this is the view of the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*. Thus, when the defining characteristics of a Purāṇa have been analyzed, one subject becomes clear.
Everywhere, the Purāṇas are accompanied by ancient commentaries. There is no doubt whatsoever regarding the antiquity of these Purāṇas and their sacred textual readings.
In this context, the connection of this term with the word ‘itihāsa’ must indeed be considered.

The term *itihāsa* is observed to be used repeatedly in the *Atharvaveda-saṃhitā* as well as in various *Brāhmaṇas*. Its meaning is: "This has certainly happened; it was thus, or it was so"—this is how it appeared.
Thus, it seems that *itihāsa* likely indicates an account of events that actually occurred in the past.
For this very reason, it is inferred that the two terms *purāṇa* and *itihāsa* do not denote the same meaning.
Furthermore, their distinctiveness and their respective spheres of activity may also be separate.
According to Yāska’s view, the story of Devāpi and Śantanu possesses the nature of *itihāsa*.
The story of Sudās Vaiśvāmitra, whose priest was Paijavana, also enters the category of *itihāsa*. Thus,
although *itihāsa* and *purāṇa* are most closely connected with one another,
nevertheless, the imaginative element within the *purāṇas* is not entirely devoid of significance.
However, its scope in history is limited;
nevertheless, the distinction between the two is neither clear nor simple.
Consequently, one such similar reading accepts itself as being ancient.
Furthermore, in other instances, this text is accepted as *itihāsa*.
The *Mahābhārata*, whether accepted as *itihāsa* or as the supreme *itihāsa*, does not relinquish its own identity as a compendium of the term *purāṇa*.
Indeed, the *Vāyupurāṇa* is one among the eighteen great *purāṇas*.
This is accepted as a venerable Purāṇa;
however, a specific verse is seen in that Vāyu Purāṇa which states: "A person reading this history (itihāsa) shall obtain great renown."
"Even his livelihood shall be endowed with righteousness"—
such [a teaching] has also been proclaimed with faith in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
This is simultaneously a Purāṇa as well as an Itihāsa.
For this very reason, out of fear of prolixity, it is said that the line of demarcation between the Purāṇa and the Itihāsa is not always easy to discern.
Kauṭilya considers the Purāṇa to include a portion of the Itihāsa;
in his view, both ancient narratives and descriptions reside within the Purāṇa.

The *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra* are situated within the *Itihāsa*. Furthermore, no distinct status is established for the *Purāṇa* apart from the *Atharvaveda* and certain *Purāṇas* themselves.
Accordingly, in the description of the earth, the *Atharvaveda* employs the term *purāṇa*.
However, the use of the term *itihāsa* is observed in that Veda regarding the subject of following the vows (*vrata*).
In his commentary on the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, Śaṅkarācārya strove to clearly indicate the distinction between the two;
in his view, the story of both Urvaśī and Purūravas is found in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*.
This story is contained within the Purāṇas;
however, the nature of the world is inherently Purāṇic— in that it is said that prior to creation there was non-existence (*asat*),
and from that non-existence the world gradually manifests.
Thus, in fact, Śaṅkarācārya himself was the first to attempt to clearly demonstrate the distinction between these two terms;
however, his view was not accepted by everyone.
The great Vedic scholar Sāyaṇācārya offered a rebuttal to this.
In his view, that which is the opposite of this is the truth.

The story of Urvaśī and Purūravas found in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa indicates a primordial nature, as it reveals something of the most ancient period. At the beginning of creation, there was only water.

The statement that "everything was composed of water" certainly demonstrates the historical nature of this creation. Thus, when there is such a divergence between the mutually contradictory views of two renowned scholars, it serves as the sole proof for the view that it is better to simply efface the line of distinction between the Purāṇas and the Itihāsas.

The condensed definition of the Purāṇa— consisting of five characteristics, namely primary creation (sarga), secondary creation (pratisarga), genealogy (vaṃśa), the periods of the Manvantaras (manvantara), and the history of dynasties (vaṃśānucarita)— as well as the duration of the Yugas, has been specified for the Purāṇa; however,
this [definition] is not to be applied to the field of the Purāṇas, even though the definition of a Purāṇa is explained in various Purāṇas.
And so,
that is firmly established in the *Amarakośa*.
Furthermore, even without the five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*), diverse subjects are generally seen in almost all the Purāṇas.
For instance: the leading of deities,
sacred places,

The significance of various types of gifts, as well as extensive geographical descriptions and the like,

Nevertheless, even this is not to be established as definitive.
In his *Kāvyamīmāṃsā*, Rājaśekhara states that there are two types of historical narrative (*itihāsa*):

one is recognized as *parikriyā*, wherein there is only a single protagonist; the other, by means of the creative imagination of ancient times (*purākalpa*), is that in which there are many protagonists.
Thus, in his view, the *Rāmāyaṇa* falls under the category of *parikriyā* (artificial composition),

Clearly, in Rājaśekhara’s opinion, the scope of history (*itihāsa*) is restricted not even by a single drop [of ink].
Apart from the five characteristics of a Purāṇa, another definition of a Purāṇa is seen twice in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and once in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.

Visarga means enclosure, protection, and interval.
The lineage,
the history of the lineage,

The cause and the basis [of this study] are as follows:

The first characteristic is recognized as "creation" (sarga).
The meaning of creation is "emanation" (sṛṣṭi).
When the equilibrium of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas within primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) is disturbed, the threefold state of ego (ahaṃkāra) arises.
From that, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and the five gross elements (bhūtas) arise;
this sequence of creation is indeed *sarga*.
For *visarga* is the creation of the world of living beings (*jīvajagat*).
Just as a second seed is produced from a single seed, so too one living being is born from another.
Brahmā alone is the creator of the universe;
by the grace of the Supreme Lord, he sustains the entire power transmitted for creation.
For subsistence (vṛtti) indeed consists of matter heavy with weight, by means of which the living being sustains its vital essence; therefore,
what portion of this world perceivable by sight remains dependent upon subsistence?
A person takes up items such as food, wheat, milk, and fruits for the purpose of sustaining life;
furthermore, certain items are taken up by him for the sake of observing scriptural injunctions.
Protection of the Purāṇa is the fourth distinctive feature.
For the protection of the virtuous and likewise for the destruction of the wicked, the Lord assumes many forms in various ages and places;
He protects those who believe in Him and brings about the destruction of those who do not.
However, this is generally the common practice of God.
For the primary intention of God is speech characterized by play (*līlā*).
A person, following God’s holy play and thus chanting and remembering God, is able to attain liberation.

Among the five characteristics of a Mahāpurāṇa, that which is called a *manvantara* is precisely this interval. According to the calculation in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, one *manvantara* consists of 30,672,000 years.
There are fourteen *manvantaras*.
Each *manvantara* exists presided over by a specific *manu*.
Generally, all the *purāṇas* maintain consensus regarding the names and the titles of the fourteen *manus*. They are as follows: Svāyambhuva, ... [and so on].
Svārociṣa,
Uttama, and Tāmasa.
Raivata,
Cākṣuṣa, and Vaivasvata.

Devasāvarṇi and Indrasāvarṇi;
these are the five Manus.
Seven thousand years, a divine year, and an Indra-year— this is the measure of these Manvantaras.
The lineage is the distinguishing feature of the later Purāṇas.
All lineages of kings were created by Brahmā;
this sequential account provides a description of these kings spanning the three periods of time.

Therefore, the *Vaṃśānucarita* (the account of the descendants) follows next.
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa examines that which is "the genealogical history of those [kings], their deeds, and those who uphold the lineage.
How many principal kings adorn this cycle?
Their glorious achievements are described here in detail.

In reality, the accounts of kings of meritorious fame are undoubtedly worthy of remembrance for the emergence of idealistic discourse;
however, in this context, the spiritual greatness of the great seers never diminishes in value.
The life stories of Yudhiṣṭhira, Hariścandra, Janaka, and others undoubtedly provide divine inspiration;
however, at that time, the few exemplary deeds of Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Vaśiṣṭha, and others undoubtedly accomplish many tasks for people.
Indeed, the eighth characteristic is designated as "institution" (saṃsthā).
This bears a resemblance to the *pratisarga* (secondary creation) of the five-lakṣaṇa *Purāṇa*.
Nevertheless, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, at the place where *pratisarga* occurs, the term *pratisaṃhāra* (re-absorption) is employed.
This *saṃsthā* indicates the complete destruction of the world.
This is described in detail according to each respective eon (*kalpa*). The name of the current eon is the Śvetavarāha-kalpa;
it consists of 432,000 years.

According to the specific calculations of the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, it is known that the entire universe will undergo complete destruction after 2,347,050,947 years. Beyond this, the cause alone remains as the sole characteristic;
this cause always points toward the living beings who are the causes of creation.
These living beings accomplish various actions through ignorance or delusion,
and these lead to another creation in the end. In reality, the destiny of these living beings is the fundamental cause of both the creation and the destruction of the universe.
For this very reason, those two alone are accepted as the cause and likewise as the fundamental cause (*mūlakāraṇa*).

The final distinction is understood as *apāśraya* or *āśraya*. That reality, or that totality, which brings about manifestation, creation, or destruction, is precisely what is indicated by the term *apāśraya*.
This very one—whether Brahmā or the Supreme Self—is the sole entity to be meditated upon alone.
All nine specific characteristics serve to nourish the tenth.
Following the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, these nine specific characteristics are examined in detail for the sake of refining the definition of the tenth.
Elsewhere, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa provides a list of its ten characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Those ten characteristics are as follows: creation (*sarga*), secondary creation (*visarga*), and so forth.
Abiding, nourishment, and protection.
The Manvantaras, the narrations of the Lord, the dissolution, liberation, and the refuge.
Thus it comes to pass that what is called the third,
fourth,

*Nourishment* (*poṣaṇam*, *ūtiḥ*).
The *manvantara* found in the second column is identical to the *antara* found in the first column.

There is no difference whatsoever between the dependent and the support. The first type of arrangement mentioned is fourfold;
namely, the occasional (naimittikī).

In this [work], the numbers of people, their practices, and their conducts are encompassed.

thus it is understood that the Bhāgavata Purāṇa fosters a clear conception of the subjects found within the Purāṇas,

However, the authors of the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*) foster divergent opinions in detail regarding this subject related to the Purāṇas. In this regard, Dharma carries extreme significance as the defining characteristic of the Purāṇas, which are full of weightiness. Certainly, here, beyond the literal exposition, the contemplation of Dharma has been grasped. Beyond the recitation of the various mantras, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa appropriately bestows mental application upon Dharma.
This claim that the *manvantaras* constitute the True Dharma (*saddharma*) applies only to one who clearly accepts the utility and gravity of the Dharma.
Therefore, this conclusion is not tenable: that previously the Dharma was not included within the consideration of the Purāṇas.
And thus, its preservation has come down solely through later ages.
In this way, in many ancient texts, there was not merely an attempt to define the characteristics of a Purāṇa,

In reality, [this applies] to the Veda and the Purāṇa, and to the Dharmaśāstra and the Purāṇa.

At that time, how many wise men again experience the unity of those two? (Compare Vātsyāyana’s Nyāyabhāṣya:
"The subject matter of Itihāsa and Purāṇa is worldly conduct.")
Setting aside this speculation, we observe that while there is scope for imagination in the Purāṇas, history abounds in actual events.
Regarding antiquity in the Purāṇas, we have mentioned several accepted ancient texts here; among them, the Purāṇa is accepted as a limited or delimited class of literature.
Among these ancient scriptures, the Atharvaveda Saṃhitā is exceedingly weighty.
In it there is a mantra whose purport is: "From the remnant (ucchiṣṭa) is born the Purāṇa, by means of the Ṛgveda and the Sāmaveda..."
And together with the Yajurveda,
the word *ucchiṣṭa* indicates the remnants of the sacrifice;
however, Sāyaṇa’s commentary attracts the mind with its diligent application of effort.
He says that at the end of all beings and their material constituents, what remains—the residue—is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
That is to say, when everything goes to destruction, only the Supreme Self remains;

In this way, the Purāṇas, like the Vedas, are not of human origin.
They are neither the products of creation nor the compilations of any mortal being.
Elsewhere, the Arthaveda describes it thus: "In the observation of the present world, no person is able to know the existence of a previous kalpa without a seer of truth."

Thus, it appears clearly that at the time of the Atharvaveda, the Purāṇas as well as the Paurāṇikas did not remain in the darkness of unfamiliarity; they had a powerful foothold in society.
Furthermore, the Atharvaveda Saṃhitā describes this in the context of the Vrātyastoma: "Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and Gāthā..."
The Nārāśaṃsīs follow this;
he who has become thoroughly acquainted with them in detail is indeed [the master] of Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
"Of the *gāthās* and the *nārāśaṃsīs*, it becomes a beloved abode.
In this context, it should be remembered that this distinguished mantra is included within the *vātyastoma* festival.
The eternal Supreme Self is revealed by the term *vrātya*.
The *Paippalāda-saṃhitā* states:
"In the beginning, the *vrātya* was the Veda."
It is certainly accepted that in the manifestation of the universe, the *vrātya* stood at the forefront of all;
he indeed attains oneness and equality with the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*).
We also observe in the *Rudrādhyāyas*: "Obeisance to the *vrātya*."
It is also indicated that the Vrātya and Rudra are non-different; thus,
it is stated according to the truth that the Itihāsa and Purāṇa are the Ṛgveda and the Sāmaveda.
Like the Yajurveda, it possesses an ancient character marked by faith;
following the Saṃhitā, the Brāhmaṇa comes forth.
At four points, the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa mentions the Itihāsa-Purāṇa, or rather, the Purāṇas.
In the first three instances, *itihāsa* and *purāṇa* do not appear as distinct entities;
those two are inseparable.
However, in the remaining example, the seer endeavors to establish a distinction between the two terms.
This description, together with the account of the *pariplava*,
makes it known to us that on the eighth night there occurs a recitation of the *itihāsas*,
and on the ninth, a reading of the *purāṇas*.
In this way, even in the age of the Brahmins, the two terms *itihāsa* and *purāṇa* existed as distinct entities and yet remained joined together simultaneously.
The first example is observed in the context of the *brahmayajña*:
the recitation of various Vedas produces various fruits.
If it be instruction, knowledge, or sacred dialogue,
Itihāsa, Purāṇa,
Gāthā, and Nārāśaṃsī are recited by certain people with the conviction that the fruit of the Madhu sacrifice is thereby obtained.
In a subsequent illustration, it is mentioned that a certain learned man should recite the Veda every day according to the instruction.
by means of sacred knowledge,
by means of dialogues, and by means of history;
Together with the Purāṇa, the Gāthā, and the Nārāśaṃsī.
If he performs this daily, then he gives complete satisfaction to the entire assembly as well as to God; regarding that Brahmin, it is said elsewhere: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda...
The Atharvaveda, history, the Purāṇas, and science.
Upaniṣad, verse, aphorism,
The Vyākhyāna and Anuvyākhyāna, along with all the Vedas, are interconnected;
any person who masters them attains universal sovereignty and supreme power.
The significance of the fourth illustration is shown here in the middle.
And thus, in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa*, the authority and greatness of the Purāṇas are acknowledged.
It is stated therein: "In this way, all these Vedas have been composed together with the Kalpas, the Rahasyas, the Brāhmaṇas, the Upaniṣads, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas.

The Piśāca Veda, the Asura Veda, the Itihāsa Veda, and the Purāṇa Veda.

In the north, the Itihāsa-veda was created, and above and below, the Purāṇa-veda was fashioned. In this context, the five great utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis)— bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, janaḥ, and mahaḥ— are mentioned.
Greater than the five Vedas, he is the ancient,
the secret, and the great.
The phrase "and that" refers to the five great sayings (mahāvākyas) which have arisen.
Thus, here a similar standard and arrangement of words is provided as in the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
It is analyzed how the Purāṇas and the Itihāsas possess both antiquity and sanctity.

In the *Jaiminīyopaniṣad* and also in its *Brāhmaṇa*, testimony from the Purāṇas is accepted as being of the highest authority in five instances (3/4/1–2, 7/1/2, 7/1/4, 7/1/1, and 7/7/1). The final portion of the *Brāhmaṇas* is recognized as both *Āraṇyaka* and *Itihāsa*.
In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, the word *purāṇa* is repeatedly employed in connection with the *brahmayajña*.

If we examine the usage and the intended meaning of the term *purāṇa* as it occurs in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, we see that the Purāṇas are accorded the same reverence as the Vedas themselves.
The value and authority of the Purāṇas remain equal to those of the Vedas;
for since there is no need for laborious effort to liberate one whose breath is obstructed,
it is said by their very nature that the source of both the Vedas and the Purāṇas is self-acting and self-manifesting.

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad endeavors to simplify this subject through one beautiful illustration. Thus it says: "Just as from a fire of wet fuel, when not yet kindled, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, these—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa—are the breath of this great Being."
This statement is supported by several citations from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, as follows:
"O Venerable Sir, I study the Ṛgveda;
the Yajurveda; the Sāmaveda; the Atharvaṇa as the fourth; and the Itihāsa-purāṇa as the fifth."
"I know the Vedas, the collection of ancestral rites (*pitrya-rāśi*)... this, O Venerable One, I study.
"The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth—this is the Veda of the Vedas.
In fact, elsewhere in this very Upaniṣad, it is seen that the Itihāsa-Purāṇa is recognized as the fifth Veda.
And to him is granted the supreme state of purity.
Thus it is clearly evident that the Purāṇas are indeed the accounts of the creative acts of such an ancient age;
and these do not merely explain various principles of conduct, but—
Rather, by adopting the specific characteristics thus described, they repeatedly draw forth praise from the people.
Regarding the literature of the Sūtras, the antiquity and age of the Purāṇas are indicated again and again.
In the Sāṃkhyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, the Purāṇa is accepted as the fifth Veda.
And likewise, the same authority that is accorded to the Āraṇyakas and the Upaniṣads is granted to the Purāṇas.
In the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra, there are numerous references related to the Purāṇas.
In several fields, the study of history and the Purāṇas was prescribed alongside the study of the Vedas.
In one place it is said:
those wise ones who have experienced the savor of the scriptures, as well as the histories and the Purāṇas, become immersed in the ocean of nectar together with the gods and the ancestors.
In that same Sūtra, in another context concerning the blazing of a sacrificial fire, this is described:
whenever there is the employment of Itihāsa and Purāṇa in the sacred rites of the gods and men, that occasion is endowed with auspicious characteristics.
However, this must necessarily be admitted: the description regarding the Purāṇas found in the Śrauta-sūtras does not refer to any specific Purāṇa or a collection of verses from a Purāṇa.
Or rather, he delineates it with particularity. In this regard, the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* occupies a unique position and holds a significant place;
from among the ancient texts extant at that time, two clear verses have been extracted by its author.
This citation praises the path of renunciation for yogins and avoids action performed with desire.
Regarding this, it is said: "The eighty-eight thousand seers who desired offspring..."
Along the path of Aryaman to the south, they have taken their place among the cremation grounds.
The eighty-eight thousand seers who led their progeny followed the northern path of Aryaman; indeed, they attained immortality.
Thus it is said.
In the commentary composed upon the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad, Śaṅkarācārya cited the two aforementioned verses.
These two verses are found in the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa,
as well as in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Padmapurāṇa.
Thus, in the Purāṇas, the origin of those two is beyond questioning;
Āpastamba recited the Purāṇas and understood two verses.
And he employed [these sources] in his own work according to his own objectives,
namely the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
The question of whether or not he had acquaintance with the *Padmapurāṇa* along with all other Purāṇas is unreal.
However, Āpastamba acknowledged his debt to the Purāṇas—those which attained prominence before him—a matter that will be discussed in the conclusion.
Furthermore, we observe elsewhere in that *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*, in the context of the ancestors who have ascended to heaven:
That which they conquered as heaven, wherein they dwelt until the destruction of the universe;
and furthermore, at the commencement of the work of creation before it had reached completion, they assumed the state of being the foundation and the cause of heaven.
This message is obtained by us from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
The mention of the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* and others requires careful consideration. By that time, the existence of the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* was accepted and acknowledged;
Āpastamba certainly studied and utilized the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
Although it is true that this verse is not found in the currently extant *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, nevertheless, one should not question its authority;
for many verses have been cited under this very name in various different scriptures.
They are not seen [in the extant texts].
What does this indicate? That all the authors of the treatises (*śāstrakāra*) themselves have fallen into error?
And thus, we observe even in the *Gautama-dharmasūtra* that the term "itihāsa-purāṇa" or the term "purāṇa" alone is mentioned as a complete work in two distinct fields.
In the first chapter, Gautama attempts to explain the meaning of the term "bahuśruta.
According to the etymological derivation of this word, it refers to that person by whom much has been heard and likewise known;
in Gautama’s view, only such a person is considered *bahuśruta*.
He thoroughly understands the customs and renown of people;
he knows the Vedas along with the six auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*),
and he acquires proficiency in dialogues, histories, and the Purāṇas.
Thus, for the sake of the proficiency of one who is well-versed, there is a need for skill in both history (*itihāsa*) and the Purāṇas.
Elsewhere, Gautama maintains that the legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) of kings among their subjects is found in the Vedas.
In the treatises on Dharma, in the auxiliary sciences, and in the Upavedas.

And regarding the remaining Purāṇas, he should be instructed with scholarly expertise. Here too, we observe that due respect has been accorded to the Purāṇas accordingly. Gautama states clearly that a king who is ignorant of all these scriptures is useless.
It never attains fulfillment.
Thus it is seen that even the Dharmaśāstras acknowledge the authority of the Purāṇas.
Like all other ancient texts, the works written upon the Arthaśāstra likewise accord due recognition to the Purāṇas.
Among all treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), Kauṭilya’s *Arthaśāstra* is the most renowned. Kauṭilya himself acknowledged the authority of the Purāṇas;
for we observe that he employed the term "Purāṇa" in numerous instances within his *Arthaśāstra* as a specialized designation.

When a certain king abandons the path of established duty and resorts to a wicked course, then ministers who desire his welfare should restrain that king from the path of evil by demonstrating examples from history and the Purāṇas. The two relevant verses are cited below.

Kautilya has stated: "One who knows the science of polity (arthaśāstra), relying on those dear to him, should instruct a king who is being constrained by his principal ministers by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
Thus.

For this very reason, certain Purāṇas dating back to the time of Kauṭilya, which concern matters of virtuous conduct, customs, and traditions, appear beneficial to kings as well, just as they serve the needs of ordinary people by providing them with their respective subjects and contents. Elsewhere it is observed that the recitation of Purāṇas constitutes a specific commencement for the daily ritual schedule.
Kautilya declares that during the first half of the day, the king should study recitations concerning the treatises on elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the Purāṇas;

While the word *purāṇa* is sometimes used in the sense of "ancient" and sometimes in the sense of "old"— just as the *Mahābhārata* is not repeatedly qualified by the term *purāṇa* in the same way as the *Rāmāyaṇa*—

The antiquity of the *purāṇa* literature is attested by numerous Buddhist and Jaina texts.

the existence of Purāṇic literature at that time is established.

The method of indifference toward worldly phenomena (dharmanirpekṣavidhi),
the systems of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, and Vaiśeṣika,
and mathematics (gaṇita).
Song, the nature of medicine, the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas—

by the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda;

This must be stated: in one of two places, the word *purāṇa* is used in the plural within a particular context.
The intention here is this: that term points to a branch of knowledge (*vidyā-śākhā*).
Thus, it indicates the existence of more than one Purāṇa at that time.
The Buddhists were not the only scribes;
the Jains likewise composed numerous literary works by emulating and following the model of the Sanskrit Purāṇas,
among these authors being one particularly ancient Jain monk named Vimalasūri.
In the first century of the Christian era, he composed the *Paumacariya*.
In more than one instance, he referred to this work as a *purāṇa*.
Another Jaina author named Raviṣeṇa wrote the *Padmapurāṇa* in the Sanskrit language in the year 678 CE.

The *Uttarapurāṇa* was composed by Guṇabhadra in the ninth century CE. From the titles of these works and from the nature of the subjects treated within them, it is clear that even from the time of the Christian era, Jains possessed an understanding of the five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*) of the Sanskrit Purāṇas.
Thus, all the facts we have gathered regarding the nature and antiquity of the Purāṇic literature compared with Vedic and other literatures have been presented.
Having examined these sources, it is seen that the Purāṇic literature had already come into existence several years before the birth of Christ.
And thus, even in that ancient time, there existed more than one Purāṇa. In fact, the popularity and authority of the Purāṇas were not such as to pervade every day or every month.
Nor is the scope of the Purāṇas limited to a single year;
rather, their scope extends over many years, by which they have established a lasting influence within the minds of people for generations.
Even slowly, the Purāṇas have firmly attracted the populace.

Narratives concerning the life stories of sages, kings, and others; edifying tales (upākhyāna) connected with the creation and destruction of the universe that captivate the mind; and a geographical description of the various regions of the world.
The various measurements and divisions concerning the duration of the *samayas*,
the determination of the time spans of the various *yugas*,
as well as the vision of *dharma* and other such topics— all these subjects presented in the pages of the Purāṇas captivated the hearts of people.
Therefore, it is well said that the Purāṇic literature is indeed self-revealing; though ancient, it is ever-new—an invaluable treasure of ancient India.

Although there is a certain ritualistic dimension not only to Hinduism but to all religions, nevertheless, when applied to its primary purpose, religion is in fact directly and consciously in conflict with the world of values;
for most ritualistic activities are essentially meaningless.
These indirect paths, for the sake of determining the magnitude of fundamental values, reflect the culture of a particular region within its own specific dharma;
there is no exception even regarding Indian culture. Each and every civilization possesses its own unique center of transformation.
For instance— ancient Greece was devoted to the arts,
and Rome to politics.

When a comparison is made between these two aforementioned civilizations and Indian civilization, it is observed that a civilization established upon secularism (dharmanirapekṣatā) tends toward forgetfulness.
However, Indian civilization stands firm and fearless even amidst a hostile environment turbulent with the storms of religious and political ideologies;
the reason for this is that its foundation is not established upon the shifting sands of a false secularism,
but rather—
It was composed by ancient philosophers as well as ethical value-knowers;
therein, from time to time, many spiritual leaders appeared in due succession.
They were indeed the true carriers of civilization—in that civilization where the integration of sweetness and truth was accomplished.
Sweetness itself reveals universal love and kindles the light of truth— that light being spiritual awakening—
and its practice is not intended merely for a particular caste or a specific tradition, but for all humanity.
Their speech and instruction are not employed merely at specific times or in specific places, but rather throughout the entire world and throughout all time;

Thus he practices a particular form of the principle of exchange: where Vedic priests, having invoked a certain deity or several deities at a sacrifice, worship them and desire abundant wealth in exchange from that deity or from those deities.
Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that within those worldly and self-interested activities, there existed a certain profound principle.

Indeed, that which was manifested spontaneously in the common rules of truthful conduct is the very principle of *satya* or *ṛta*. This ethical practice, seen in ancient *dharma*, assumed a specific form in later times; having transcended the era of great epics and Purāṇas, it evolved into a designated social ideal.
The discernment between virtues and faults, as well as merits and demerits, generally rests upon this mirror;
transgression of it entails grave sin,
and deliberation follows accordingly.
In general,
there is an acceptance of those duties prescribed by the system of ethical obligation;
those duties, along with one's caste, [are to be fulfilled].
These are intertwined with the cycle of life;
even apart from these,
there are certain duties that must be performed by everyone in the world.
Society is formed by including all kinds of people engaged in reciprocal activities;
it is not merely a gathering of those who share the same birth, the same occupation, or the same mental disposition.
Therefore, it is a gathering of people from all traditions who share the same occupations and the same mental dispositions.
For this very reason, certain rules must necessarily remain in force for all traditions or for all castes.
These rules indeed serve the purpose of the prosperity of the social vehicle;
among them are certain supreme functions which desire some form of conduct from everyone.
Thus, there is assistance for the sake of others,
service to guests,
and the tending of domestic animals.

The offering of oblations to the ancestors (pitṛ-hutidāna) and other such duties were necessarily to be performed by all. And thus, there was the imposition of constraints upon living beings, as well as the forcible and unjust seizure of the property of others.
Such activities as these are to be censured;
however, providing assistance to those in distress and showing respect to elders and the like are duties that constitute the fundamental causes for the existence of society.
For this very reason, such a practice must indeed be observed by everyone in the world:
namely, purity regarding sexual relations,
and marriage to a woman only once.
These subjects concerning the observance of marriage rites are analyzed as being useful both for individual happiness and for the establishment of social unity.
Furthermore, there is a need for certain subjects for the sake of moral purity;
for example, self-control (*jitendriyatā*).
The practice of purity through speech, thought, and action;
hospitality, generosity, and compassion.
Forbearance and endurance are the fundamental virtues;
these subjects have been accepted with conscious awareness since the Vedic age.
By way of an indirect method,
these states have become more clearly manifest through contact with the contemplation of other doctrines.
By "other doctrines," it is indicated that the Buddhist doctrine and the Jaina doctrine are meant.

Between those two principles, it was *mānavatā* (humanity) that established a distinctiveness characterized by a commitment to the duties of a *brāhmaṇa*. This ethic brought about a subtle transformation in ritual practices toward those who were merciless.
For this reason, it is observed that in the Puranic age, Hinduism was, for the most part, transformed.
The treasury officials (*koṣādhyakṣas*) of the Jātīya-dharma were primarily occupied with the ranks of those who live by their intellect (*buddhijīvī*), as appointed by Brahmā.

rather, drawing strength from Buddhism and Jainism, they made the Hindu religion most powerful.
Thus, narratives such as the greatness of the gift of self-sacrifice, like signals of light, pervaded age after age, casting a flood of illumination upon the path of Hindu practice.
Describing the rules for domestic life, the *varṇāśrama-dharma* bestowed gravity upon various duties;
for instance, faith toward one's teachers (*guru*).
Providing assistance to the weak,
the spreading of generosity,
and the planting of trees.
The construction of royal roads,
the digging of wells,
and the excavation of lotus ponds.
The giving of food, shelter, service, and so forth,
to those who have fallen into misfortune and to living beings.
Service to the sick and to those who are incapable;
herein lies the question concerning compassion.
Having stated this analysis, an effort is made to provide proof for its truth: that Hinduism is fundamentally a religion of compassion.
A compassionate disposition cannot have entered [Hinduism] only last night;
therefore, if we seek to observe a compassionate spirit within the Purāṇas, [we shall find it].
Thus we see that this phenomenon has emerged progressively from the very earliest stages.
For compassion is the fundamental truth of any dharma;
otherwise, a dharma devoid of compassion can never survive the test of time.
The light of compassion removes the obscurity from legends and ancient accounts that have become disjointed;
that compassion shines forth spontaneously before the eye of the observer and diffuses beauty among those who appreciate beauty.

And thus he establishes that the Hindu religion is, above all, eternal, great, and sublime. While the Purāṇas are designated as belonging to the domain of religious ritual (*kalpa*), they also contain subjects independent of religious duty;
nevertheless, their status does not fall below that of the Vedas.
If the Vedas are the primary ornaments for the high-born,
