Etymologically, the word *purāṇa* indicates an ancient narrative (*ākhyāna*).
This word also indicates a specific literary tradition—
that literature which was preserved in verses and narratives throughout every age.
These verses, narratives, and tales occupied a prominent place within the extensive body of literature.

Within that literature, the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas as well as the eighteen Upapurāṇas became included. It is noteworthy that, regardless of when the compilation of the Purāṇas actually took place, the individual narratives contained within them likely originated at the very dawn of the Vedic age.
An account that deals with ethical matters— even without being based on a religious, social, or political doctrine— illuminates the moral code of its time.
That question will be discussed further below.

Merit (*puṇya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are the primary subject matters of Vedic literature; therein, secular subjects are generally merely incidental. Such a subject pertains solely to the sphere of religious activity.
From the reading of ancient texts, it is perfectly clear that two principal traditions were primarily prevalent in ancient India;
namely, the Brāhmaṇic tradition and the Kṣatriya tradition.
The distinction between these two is of profound importance.

The Vedic texts bore the burden of addressing matters pertaining to dharma; at that time, other texts were characterized by an effort toward secular aspirations. Vedic literature, or Brahmanical history, does not benefit from the religious reflections and activities of the ancient age.
However, the Kṣatriya tradition reflected in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas assists us in constructing a conception of a secular environment;
nevertheless, the analysis of both traditions brings completeness to a picture that is mutually interconnected.
Whether there is unity or non-unity between the two is not a matter of substance.
However, these two traditions are bound together by a certain common bond;
that bond is one of humanity and nobility.

And compassion— this inclination, like an invisible thread— enters into all of Indian thought and faith, whether pertaining to dharma or adharma. Furthermore, there is the influence of entirely distinct domains such as pilgrimage, medicine, science, and expiation upon the compassionate activity of universal benevolence.
Forbearance is indeed the pivot of transformation; patience is truly the opening word of Indian life.
From these two principles, social norms, laws, and codes of conduct arise.
Upon this foundation, the excellence of the history of celebrated Indian philosophy arose;
for there is no entity whatsoever that exists without the welfare of humanity and the collective well-being of individuals.
It is generally analyzed that the Purāṇas are subsequent to Vedic literature.
Although some stories are indeed authentic and extremely ancient,
these *purāṇas* have undergone transformation from time to time, much like intimate matters shared with ordinary people;
yet it is precisely this that preserves the substance appropriate for the life and thought of common folk.
The dharma of the Hindus has never been indifferent to worldly desires; rather, it possessed the magnanimity to provide for the knowledge and acceptance of those who yearn for a changing time.
To demonstrate the vitality of life, there must necessarily exist within a living society the power of flux and transformation.
The flow of Dharma always effects a transformation in its course by following the currents of distinct ages (*yuga*),
and likewise establishes the necessary correspondence.
Thus, the Purāṇas clearly demonstrate the popularity of various deities by adopting conformity with the diverse ages.

Following the tradition of the Brāhmaṇas, as it is recorded in both the Atharvaveda and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is seen that the Purāṇas possess a sacred foundation just like the Vedas. The Atharvaveda states that from the remnants of the sacrifice, along with the Yajus formulas, the Ṛks, Sāmans, meters, and Purāṇas were born.
Furthermore, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad describes the origin of the Vedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, as being the breath of the Great Being (Mahābhūta).
Although these two views are fundamentally independent, they nonetheless maintain a consensus regarding the sanctity of the Purāṇas;
it is precisely because of this sanctity that the Purāṇas have been accorded the designation of the "Fifth Veda."

It is prescribed that there are five characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in the Purāṇas. Namely: "Cosmogony (*sarga*), secondary creation (*pratisarga*), genealogy (*vaṃśa*), the periods of the Manus (*manvantara*), and the history of the dynasties (*vaṃśānucarita*); such is the Purāṇa with its five characteristics."
(Prasaṅga: Vāyupurāṇa, 4.10.92;
Matsyapurāṇa, 53.63;
Agnipurāṇa, 1.14)
In a technical sense,
the Purāṇas contain the principles of creation and re-creation, as well as the genealogies of the gods and the virtuous.
The description of the universal wheel and the detailed account of royal lineages—
the foundation for all these characteristics resides within the narratives.
In discourses, verses,
and ritual treatises— whatever emerges from the midst of sacrifices: through narratives, legends, verses, and ritual expositions.
Expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed a compendium of the Purāṇas.
(Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, 2.34.21; Vāyu Purāṇa, 60.21;
Viṣṇu Purāṇa, 3.6.25)
The eighteen Mahāpurāṇas:
1. Vāyupurāṇa, 2. Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
3. Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, 4. Viṣṇu Purāṇa, 5. Matsya Purāṇa.
6. Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 7. Kūrma Purāṇa, 8. Vāmana Purāṇa.
9. Liṅgapurāṇa, 10. Varāhapurāṇa, 11. Padmapurāṇa.
12. Nāradīya Purāṇa, 13. Agni Purāṇa, 14. Garuḍa Purāṇa.
15. Brahma Purāṇa, 16. Skanda Purāṇa, 17. Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
18. Bhaviṣya Purāṇa. Due to various recensions, the sequence of the Purāṇas may differ;
indeed, some discrepancies are observed among them.

Nevertheless, it is the analysis that the eighteen Purāṇas mentioned are exceedingly weighty. Alternatively, these Purāṇas may sometimes be divided into three types: namely, Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa.
1. Among the Sāttvika Purāṇas—there are the Viṣṇu, Nāradīya, Bhāgavata, Garuḍa, Padma, and Varāha Purāṇas.
2. Among the Rāja Purāṇas—the Brahmāṇḍa, Brahmavaivarta, Mārkaṇḍeya, Brahma, Vāmana, and Bhaviṣya Purāṇas.
3. Among the Tāmasa Purāṇas—the Matsya, Kūrma, Liṅga, Vāyu, Agni, and Skanda Purāṇas.

This kind of categorization was made by specific traditions in order to grant authority to their own respective lineages; this profundity is not understood. In reality, this categorization is a meaningless preoccupation with religious fanatics.
Indeed, the intention of the Purāṇas is to describe Hinduism through some independent means.

That which was described with severity in the Vedas and Upaniṣads is recounted in the Purāṇas by means of narratives and other forms— so that the simplest mind may be able to grasp the pure speech of the Purāṇas.
Here, even the ritual acts prescribed in the scriptures have been described in a simplified manner.
Vedic dharma is extensive in its meaning and possesses many arguments;
therefore, there is ample scope therein for numerous Puranic stories, sub-stories, and the like.

Moreover, like the Vedic dharma, the dharma that speaks of many deities is by its very nature tolerant. For this reason, a process of harmonization occurred among the various conceptions of the divine; specifically, a state of humility arose within the inner disposition of the Brāhmaṇa class.
That method was entirely immersed in the ritual practices prescribed by the scriptures;
for the sake of winning public favor, it employed a certain dharma with simplicity, impartiality, and truth,
as well as abundant historical narratives.
There was a need for a simple mode of worship and a common, humble mental disposition.
In this field, the Brahmins and the Upanishads rendered their purpose void, secretly instigating enthusiasm for non-Vedic streams of thought.
While these streams of thought gradually attained preeminence through certainty,

in the meantime, non-Vedic religions such as Buddhism and Jainism— having found a favorable environment created by the Upaniṣads— rapidly gained widespread expansion without accepting the authority of the Vedas.
Those teachings gathered various auxiliary materials from Vedic deities and principles, from the ritual cycles of Brahmanical practice, and from the Upanishadic doctrines concerning the inner self.
At that very time, they discarded those weak elements;

although the existence of these un-Vedic religious activities was not preserved in the consciousness [of the tradition], nevertheless, they established a profound influence within the general stream of being of the entire Hindu religion.
The Hindu religion of the pre-Buddhist age was certainly distinct from the Hindu religion of the post-Buddhist age.
In this regard, an extremely profound transformation was accomplished. To illustrate: the earlier religion had been rigid and even somewhat harsh.
However, later Dharma became more complex, providing an occasion for the discernment of differing opinions.
Just as it prescribes punishment, it likewise provides means for its avoidance;
for instance, liberation from various terrifying sins is achieved through the method of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
For this compassion, even while accepting futility and weakness, does not abandon the true path;
rather, it simultaneously demonstrates the means for purification.
It is precisely here that the influence of non-Vedic religious practices is undoubtedly at work.
Those activities are indeed greater and more sublime than Vedic dharma;
in this field, it is the Puranic dharma that would be so described.
In spirit, it is independent of Vedic dharma.
Although this dharma, having emerged from the ocean of knowledge of the Purāṇas, appears at first glance to imitate ancient dharma, yet that dharma is peaceful and noble.
Here, accounts of deities abound.
However, among them exists a certain mirror-like dimension which reveals either truth or falsehood and provides instruction regarding faults and other matters.
The Purāṇic literature is regarded as a complement to the Vedic literature.
In what manner does peace arise in life, how is fulfillment born, and how is the ideal of life attained?
The question of life is resolved: through narratives and sub-narratives, the Purāṇas show them the simplest path.
It is marvellously illustrated how, by this means, the Purāṇas establish a synthesis among diverse principles.
They bring together Vedic and non-Vedic perspectives concerning the conduct of life.
Puranic literature, with great faith, presents a comprehensive body of religious conviction and establishes unity amidst diversity by synthesizing everything into one.

The synthesis established by the Purāṇas regarding the principles of knowledge, action, and devotion— encompassing both Vedic and non-Vedic systems concerning the conduct of daily life— exerted its influence across all levels of Hindu society. As a result, even today, the lives of almost all Hindus have become well-ordered, wherein [they accommodate] those of different eras, different religions, and different...
Through the equalization of the intervals between meditative states, the integration of various phenomena has been accomplished.

Even such an unlearned Hindu, though living far from the fields of formal knowledge, does not foster total ignorance regarding the philosophical truths taught in the Purāṇas. Consequently, he adopts an exceedingly noble view concerning life.
He experiences the profound meaning of forbearance as well as the establishment of harmony— a function that is indeed rare elsewhere.
It is for this reason that it is said that the Mahākāvyas and Purāṇas play an exceedingly significant role in the lives of Hindus for more than two thousand years.
Throughout their time,
they never engaged in any dispute, but instead imparted the knowledge of the great seers (maharṣis) to common people.
The authors of these literary works provided beneficial instruction for the social and religious lives of each individual by examining every person.
Through these literary works, an elevated sense of value and ethical discipline remains conjoined with practical knowledge.
Just as these works acknowledge certain flaws in human character, they likewise demonstrate the means for their transcendence;
in this comprehensive grasp of humanity, they constitute the fundamental authority for the human activity reflected in the sacred scriptures.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is an unprecedented word;
therein reside many mental states (*manas*).
For instance—love (*prema*),...
devotion, greatness of soul, and affection.
Forgiveness, empathy, and so forth are experiences;
these experiences constitute the very nature of the stages of life.
The practice of giving and receiving,
as well as the practice of forgiveness and forgetfulness, sustains the life of certain individuals and their companions in a fitting manner.
This voice is repeatedly conveyed through numerous narratives and legends within these beloved literary works by Dhruvak.
Humanity is indeed in error; nevertheless, the very effort made to purify that error leads humanity toward the state of a "Great Man" (*mahāmanava*).

That time has arrived when there is no further need for re-interpretations of the divine narratives and ancient histories composed in the *Purāṇas* and *Itihāsas*. Within these stories, one must investigate the social reality reflected therein.
In this context, an attempt is made to analyze Hinduism as expounded in the Puranic literature as a religion of compassion (*kāruṇika-dharma*).
In it, customs and rituals are not paramount; rather, greatness and compassion are established as its fundamental nature. Hinduism has always been an expansive religion.
This is as deep as the ocean,
wherein the diverse streams of the thoughts and beliefs of the traditionalists have converged and become one.
Although Vedic religion was ritualistic, it...
Nevertheless, a certain philosophical ground was implicitly present there, which supported all the fundamental truths when considered in their natural context;
these truths shine forth within the impulses of nature,
and compassion is their common foundation.
This sound possesses variegated colors like a rainbow;

herein, the integration of as many states of being (*bhāva*) and aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) as possible is established. For those states of being are—affection (*prīti*), devotion (*bhakti*), and so forth.
The duties appropriate for women, sympathetic participation, and devotion to affection.
The activity of the teacher toward the disciple, or the duty of the disciple toward the teacher;
the compassion of the deity toward the devotee;
and ascetic practice.
And there is lamentation.
These states have an influence upon compassion;
they promote the propagation of that very same ancient Hinduism.
Like Vedic texts, yet in a different manner;
they teach primarily through narratives.
Many stories, at first glance, appear simple and devoid of religious sentiment; however, through subtle observation, one establishes that within these stories shines a compassionate reflection.
This is true: a religious spirit exists within the Purāṇas.
For this reason, virtue plays a significant role in the narrative portions [of the Mahābhārata].
This virtue is explained in many ways in relation to the duties of a son, a wife, and a disciple.
Devotion (*bhakti*) is another form of agitation (*āvega*) that is observed in many activities. While a truly exhaustive classification of all forms of agitation is impossible,
all agitations are included within compassion (*karuṇā*).
Now, the impulses impelled by compassion are described.
Bhakti—bhakti is divided into two types: that of a human toward another human, and...
A human being's devotion toward a deity and toward another human being is of many kinds; for example,
that of a disciple toward a teacher.
Women toward their husband, and a servant toward his master—
many illustrative stories demonstrate this surge of emotion born of devotion, which is imbued with reverence.
In devotion, a principle governing both receiving and giving is established.
From a superficial perspective, there appears to be no goal here directed toward self-interest;
however, when a devotee offers themselves to someone, a certain response will inevitably arise.
Beyond that, it ought to be of the nature of pure bliss, or rather, of the nature of honor.
It is considered sufficient as the sole joy for the elders and the venerable ones;
that bliss which serves for the enjoyment of good fortune both in this world and in the next.
Virtuous conduct never perishes,
and a sacrifice performed according to one's nature is never in vain— such is the very lesson derived from ancient legends.
In this regard, there are several excellent examples related to devotion.
In the Purāṇas, the devotion of women is described as preeminent;
these passages concern their status as chaste wives and the practice of marrying only once.
They attribute gravity to a transaction that lacks self-interest and persists across lifetimes toward one's master.
We find the account of the king Śatadhanu in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (3.18).

His wife, Śaivyā, was exceedingly virtuous and devoted to righteousness; that couple was always engaged in religious duties. Once, as they were returning from their daily bath in the Gaṅgā, they saw a sinful person on the road.
Because that sinful king had engaged in conversation with him during the time of his religious observance, he was reborn as a dog in his next life.
The queen, however, became a princess;
she remembered her previous birth.
By means of that [knowledge], having investigated the specific nature of the dog, he remembered its lives in previous births.
Thus, after several births had passed, it took birth as the son of King Janaka.
At that time, his marriage with the princess took place.

In one place, the two of them enjoyed their livelihood together; yet they underwent births in different low castes. The princess’s determination toward her master, as well as her effort to see him through the sequence of successive births, was a marvelous undertaking.
This singular devotion is by its very nature worthy of praise.
Relying upon such an object that is devoid of self-interest, there is a single narrative in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* (Chapter 64).
It concerns the Brahmin Kauśika, who, though afflicted by leprosy and unfortunate, [attained success].
It was indeed his good fortune that his wife, a great *satī*, thought of his livelihood.
That brahmin was by nature wicked;
once, he desired to see a beautiful courtesan.
His wife led him there.
A certain sage, having been insulted by that Brahmin on the road, cursed the Brahmin, saying, "His death shall occur simultaneously with the rising of the sun.
Such was the power of her chastity that his wife warded off her husband's death along with the rising of the sun, for she never desired her husband's death.
Since her husband was unwell in both body and mind, she faced no legal accusation regarding her husband’s unjust or wicked conduct.

At the conclusion of this narrative, that Brahmin, through Anasūyā’s intervention, obtained the favor of the gods and became free from disease. This third episode, which conveys the essential meaning, is found in the *Brahma Purāṇa* (Chapter 111).
There was a certain serpent who was the son of Surasena, the king of Pratiṣṭhāpura. This matter was kept secret by both the king and the queen.
When he had reached a suitable age, that serpent desired to marry.
Without revealing his secret identity, his marriage was arranged with Bhogavatī, the princess of Pūrvadeśa.
After the wedding, Bhogavatī desired to know her husband’s true background;
however, she did not become deluded by him.
However, she served him as a single woman might;
through this greatness, she attained a power by which both the master and the woman were able to remember their past-life history.
The serpent remembered that in his previous birth he had been a follower of Śiva.
At that time, Bhogavatī was his wife.
Due to the curse of Śiva, he took birth in the form of a serpent.
Having gone to a sacred place, he was urged by Bhogavatī to perform the worship of Śiva.
By the grace of Śiva, he regained his natural life.
We always reflect that the ancient system of conduct desired such selflessness from women;
in the field of the master, the moral law assumes a different form.
Nevertheless, in many narratives it is observed that masters made efforts for the welfare of their wives even when those wives were truly devoid of devotion and lacking in virtue.
From these narratives it follows that there is an extreme necessity in conjugal life for affection characterized by firm bonds of love and a profound understanding of one another;
this very thing is called *prema*.
She abides in that love which exists within the circumference of compassion.
A brilliant illustration of this is found in the legend of Sūrya and his wife Saṃjñā;
independent versions of this legend exist in various Purāṇas.

However, the primary outline is identical everywhere. The personification (bearing a different name elsewhere), being unable to endure the sun's fierce radiance, created a likeness of herself named Shadow and departed elsewhere.
That Saṃjñā, whose nature was characterized by conceptual construction, behaved unfairly toward her sons.
At that time, Sūrya assumed the disguise of a horse and went to the land of Uttarakuru to seek out Saṃjñā,
because at that moment Saṃjñā had herself taken on the form of a mare.
From the very beginning, he had resolved to relinquish his own vital energy for the sake of his wife;
although this state was the cause of his physical ailment, he had made a firm determination to endure it for Saṃjñā’s sake.
This, indeed, is our relevant field of inquiry.
For the sun was unable to abandon Saṃjñā alone; he could neither curse her nor punish her. Yet, instead of doing so, he established a painful union with his wife in order to dwell happily together.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* (Chapter 100),
there is a beautiful narrative concerning the two wives of Kaśyapa, Vinatā and Kadrū;
it appears that these two women were exceedingly submissive.
When they both became pregnant,
Kaśyapa went elsewhere,
so that those two women became exceedingly difficult to control.
When they were pregnant,
Kaśyapa went elsewhere so that they would not perform even the slightest unwholesome act.
In that manner, he instructed them both;
however, as Kaśyapa’s return drew near, they became involved in an evil deed.
They went to the sacrifice performed by the seven ṛṣis.
And there they committed improper conduct;
those great sages cursed them,
and consequently, they became inclined toward the state of rivers.
Having returned and heard everything, Kaśyapa propitiated Śiva with hymns to support his wife's side and recovered his two wives without any loss.
Nevertheless, because she was incorrigible, Kadrū again mocked the Brahmins and committed another sin;
due to their curse, she became blind.
Furthermore, Kaśyapa performed his duty by supporting his wife's side.
This narrative serves as evidence of how Kaśyapa did not perceive any fault in his wife;
therefore, she was protected by him in every respect.
Although those two were stained by evil deeds,
a splendor befitting love is seen in the account of Kaṭha Muni (Brahma Purāṇa, Chapter 182).
There, that sage made his despicable wife beautiful by means of the power of his asceticism.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, there is a story concerning King Uttānapāda;
he was exceedingly fond of his daughter Bahulā.
However, Bahulā had no love for the king at all;
she always behaved ill toward him,
yet the king did not take any offense.
Once, Bahulā, having completely transgressed all propriety, insulted the king in the full assembly of his court.
Thereupon, the enraged king banished his wife Bahulā to the forest.
In the meantime, a certain brahmin arrived and delivered a message concerning the abduction of Bahulā.
The king went outside; after a long search, he recovered her. He gradually came to realize that Bahulā had been taken to the kingdom of the serpents.
There, Nandā, the daughter of the serpent-king, protected Tāmra.
Out of detachment for his wife, the king, with the assistance of the aforementioned Brahmin, brought Bahulā into his home so that he might be liberated.
Due to her father’s curse, the serpent-king’s daughter had become mute.
Queen Bahulā assisted the daughter of the serpent-king in order to liberate her from that state of muteness;
the Brahmin, through the power of his sacrifice, brought about the restoration of the princess’s faculty of speech.
This narrative is presented as an illustration of the love a husband bears for a wife who is unrestrained.
In many Purāṇas, the narrative of Yayāti and his city is well known as an illustration of devotion to one’s father.
It appears that because of the captivating nature of this narrative, it gained widespread circulation from an early period and occupied a prominent place in almost all the Purāṇas:
even though Yayāti was old, he was not satisfied with the enjoyment of pleasures.
For this very reason, he desired to obtain youth from one among his sons by means of offering his own old age.
One by one, none of all his sons were willing to grant it;
however, the youngest son, Puru, offered his own youth to his father in exchange for accepting the old age.
Then, being satisfied, Yayāti restored his youth to Puru,
bestowed his blessing upon him, and made him the successor to the empire.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is a corresponding narrative:
therein, Sumati, the son of Pramati, liberated his father from a state of bondage inflicted by a Gandharva.
In one narrative of the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, the distress of a disciple toward his teacher is described.
The sage Bhūti was exceedingly prone to arrogance and agitation;
he suddenly fell under the sway of anger.
Once, having entrusted the responsibility of attending to the fire to a disciple named Śānti, he departed elsewhere.
By ill fortune, the purifying fire was extinguished due to a certain cause.
Thinking, "Because of this, the Guru will become enraged," Śānti became exceedingly afraid;
he knew that there would be no deliverance whatsoever from the wrath of the Guru as thus described.
He strove exceedingly for the satisfaction of his limbs.
Then Agni, overcome by compassion, granted him boons.
Śānti first requested a boon: "May the sacrificial fire blaze forth."
Then he desired one son for his teacher;
he even requested a transformation of the teacher’s heart.
When the sage returned, he perceived a certain change in his own nature.
Then, having investigated the cause, he was unable to know everything.
This narrative not only demonstrates the student's lack of self-interest, but also validates his complete devotion toward the teacher.
With such devotion, disregarding the faults of the guru, he acts in such a way that the guru obtains whatever object is desired.
Ancient texts observe a profound intimacy between the human being and the divine.
It is true that the gods were established in positions of great advantage;
nevertheless, they remained ever-present and close at hand.
The yoga between gods and mortals was uninterrupted.
Everywhere we observe that whenever even a god is summoned with single-minded devotion,
that god not only manifests himself, but...
Rather, he delights the sacrificer by granting the desired object.
There is a praiseworthy focal point in this association:
the deity is always the very embodiment of compassion.
He gives— even when he himself is suffering, he gives.
The gods never cease from thoughts of compassion,
nor do they ever consider virtue and fault as equal.
At times, they do not even keep account of gain or loss;
for this very reason, at times the donor suffers a depletion of what he has acquired.
Such a state leads him to that uncertain condition.
He causes him to lose either his land or his heaven;
moreover, it becomes the cause for his wandering from forest to forest.
Nevertheless, the gods do not cease from granting even greater boons.
For the benefit of mortals, they accomplish auspicious deeds that transcend all questioning.
By this granting of boons, it is indicated that their profound love and compassion are directed specifically toward those living beings who are lower [than themselves].
Indeed, such selfless love is inevitably accompanied at once by both affection (*anurāga*) and devotion (*bhakti*).
In these accounts, the state of complete self-surrender is indicated.
Such activity is also found in the narratives of Prahlāda, Dhruva, and Bali;
all three of these narratives are seen in various Purāṇas, wherein the Lord Nārāyaṇa is described as the Supreme Deity.
Prahlāda’s birth took place in the lineage of the Daityas;
however, from his very childhood, he was a devotee of Nārāyaṇa.
His father, Hiraṇyakaśipu, recognizing Prahlāda’s conduct as characteristic of a Daitya, strove by every means to prevent it.
There was no limit to the excesses [of his enemies],
yet Prahlāda remained fearless;
thus, by the grace of his chosen deity, he remained free from calamities everywhere.
In the remainder [of the narrative], Nārāyaṇa, in order to protect the creation from his excessive conduct, slew Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The account of Prahlāda’s life demonstrates the constant and visible attention that Viṣṇu bestows upon His devotee.
Prahlāda is a specific emblem of supreme devotion.
In this matter, Viṣṇu acts as the authority: that perfect fullness sometimes turns into fruitlessness. Otherwise, Dhruva’s story would have been misplaced;
having been struck by his stepmother, he went into the presence of Viṣṇu.

This alone was his humiliation: that he became firm in his resolve to obtain something rare in order to determine its value. Thereupon, renouncing the comforts of home, he began to search for that unknown object.
The sages were sympathetic toward him.

From the very beginning, they showed him the right path. By means of steadfastness and sincerity, he moved through the midst of all calamities. Having crossed over all calamities, he attained the supreme goal through subtle application.
Viṣṇu, having manifested himself, granted him an unprecedented and extraordinary boon;
this narrative is an unparalleled example of compassion,
wherein an abandoned infant found refuge in the sheltering shadow of the wings of the omnipotent Viṣṇu.
That is to say, even an ignorant child is not disregarded by that Supreme Lord;
He protects him by granting consolation and provides for him with his desired objects.
The story of Vali is known to all and is seen in various Purāṇas.
Although he was a Daitya, Bali was exceedingly righteous and a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu. Once, he took possession of heaven.
The gods went to Viṣṇu in order to regain their beloved earth.
Viṣṇu descended as Vāmana, having become the son of Aditi. Bali used to grant all things to every petitioner;
at that time, Vāmana arrived there as a petitioner.
He requested only three-quarters of the land.
Śukrācārya, the preceptor of the Daityas, perceived everything;
he caused Bali to desist.
Nevertheless, Bali remained bound by his own vow, even at the cost of exchanging heaven for his own life;
with one foot Vāmana covered heaven, and with the other, the remainder of the world.
When the third foot was revealed beyond the base of the navel, he desired to place that foot there;
Bali offered his own head,
and then he himself went to Pātāla.
Here, the scent of pure devotion exists;
through his ethical integrity, the devotee is placed above his beloved deity.
For the sake of achieving his own ends, the deity resorts to deception.
Even though a devotee knows everything, he does not stop after that.
There are numerous narratives concerning the greatness and the majestic power of various deities;
among these, some are like natural jewels of literature.
These reveal the sweetness of the great deeds of the Lord.
A similar narrative is found in the *Brahma Purāṇa* (chapter 86),
which describes how Yama went to bring back the deceased son of certain elderly parents.
However, seeing the extent of their suffering, he was unable to take his son with him;
therefore, he went out to perform austerities in order to remove the suffering of the human race.
This undertaking was exceedingly purposeful.
Since Yama is the King of Death, he should not be shaken by the sight of death; however, this follows:
that he is not satisfied.
Even that suffering which is real touches him.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is a narrative concerning the supreme state of equanimity;
herein, Yama takes the side of the recipient.
He went to fetch food for Mahādeva, but he was unable to bring it.
Mahādeva not only protected his food, but also slew Yama in order to bring an end to the harassment caused by Yama.
Subsequently, at the request of the gods, Mahādeva restored Yama to life.
However, Yama accepted [the request], thinking that he would not show the fear of death to the devotees of Mahādeva.
This acceptance was not logical;
nevertheless, Śiva intends to protect his current devotee by whatever means possible.
This serves as proof that the Blessed One remains perpetually blind to the faults of His devotees.
Furthermore, the various deeds of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa are described in detail in both the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa;
among ordinary people, He performed many significant acts.
By him, the subduing of the Naga Kālīya was accomplished;
consequently, the people of the land of Nanda obtained protection from poison.
Yet, even there, he displayed compassion.
The wives of Kālīya prayed to Kṛṣṇa for mercy.
Kṛṣṇa made such an arrangement that they were able to cross the ocean without danger. Such an inclination toward forgiveness and compassion is exceedingly common among the gods.
If an adversary who is difficult to overcome seeks protection or bows down in remorse,
he should be forgiven at that very moment.
In this regard, the account of the battle between Mahādeva and the demon Andhaka must certainly be cited.
This asura was not only ill-behaved, but he also cast a gaze full of passion toward Pārvatī;
somehow, Pārvatī must obtain protection from his wicked grasp. However, a terrible battle took place between Śiva and Andhaka.
Seeing that his defeat was inevitable, Andhaka sought protection from Śiva.
Śiva granted him forgiveness at that very moment;
however, being pierced by Śiva’s trident, Andhaka became liberated from all his sins.
Having thus purified himself, he attained supreme bliss.
It is our firm conviction that Śiva is the God whose heart is always moist with compassion;
he becomes tranquil with the utmost ease.
And so, He grants everything desired by His devotee.
By performing this repeatedly, a state of complexity is created;
here, the field of the demon Bhasmasura is taken as the example.
He obtained a boon from Śiva and became invincible;
through the skill of the Lord Viṣṇu, the gods were liberated from their miserable state.
A similar compassion is experienced in the case of Bhagīratha as well.
Out of anger toward him, Śiva bound the Gaṅgā within his matted locks.
Bhagīratha endeavored in many ways for her release, but all his efforts proved in vain.
Śiva, showing compassion toward him, released the Gaṅgā;
Bhagīratha, for his part, received a certain instruction.
In the 169th chapter of the Brahma Purāṇa, there is another brilliant narrative describing Mahādeva’s activity of rescuing a devotee.
A hunter of low caste, a Bhilla, worships Mahādeva by means of a method that is utterly unconventional.
The very image of Mahādeva that he worships belongs to a Brahmin named Veda.
In the absence of Veda, the Bhilla would come there and worship his beloved god Mahādeva with raw meat and other such things.
However, Mahādeva was satisfied by his steadfastness.
Once, while disguised as a hunter, Veda saw the Bhilla acting in such a manner;
what he witnessed was beyond belief.
He desired an explanation of why such an action was performed by nature itself near Śiva.

To support his position, Mahādeva presented the example of the Bhilla’s steadfastness and devotion. There is an extremely captivating narrative in the eighth section, the Uttarakhanda, of the Garuḍa Purāṇa.

This demonstrates the extent to which the nature of the god who nourishes from behind can extend as a protector. This describes how many hungry ghosts (preta) had committed exceedingly blameworthy sins;
by chance, a single righteous brahmin came into their company.
The hungry ghosts (pretas) desired to devour him;
however, that brahmin, a devotee of Viṣṇu, began to utter the name of his beloved deity. By its very nature, this became conducive to his liberation.
Not only for the brahmin, but also for the departed spirits;
for all of them were able to perceive the Blessed One directly.
This demonstrates that association with the virtuous is beneficial to everyone.
This association bestows good fortune even upon the most wicked.
Its mention in the context of self-inquiry is not irrelevant, for in the Purāṇas, compassion toward one's own insatiable selves is described as an exceedingly common activity;
[it is directed] toward their liberation from fear and their liberation from suffering.

There are many means for liberation from a state of degradation. One such means is said to be: lamps are placed in a particular elevated location so that the wandering spirits (*preta-ātman*), who are prone to roaming, may see them without effort.
Compassion—compassion indeed is another great impulse by which the dignity of the giver increases.
This great momentum is reflected everywhere in the ancient texts:
the gods grant boons to their devotees and protect their devotees from sufferings.
They protect one from activities consisting of deception. All this is validated by the fact that the stream of compassion flows at all times.
From time to time, gifts are given to those unworthy of them, or there may be the improper application of a boon.
Nevertheless, that cannot be fully calculated.
Like the gods, the virtuous also possessed a similar nature;
they too possessed great power.
They generally employ their power for the benefit of the human race;
liberation alone is their supreme goal of human endeavor, yet they act for the welfare of people.
However, they harbor no expectations.
They assist even when unasked;
this demonstrates that their selves have been purified through austerity,
whereby they are able to transcend the bounds of self-interest.

The emptiness of self-interest, or rather the dissolution of any individual self within the entire universe, is the primary object of asceticism; it is that which reaches the culmination of that path, as one experiences the happiness and suffering of others as one's own.
Taking such accounts as their basis, many stories exist within the Purāṇas.
In this context, several stories are presented as incidental.
Regarding the praise of Kṣudhātīrtha, it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa (Chapter 35) that once the sage Kaṇva brought about the satisfaction of both Gaṅgā and Kṣudhā.
Only the two appeared;
only the two desired to grant a boon to that sage.
He did not desire anything for himself.
Yet he prayed for his own children that none among his people should suffer from hunger;
even in this, he found no rest.
He opened up his own good fortune for the whole world.
He prays: "If anyone worships hunger, he shall certainly be liberated from hunger.
The story of Śunaḥśepha is an ancient narrative;
it is found in the 104th chapter of the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
To this it is replied: Hariścandra obtained a son through a boon from Varuṇa.
He made a solemn resolve (saṃkalpa) in the presence of Varuṇa that he would perform a sacrifice with his newborn son.
However, when that time arrived, he began to delay again and again.
The remaining gods, being enraged, communicated their intention for the king's welfare through a spy.
At that time, the king, resorting to deceit, said, "I do not know what ought to be done.
When someone instructed him that he should purchase the son of some person and perform a sacrifice with that son as a substitute for his own son, [he agreed].
Then he purchased Śunaḥśepha,
whose father was in dire need of wealth, and moreover, that father had two other sons.
However, in reality, Śunaḥśepha was not actually sacrificed at the sacrifice.
This indicates that the cruel sacrificial system was rejected at will by one of a compassionate disposition;
consequently, the performance of the sacrifice was permitted without the immolation of a human being.
This task is not easy;
the purpose of transgressing established rules is exceedingly great.
It is only through profound compassion that one acts for the sake of the poor, the destitute, and the child.
The Lord was impelled to protect him who belonged to no one else;
this narrative is exceedingly permeated with the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇarasa*).
For his father desired the eldest son for the sake of protection against calamities in the next world,
while his mother, out of great affection, would not abandon the youngest son. At that time, he desired only that which the king might protect.
For this very reason, there was no one to serve as a protector for this child;
at that time, he offered everything to the Divine,
who protected him with compassion.
In the 125th chapter of the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is a captivating narrative.
It is seen here that compassionate conduct is found not only among gods, saints, or high-born men, but even among beings of low birth, who possess an exceedingly noble heart.
In this regard, there is a certain narrative concerning a bird.
Through it, the incomparable greatness of that bird’s character is revealed;
its introduction serves to praise the holy site of Yamatīrtha.
There, an owl and a pigeon lived together for generations and so forth;
however, their association had turned into enmity,
and consequently, a battle broke out between them.
The two wives of the two birds did not wish for war;
they invoked Agni and Yama,
for those two gods are the presiding deities over the pair of spouses.
Consequently, both deities became manifest;
however, the birds of the two retinues desired nothing other than the end of their enmity.
They sought only a common auspiciousness.
In the Mahākāvyas and Purāṇas, the two sages Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra are exceedingly renowned. There exist many sentiment-rich narratives concerning these two.
Sage Viśvāmitra was a Kṣatriya by birth, but through ascetic penance he became a Brāhmaṇa.
This establishes his character as being singularly focused and full of power;
however, Vasiṣṭha was an exceedingly free from illusion (amāyika) sage.
Both sages performed great deeds for the benefit of the world.
This indicates the greatness of these two.
The Vāmana Purāṇa (Chapter Twenty-one) describes the narrative of Saṃvaraṇa, a king of the Lunar dynasty.
That king was a disciple of Vasiṣṭha.
Once, by chance, the king beheld Tapati, the daughter of the Sun;
at that very moment, the king became enamored of her.
Not realizing the nature of the maiden, he fell into a state of distress.
Vasiṣṭha, the foremost sage, perceiving his condition, considered the quality of the Sun's region;
yet, even though the teacher recognized the fault of the disciple, he acted in such a way that the disciple obtained the desired object.
In ancient times, a very intense conflict existed between Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra;
the account of this is found in the fortieth chapter of the Vāmana Purāṇa.
Once, the river Sarasvatī became beset by calamity.
Viśvāmitra formed the intention to kill the most distinguished [Vasiṣṭha].
He commanded Sarasvatī: "Bring Vasiṣṭha here;
otherwise, he will become the cause of her suffering."
Having no other means, Sarasvatī went to Vasiṣṭha and reported everything to him. Vasiṣṭha felt compassion for her;
he gave his consent to Sarasvatī, saying, "Lead me to Viśvāmitra."
Then Sarasvatī brought Vasiṣṭha to Viśvāmitra’s hermitage;
however, that sage began to aim the weapon intended for his destruction.
Sarasvatī was leading Vasiṣṭha elsewhere to escape the grasp of the harsh-minded muni.
For this reason, a single curse was inevitable.
After a long period of agitation, Sarasvatī was finally released from this state.
On the side of the sage Vasiṣṭha, there was no purpose whatsoever in fulfilling Viśvāmitra’s wicked desire.
He was always on equal footing with Viśvāmitra,
even though he was not suited for battle;
however, he showed compassion toward Sarasvatī.
For her benefit, he became intent on performing a sacrifice;
meanwhile, Sarasvatī, disregarding the sage’s anger, strove to protect Vasiṣṭha to the best of her ability.
In this context, the greatness of King Kuru is also worthy of mention.
We find this narrative in the twenty-second chapter of the Vāmana Purāṇa.
Once, the King of the Kurus desired to perform a certain act by which he would become the possessor of imperishable fame.
Therefore, with the assistance of Śiva’s bull and Yama’s buffalo, he began to plow the earth with a golden plough.
Being curious, Indra went there to learn the message.
The king said to Indra that he wished to sow the seeds of dharma, truth, charity, forbearance, purity, and other virtues.
When questioned, he replied that those seeds were present within his own body.
Viṣṇu, having gone there to test him, asked for some seeds.
The king extended his right hand first;
however, that hand was severed by the discus.
In the same way, he offered his other hand, his thigh, and his head;
then the Blessed One, being pleased, bestowed a blessing upon him.
The king did not ask for anything for himself,
not even liberation;
he desired only this— that this place become sacred.
"May whoever performs the sacrifice there attain liberation.
This is an illustration of incomparable greatness. It demonstrates that human character ought to be exalted where self-interest is completely eclipsed.
For the welfare of human beings, this exaltation of the Self is truly worthy of being extolled.
There are many such narratives in which compassion devoid of motive is described.
One story from the Viṣṇupurāṇa (4.3) [illustrates this].
He relates that the sage Aurva protected the life of Bāhurāja’s son while he was still unborn. When the queen was pregnant, a certain co-wife, overcome by jealousy, administered poison;
consequently, the birth of the son was delayed for an indefinite period.
Thus, when seven years had passed and the king had gone to the world of death, and the queen was intent on taking her own life,
the sage Aurva experienced grief on account of his unborn son—
the son who would be capable of bringing about auspiciousness and good fortune for mankind.
For this very reason, the sage, acting as a leader, restrained the queen from taking her own life.
By his blessing, the birth of a son occurred;
that son was nurtured through the efforts of the sage.
Regarding that which was performed here by the Sage, there is no causal basis rooted in the nature of things;
rather, it is solely pure compassion.
Such greatness of the *Brahmapurāṇa* is also seen in the 164th chapter.
It is stated there that Pavamāna brought a certain two-faced bird for its liberation to the sacred site of Gadādharatīrtha;
at that place, there was no hope whatsoever.
There was no bondage whatsoever;
he accomplished only that which is beneficial for the sake of welfare.
(Vāyupurāṇa, Chapter 90)
There is one account that describes a difference in taste as well as a state of equanimity;
this is also found in other Purāṇas.
This concerns Jamadagni, the father of Paraśurāma.
The sage Ṛcīka desired to obtain one son from his wife Satyavatī;
at that time, his mother-in-law also desired to obtain another son.
Thereupon, the sage prepared two sacrificial offerings (*caru*) and gave separate portions to Satyavatī and to her mother-in-law.

Due to ill fortune, Satyavatī consumed the portion intended for her mother-in-law, and the mother-in-law likewise consumed the portion intended for Satyavatī. Having learned of this, the sage informed Satyavatī that she would give birth to such a son of wicked conduct that he would even be capable of killing his own mother.
Upon hearing this, Satyavatī became exceedingly distressed.
She did not comply with her husband's command in that manner.
Out of compassion for the unfortunate girl, he wiped away the curse, saying:
"Not a son, but rather a grandson shall be born to you who will be such as this."
Observing his wife’s state of great misfortune and lack of renown, the sage was deeply pained and employed his power elsewhere;
consequently, the birth of Paraśurāja was delayed.
Devotion to duty exerts an influence over compassion through the awakening of a sense of duty.
For this is that experience wherein a person accomplishes their duty with steadfastness,
so that no one else may become a partaker of suffering;
this experience belongs to the same lineage as compassion.
This indicates the natural nobility, greatness, or majesty inherent in [the person].
There are numerous accounts in the Purāṇas which serve as evidence that such an intensity of emotion graced a high position even in ancient times.
Indeed, this is analyzed as a quality of the human being in their original state, characterized by extreme gravity.
Here too, the pure value of knowledge is reflected—that knowledge which is praised in every way and at all times;
among the well-known narratives, the bringing of the Gaṅgā by Bhagīratha is one such narrative. In this regard, there exist many perspectives worthy of examination.
Thereupon, Bhagīratha was indeed moved by a certain sense of duty;
having been awakened by it, he performed rigorous austerities for the sake of liberating his ancestors who had been cursed.
He truly caused both heaven and the mortal world to tremble in order to bring down the Gaṅgā.
Because of that, he experienced all kinds of sufferings and hardships;
at times he became bewildered, and at times he fell into despair. Nevertheless, in the end, he emerged victorious.

In this regard, an extremely intense attachment is observed, by which even the power of the mind is adorned with purposefulness. In the eightieth chapter of the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is a captivating narrative;
herein, the story of a monkey couple is recounted.
Once, a female pigeon was captured by a certain cruel hunter.
That hunter remained at that tree where the birds dwelt, having built their nest, throughout the entire night.
Not finding his mate, the female pigeon, he began to weep piteously.
Having heard that, the female pigeon made herself known to him;
thereupon, the pigeon made an effort for her liberation,
but she rejected his proposal.
Moreover, she justified the hunter’s occupation;
for hunting is the duty of a hunter,
and therefore he is not considered blameworthy for that purpose.
Again, she said to the pigeon, "This hunter should be honored as a guest;
comfort should be provided for him according to one's ability.
In the final instance, the pigeon offered his own body for the hunter's meal.
Observing the entire situation, the hunter became speechless and utterly bewildered;
then, reproaching his own conduct as something to be cursed,
he began to lament and desired to begin a new life.
Such a quality is certainly worthy of praise;
for even at that age, such conduct is not natural.
This is also well-known from the story of Śunaḥśepha (Brahma Purāṇa, Chapter 150).
In the end, the son Śunaḥśepha, though bound by circumstances, did not abandon his father in his mind.
His father went to hell as a result of his own evil deeds;
however, the son, having understood this and feeling sorrow for his father, undertook a righteous vow by which his father was able to go to heaven.

Is there any greater illustration than this for the understanding of what ought to be done and the understanding of universal compassion? Regarding affection, we previously considered that the word *karuṇā* (compassion) signifies many meanings;
namely—*dayā* (pity),...
friendship, shared experience, and affection.
Generosity, forbearance,
love, and all [other virtues] as well.
Wherein lies the remnant of compassion, or where is there a sign of equanimity; and what is the relative intensity between affection and love?
Such a definitive determination is not possible;
for this very reason, there is no purpose in such a classification.
This classification is made solely for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctions between experiences.
Just as the rays of the sun are reflected in seven ways upon a crystal with three facets, so too does the analysis of the word *karuṇā* (compassion) occur in many ways.
For this very reason, the classification mentioned previously is not presented here as the primary subject, but is undertaken for the sake of ease of contemplation.
Be that as it may, several narratives concerning affection (*sneha*) will now be described below.
This passage describes two types of agitation (*āvega*): the story of the sage Saubhari and impartiality (*apakṣapāta*), as well as affection (*sneha*).
Having observed the contented life of a certain fish, that sage desired to attain the life of a householder.
Thereupon, he approached King Māndhātṛ and expressed his desire to marry one from among the king's fifty daughters.
However, the king did not wish to give his daughter to such an old man;
nevertheless, he became afraid of the sage’s wrath,
for that anger portended ruin for him and his entire family.
To prevent the dilemma of both [parties], the sage will go forth; that maiden will be sought after by the sage.

In this, the sage displays a profound inner vision of human conduct. He made himself exceedingly youthful and beautiful, such that upon seeing him, all the maidens became filled with desire to obtain the sage as their husband.
After the wedding, this sage began to look upon all of them with an impartiality free from partiality;
thus, the sage made them exceedingly happy.
When their father desired to know [their state], all the daughters said that their husband spent his time with them in a most joyful manner.
There is no comparison for such balanced treatment in the entirety of literature.
In the eighty-second chapter of the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is a story concerning maternal affection;
herein, the actual setting of the narrative is present.
After the slaying of the demon Tāraka, Kārttikeya spent his time experiencing bliss together with celestial nymphs.
Upon hearing this, Pārvatī became truly distressed;
for as her son reached maturity, the mother’s hands were bound.
She was unable either to reject or to kill her son;
however, such a blameworthy act had to be prevented by all means.
Therefore, she divided her own being into two parts and placed one portion within the bodies of the gods.
After that, when Kārttikeya went to play with a certain celestial nymph,
he saw the reflection of his mother in that woman and was unable to play.
A mother never feels affection for a son who is intent on wicked deeds.
Moreover, she censures him;
she always desires to see her son endowed with reverence.
This fall of her son from his reverence causes Pārvatī, his mother, to be exceedingly distressed.
Then, through her discernment and the successful execution of her efforts, she accomplished her own task.
Such a system of instruction is not difficult to find between a teacher and a disciple, or indeed between the Lord and his devotee.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* (the 90th chapter), there is a narrative concerning equanimity;
that narrative concerns the Lord Viṣṇu and his devotee Garuḍa.
Once Garuḍa became exceedingly arrogant;
even when commanded, he would not release a single serpent.
Then Viṣṇu, by treading upon his foot, gave Garuḍa this lesson.
Such actions do not lead to purification, but rather to the exaltation of someone's own self;
the intention here is that the mirror of conduct must not be lowered.
Empathy— this empathy alone is one thing that possesses an exceedingly great momentum;
it melts the heart and causes the heart to expand.
This carries a distinct acquaintance with individual life-forces (*prāṇa*), and moreover, the sufferings of a person whose *prāṇa* is integrated appear as if they were one's own personal sufferings.
By this single means, it removes the external obstacle existing among divided people.
Throughout the entirety of classical literature, there are numerous examples related to empathy. A complete conception of greatness exists regarding several matters;
one such matter is indeed empathy experienced toward other people.
In the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is a unique narrative. It is a popular story concerning Umā’s ascetic penance for the sake of obtaining Mahādeva as her husband;
after the completion of her penance, she attained her desired object.
Mahādeva himself came to grant her a boon;
however, at the time of departure, he desired to test Umā’s worthiness,
since she was going to occupy the position of the Mother of the Universe.
Śiva assumed the disguise of a child.
Whenever that boy bathed in the lake, he would be seized by a crocodile.
Hearing his cries of distress, Umā ran to rescue him.
She entreated the crocodile for the sake of the boy's release;
however, the crocodile could only release the boy in exchange for the fruit of the penance performed by Umā.
Her intention was the relinquishing of her own fitness for the sake of attaining Mahādeva as her husband.
This doctrine is exceedingly harsh; nevertheless, Umā made a firm resolve to grant the fruit of her own penance for the sake of the child’s liberation.
By acting thus, she demonstrates that her devotion extends not only toward Mahādeva, but toward all people at all times.
Pārvatī possesses that very qualification which is required of a mother.
She is capable of setting aside her own suffering for the sake of all others;
at that time, her own happiness never becomes an object of deliberation.
This alone is the ideal of a mother.
The compassion, affection, and protective nature of such a mother are tested from time to time;
she renounced that happiness which she had acquired at great cost, even though her child was entirely unaware of it.
In the seventy-fourth chapter of the aforementioned Purāṇa, within the account of the descent of the Gaṅgā, there is a certain modified form [of this narrative].
In this instance, Bhagīratha is not described as the primary agent of the great catastrophe;
rather, it was the sage Gautama who realized that Pārvatī was experiencing mental anguish on account of her co-wife Gaṅgā,
for she was, in truth, the beloved wife of Mahādeva, and because of that, she had become intensely consumed by jealousy.
Gautama became the leader in alleviating the mental distress caused by the yogic disciplines of Pārvatī;
meanwhile, Gaṅgā was falling away due to her excessive intimacy with Mahādeva and Pārvatī.
Consequently, he made an effort to bring Gaṅgā down to the mortal realm.
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa relates a unique narrative;
herein, an exceedingly intense compassion for living beings is described.
Once, the righteous King Bharata beheld a doe who had reached the point of death at the time of giving birth to her fawn.

Then the king, feeling intense compassion for the fawn who was bereft of its mother, protected that young deer. Consequently, because of his excessive affection for that animal, he had no mental application toward ascetic practice;
even at the time of death, his mind was occupied solely with thoughts concerning the deer.
For this reason, he was born in a future life in the form of a deer;
in the end, he became the famous and dull-witted Bharata.
The essential point of this narrative is that the king, because of his compassion, did not go so far as to abandon his own priceless Dharma.
Forgiveness, forbearance, and a disposition toward endurance are established as the very essence of Dharma.

In the capacity for tolerating the views of others, as well as in the ability to accept being overpowered by another, there exists the nobility of a certain quality of Dharma. Such a person never forcefully imposes their own opinion.
Among the primary principles, the policy of establishing alliances and forming associations would be of the utmost importance.
We can state without doubt that forbearance is indeed the central distinguishing feature of Hinduism;
the curses resulting from its consequences serve as proof that defects such as weakness are always insignificant in practice.
However, their victory contains within it the greatest form of dharma, both in its disregard and its acceptance. A certain curse is a specific kind of punishment;
there is a need for punishment for the sake of ensuring conformity to the rules.
However, remorse,
the desire for purification,
and the effort toward self-elevation carry an extreme gravity.
This is accepted in general,
and we see again and again that one who is under a curse forgets and forgives.
The leader becomes one for whom sins are diminished;
this fruit never perishes entirely,
because no action performed in accordance with the rules ever goes to waste.
However, a means to diminish the blow is always perceived;
every narrative that contains a curse may serve as an illustration of this sentiment.
Several narratives are presented here to support these thematic points.
First, the well-known narrative of Ahalyā is related.
This narrative, in which Indra’s conduct is marked by a shameful situation, is found in almost all the Purāṇas.
*Brahma Purāṇa* (Chapter 87).

He set aside the relevant subject matter of the conversation for a moment and spoke of that which he had received following the imposition of the curse: that it was impossible for him to appear before the world in his present form.
Consequently, he earnestly entreated him to effect a transformation of the physical characteristics rooted in his bodily transgression.
At that moment, Gautama forgot the great sin committed by Devarāja and instructed him on the means to mitigate the curse.
In the ninety-second chapter of the *Brahmapurāṇa*, there is an exceptionally extraordinary narrative.
Just as it draws the reader’s mind far away, so too does it melt that very mind.
This was composed concerning a woman named Mahī.
In her youth she became a widow. Due to instability in the household, she placed her son under the care of the sage Gālava and went abroad to see the world.
By her very nature, in the course of time, she became a courtesan.
After some years had passed, that son, having reached maturity, went abroad to see the world.
By the turn of fate, a meeting between mother and son occurred;
however, the mother did not recognize her son.
And the son [approached] his mother; the earth became the concubine of that son. Then, as time passed,
Furthermore, through destiny and diverse karma,
both mother and son were able to recognize one another;
what then transpired was exceedingly heart-wrenching and poignant to the core.
Both of them desired the end of their lives;
however, the sage Gālava, seeing their condition and being pained with compassion, pointed out the cause to the mother and son, restrained them from performing actions befitting fools,
and established mental peace for the two of them.
In the 170th chapter of the *Brahma Purāṇa*, there is another narrative concerning his friend Maṇikuṇḍala and Gautama, in which the rare quality of forgiveness is found.
Gautama was a wicked person,
but his friend Maṇikuṇḍala was righteous.
Gautama calls his friend Dharmāya;
thus, in this sequence, for the sake of that merciless relative, he [is deprived] of his wealth and his two hands.
He was deceived even by his own two eyes;
consequently, Gautama abandoned him,
yet he did not die.

Seeing him, Vibhīṣaṇa, by means of the application of medicinal herbs brought from Mount Gandhamādana by Hanumān, freed him from that disease. Through his grace, Maṇikuṇḍala became prosperous once again as before.
In this circumstance, Maṇikuṇḍala remembered his first friend, Gautama.

After long deliberation, Maṇikuṇḍala beheld Gautama, who was seized by misfortune; bringing him into his home, he gave him a share of his own good fortune— for there is no need here to analyze the sentiment of compassion as it is the subject at hand.
Nobility—nobility is indeed another great agitation;

For since the sages know the Self and perceive the fundamental reality of the world,
they likewise forget their own separate existence.
In the description of the fruits [of their actions], they embrace the notion of self along with all sentient beings and experience the suffering experienced by others as if it were their own.
An unprecedented illustration of this, characterized by the contact of compassion and empathy, is seen in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
Therein, the empathy and compassion of Umā, the consort of Śiva, are reflected toward a child being attacked by a crocodile.
Even the royal sage Bharata showed compassion toward his younger brothers;
we see this account in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Through the presence of an assault, the experience of forgiveness arises—that forgiveness which is exercised toward a person who has committed an offense.

In the Purāṇas, numerous accounts are found concerning the demonstration of compassion and forgiveness toward wrongdoers by the sages (*ṛṣis*). In the narratives of the Purāṇas, we observe that a certain sage, out of compassion, rescinds a pronounced curse. In a particular narrative in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, we see that the sage Gautama mitigated the punishment resulting from a curse he had uttered.

Thus we observe that there exists a close proximity between the tenets of the Buddhist philosophy and those of the Vedic and Paurāṇika systems of thought. This proximity indicates a mutual affinity between the two philosophies. Given this historical relationship between the two systems, Buddhadeva was accepted by the Hindus as one of the incarnations among the ten avatāras.
